#7975. ‘The Garden Brought Me Back to Life’: A Revitalized Yard for a Sag Harbor Couple

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

When Bette Lou Fletcher and her husband Bruce moved to Sag Harbor, New York, during their retirement, Bette Lou was determined to build the garden she’d always dreamed of. She connected with local landscape designer Daria Szalinska, who had just established her own design practice, Landelier Landscape Atelier.

Bette Lou told Szalinska she longed for a garden room, an abundance of flowers that would feed and attract wildlife, and a deer-free zone to grow vegetables and cut flowers. One thing she didn’t need? A lawn. “I was beyond excited when Bette Lou told me she did not want a lawn,” says Szalinska. “I had been following Meadow Lab for some time, waiting for their wildflower sod to become available and for the right project where I could use it.” Bette Lou was game to try it out. In Szalinska’s redesign of the Fletcher’s yard, turf grass is used only for pathways and parking, with meadow sod replacing much of the former front lawn.

Bette Lou was also keen to keep the brick walkway, picket fence, and trellis that Bruce had built, a request that at first felt like a design challenge to Szalinska. As is so often the case, the constraints brought about especially lovely solutions. After debating the idea of weaving brick into a larger patio, Daria decided to use organic bluestone pavers, pushed right up against the existing brick, creating a moment of contrast. And surrounded by meadow and perennial plantings, the fence “took on a much softer, almost nostalgic character,” says Szalinska. To create the “rooms” that Bette Lou desired, Szalinska leaned on rigid geometry for the patio and paths; she also designed a fire pit surrounded by a ring of crepe myrtles and a fenced area in back to grow fruits, vegetables, and Bette Lou’s beloved dahlias.

One of the biggest changes Szalinska made is not visible in the photos because it was an act of concealment. She shifted the driveway closer to the edge of the property line, carving out more space for the garden. The landscape contractor Coastal Arborcare raised the grade of the garden, which helped hide the driveway. The final touch was to plant a hedge of native northern bayberry, which screens the driveway from the garden in a naturalistic way. “Bruce got a practical working area and Bette Lou a beautiful garden—making both of them happy,” says Szalinska.

Already, in its first year, the garden is lush, filled with blossoms and wildlife. Bette Lou finally has the garden she’d always imagined, but more significantly, she says, “The garden brought me back to life.” Not only is she surrounded by beauty, she’s been inspired to pick up her camera after years away from photography. “I can’t express the joy that it’s brought me,” she says.

Let’s take a tour of this Sag Harbor garden. (And be sure to scroll to the end for the “before” shot.)

Photography by Laura Castrillón, courtesy of Landelier Landscape Atelier.

Smooth boards and prepare furniture for finishing with this random orbital sander. Variable-speed control lets you adjust the sanding action for the material, and a removable dust bag collects debris as you work; a battery and charger are sold separately.

Remove These 7 Flower Thugs Before They Self-Seed Everywhere – Or You’ll Be Digging Them Up Next Year

Some well-intentioned fall gardening chores can damage plants, weaken bulbs, harm wildlife, and rob you of next year's blooms. Here's how to avoid them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Have you ever cleaned your house so thoroughly that you tossed out important papers or other things you need? Well, the same can be true in the garden. A tidy garden isn't necessarily a healthier garden, and some common fall cleanup habits can actually compromise next year's flowers.

Yes, fall cleanup is as important as spring cleanup, but there is more room for error. At this point, plants have buds or seeds that will turn into flowers in springtime. The foliage is still storing energy to keep the plants alive through winter. Prune wrong – or make any of a dozen wrong garden moves – and you’ve set up problems for yourself and your plants.

So which autumn cleanup tasks are actually bad for your garden? I'm here to help you avoid the fall missteps that will keep you from getting a spectacular display come spring. Here are the key fall garden mistakes to watch out for – and what you should do instead.

Most spring-blooming shrubs bud on old wood. These include some of your favorite perennials, such as azaleas, lilacs, forsythia, and magnolias. If you go wild pruning in fall and chop these shrubs too, you'll cut off next spring's flower buds.

This doesn’t kill the plant, of course. The shrub will still grow healthy green leaves, but you will get very few or no blossoms when spring arrives. You’ll have to wait another 12 months to see most of those flowers.

Instead, prune spring-flowering shrubs that bloom on old wood immediately after the flowers fade. This allows them plenty of time to develop buds that will fill your garden in spring. For clean cuts on woody stems, use a sharp pair of bypass pruners, such as the Felco 8 pruning shears, which can cut branches up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick.

Summer-flowering bulbs, corms, and rhizomes use their green foliage to make food and store energy for their next flowering cycle. If you cut back the leaves of summer-flowering plants such as lilies, gladiolus, cannas, and crocosmia too early in fall, you risk depriving them of the energy they need. As a result, they may produce fewer flowers next year, or even fail to bloom altogether.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Fortunately, this mistake isn't usually fatal, but it can weaken plants and affect their flowering performance. Instead, leave the foliage in place for as long as it's green and healthy, then cut it back once it naturally yellows and dies. However, frost-tender plants such as gladiolus and cannas may need to be lifted after frost damages their foliage, rather than waiting for it to die back naturally.

Tender plants such as dahlias are a little different – wait until the first frost blackens their foliage before cutting back the stems and lifting the tubers for winter storage, where necessary. Don't leave the tubers in freezing or waterlogged soil for too long, though, as they can rot.

Once lifted, store bulbs, corms, and tubers in a cool, frost-free location. Ventilated storage crates, such as these stackable, collapsible crates from CleverMade, are ideal for keeping different varieties organized while allowing air to circulate. Gladiolus corms can be stored dry after curing, while dahlias and cannas benefit from being packed in a suitable material, such as vermiculite (available on Amazon), to prevent them from drying out.

A thorough fall cleanup might leave your garden looking neat and tidy, but it can also strip away valuable food and shelter for wildlife. Many perennials produce seed heads that feed birds through the colder months, while their hollow stems and dead foliage provide overwintering habitat for beneficial insects. Cutting everything back in fall can leave these creatures with fewer places to shelter when they need them most.

Instead, leave plants such as coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, asters, and ornamental grasses standing through winter. Their seed heads provide food for finches and other backyard birds. If your garden is short on birdseed-bearing plants, you can supplement this natural food supply with a nyjer seed feeder, like this easy-clean feeder on Amazon, which is particularly attractive to goldfinches.

Standing stems can also offer nesting habitat for native bees in the following growing season. Wait until spring to tackle the cleanup, and even then, consider leaving some hollow or pithy stems standing at a height of 8–24 inches (20–60 cm). Cutting the stems creates openings that certain native bees can use for nesting, often in the following year. It's also worth leaving some fallen leaves in garden beds, as these provide overwintering shelter for butterflies, moths, and other beneficial insects. However, you should still remove diseased foliage to prevent problems from spreading next year.

Soil structure is important. If, in a flurry of fall cleaning, you dig or cultivate your garden beds too aggressively, you are actually destroying that natural soil structure. More specifically, that type of aggressive digging disrupts the habitats of beneficial earthworms and microbes. It also damages the delicate fungal networks that nurture the plant roots.

But that’s not all. When you do a lot of heavy tilling, you also run the risk of bringing up weed seeds into the upper soil, where they have a wonderful time filling your empty garden beds. Over time, repeated tilling can also break down the soil's natural structure, making it more prone to compaction, especially if you work the soil when it's wet.

Instead, choose a gentler alternative. You might layer on compost or straw right on top of the soil, allowing worms to do the work for you as they pull down food. Alternatively, install deep-rooted cover crops (like Tin Shed Seed Company's No Till Cover Crop Mix) or just loosen soil with a garden fork. Push it straight down, then just wiggle it a little.

The very word “smothering” should give you pause. If you pile on so much mulch that it smothers the plant crowns, it blocks sunlight, traps excess moisture, and keeps oxygen out of the roots. These conditions can lead to stem rot, fungal diseases, and plant death.

Instead, apply several inches of mulch (no more than 2 inches) to regulate soil temperature. Keep the mulch about 3 inches (7.5 cm) away from plant crowns. For that matter, keep it away from trunks too. A small hand rake, like this Ames one from Home Depot, makes it easy to redistribute mulch that's piled up too close to stems without disturbing the plants.

You may have heard that healthy leaf litter can decompose over time, providing nutrients for the soil. It can also shelter wildlife.

But leaving diseased foliage provides a reservoir for problems – like bacteria, pests, and fungal spores. If that happens near vulnerable plants, rain or wind can splash these pathogens onto healthy new growth. That means that the garden can be reinfected with powdery mildew and black spot.

Instead, clear fallen foliage from vulnerable plants (like roses) in fall, but dispose of it properly. Never put it in the compost; instead, bag it and put it in the garbage – these Kraft Lawn and Leaf Bags will decompose with garden waste. Then, lay down clean mulch.

With so many fall garden jobs competing for your attention, it's easy to overlook tender flowering plants that need protection before winter arrives. Dahlias, fuchsias, and tuberous begonias are all vulnerable to freezing temperatures, and forgetting about them until the first cold snap can put next year's flowers at risk.

If frost has already struck, don't panic. A little damage doesn't necessarily mean the whole plant is lost. However, the next step depends on what you're growing. Dahlias can be left until the first frost blackens their foliage, then cut back and lifted for winter storage in colder climates.

With other tender perennials, avoid rushing to prune away frost-damaged growth, as leaving it in place temporarily can offer some protection to the stems and crown. Instead, move containers somewhere sheltered or use frost cloth to protect plants from further cold. If you're using plastic covers, keep them from touching the foliage and remove them once temperatures rise to prevent overheating.

This versatile plant cover is ideally used for protecting crops from frost and pests, but can also be used for other plants.

These zip-up plant jackets protect shrubs and small trees from frost and feature drawstrings for a secure fit.

These heavy-duty planter dollies make it easy to move large pots indoors or to sheltered outdoor areas.

The best rule for fall cleanup is to keep it selective. Stripping garden beds bare is thorough – but very short sighted. So hold onto the reins before letting the autumn garden tidying run away with you.

As a final reminder, be sure to leave some seed heads and stems standing. They can make the landscape more interesting in winter, while providing food for birds and shelter for beneficial insects. It makes your garden more eco-friendly and welcoming.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7972. A Scottish Fisherman’s Cottage Gets an Update, with Make-Do-and-Mend Spirit

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

On the rugged coast of Scotland’s Isle of Mull, a small stone cottage sits just feet from the chilly water. The old bothy was a fisherman’s refuge and a sheep pen before it was purchased by Peter Harford-Cross’s family, who used it as a camping-style accommodation for years. Recently, though, the architect and his partner Rachel turned the semi-derelict structure into a cozy seaside getaway—while maintaining its original charm.

The duo, also known as Harford-Cross Architects, were careful to preserve the existing windows and pitched roof that Peter’s uncle installed in the 1980s—then infused the interior with modest contemporary comforts. “Our approach was fairly minimal,” says Rachel. “We needed surfaces that were hard-wearing and robust because of the location. There’s an element of the stone that we’ve kept and painted, but we’ve lined out the walls in durable plywood where it was necessary to provide improved thermal quality. Hopefully it has longevity and visual warmth, too.”

When it came to furniture and fittings, the couple reused and recycled as much as possible, reflecting the make-do-and-mend spirit of the island and of Peter’s grandmother, who once lived there. Nearly everything was bought on eBay or from local vintage shops. “Even though it was all secondhand and relatively inexpensive, we sourced the pieces quite carefully,” Rachel says. “It was about having a little bit of respect for the property. We chose fine pieces with their own inherent character.”

Photography by Alexander Baxter, courtesy of Harford-Cross Architects.

#7971. The Best Soundproof Curtains of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

By Stacey L. Nash, Additional research provided by Deirdre Mundorf, Jasmine Harding

Published Oct 25, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

After researching dozens of popular noise-canceling curtains and testing 10, we found seven sets we recommend. Our favorite is the Pony Dance Blackout Insulated Soundproof Curtains, which offer excellent sound reduction, are easy to clean, and aren’t overly heavy or hard to hang. Plus, they come in over 20 colorways and almost twice that many sizes. Read on to see what we like about each of the rest of the best soundproof curtains that made our list.

Bottom line: Soundproof curtains can significantly reduce noise and light, with options ranging from budget-friendly to high-end designs, catering to various needs and styles.

We selected the sound-absorbing curtains below for their appearance, performance, ease of hanging and cleaning, and value. Any one of these sets of noise-blocking curtains can aid in preventing ambient noise and light from infiltrating indoor spaces.

Our Ratings: Appearance 4.5/5; Effectiveness 4.5/5; Ease of Cleaning 5/5; Value 4.8/5

If you’re looking for sleek and effective soundproof curtains, this set from Pony Dance may fill the bill. In testing, these sound-deadening curtains​ reduced noise levels by 10 decibels, making them one of the top performers despite their lightweight construction. Made from 100 percent polyester, the panels feel luxurious and come in over 20 colors and almost 40 sizes to fit virtually every style and window.

While this pick is available in everything from black, brown, and navy to mint green, blush pink, and pure white, the manufacturer recommends darker shades if you want significant light blocking in addition to sound reduction. However, even the lighter shades are estimated to filter 85 to 95 percent of light, and the gray curtains we tested proved that to be true.

Installation is versatile, as these curtains are designed to accommodate both rod pocket and tab installation. Also, the fabric held up well to washing, but we did have to steam it afterward to fully remove the wrinkles.

What our tester says: “Even though hanging these using the rod pocket was a bit trickier than simply sliding the rod through the tabs, we really liked the sleek final look. Plus, once we had them in place, the soundproofing and light-blocking they offered made them a definite favorite.”—Stacey L. Nash

Get the Pony Dance soundproof curtains at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Appearance 4/5; Effectiveness 4/5; Ease of Cleaning 5/5; Value 4.5/5

These budget-friendly soundproof blackout curtains from BGment are a solid choice for effective noise reduction at a reasonable cost. Made from polyester, they are insulated to absorb sound while balancing and maintaining room temperature to reduce thermal energy usage.

These curtains are surprisingly lightweight given their light-blocking, temperature-control, and soundproofing capabilities. Not only did they absorb about 5 decibels of noise in our sound test, they also kept our room noticeably cooler during the day and warmer at night. Plus, the triple-weave polyester fabric had a nice drape and blocked out a significant amount of sunlight.

BGment’s curtains for sound reduction​ come in almost 40 colors and about 20 sizes, ranging from 45 to 120 inches long and 38 to 70 inches wide. The two-panel set has metal grommets for easy hanging, and the fabric is machine washable in cold water on a gentle cycle and can be tumble dried on low heat.

What our tester says: ”We love being able to wash and dry these curtains. Even though they always come out with a few wrinkles, they’re easy to smooth with a quick steam, which is way better than hauling them to the dry cleaner.”—Stacey L. Nash, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the BGment soundproof curtains at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Appearance 4/5; Effectiveness 5/5; Ease of Cleaning 5/5; Value 4.5/5

These high-performing soundproof blackout curtains from RYB Home are a worthwhile upgrade for those wanting heavier-duty curtains. Designed with a detachable felt liner between two layers of fabric, they offer excellent sound-reducing capabilities, cutting noise by 10 decibels during testing. Because both exterior layers are the same color (as opposed to showing color on the front and white on the back), this set also provides a more high-end, polished look.

Beyond aesthetics and soundproofing, the three-layer design also blocks all sunlight and ultraviolet (UV) rays, which helped keep our room warm at night while preventing rising temperatures during the day. Available in a variety of colors and sizes (including customizable dimensions if ordered directly from the brand), these acoustic curtains offer easy maintenance. Though the inner liner isn’t machine washable, it is removable via a hook-and-loop system, which allows you to clean the rest of the curtains on a gentle cycle and dry them on low. Like the other washable curtains we tested, they will need a light steaming to get rid of their wrinkles.

Get the RYB Home soundproof curtains (various sizes and colors) at Amazon or RYB Home.

Our Ratings: Appearance 4.5/5; Effectiveness 4.8/5; Ease of Cleaning 2/5; Value 4.5/5

The multilayered design of these Moondream 3-in-1 curtains makes them a top pick for blocking sound and light while providing thermal insulation. Each panel combines a blackout fabric, an insulated lining, and a thick cotton fabric backing to create a heavy soundproof curtain. In our tests, they reduced noise by up to 6 decibels, just shy of the manufacturer’s claim of 7 decibels. They also kept the temperature of our room more consistently and blocked all incoming light.

While this pick only comes in four sizes, each curtain has a surged bottom edge that allows you to customize its length using the included hem tape. Even though it took us a few tries to get everything straight, being able to adjust the hem is a definite bonus, especially if your windows aren’t a standard size. Also, installation is easy thanks to reinforced, rustproof grommets, but care isn’t quite as simple since these curtains are dry clean only. They’re also a bit spendy, even if you only need a single curtain.

Get the Moondream soundproof curtains (various sizes and colors) at Amazon or Moondream.

Our Ratings: Appearance 5/5; Effectiveness 4/5; Ease of Cleaning 5/5; Value 3.8/5

These thermal-insulated curtains from H.Versailtex not only absorb sound but also reduce energy costs by preventing warm or cool air from entering or escaping. During testing, they helped regulate room conditions, even when outdoor temps changed by 30 degrees Fahrenheit from night to day. They also reduced sound by up to 5 decibels in our sound test.

Made of a woven polyester blend that looks like textured linen, these sound-absorbing curtains block at least 85 percent of sunlight and UV rays. They’re available in over 20 colors and patterns and have attractive copper grommets, which increase their durability while making them easy to hang and adjust. They’re also machine washable, tumble-dry safe on low, and safe to be smoothed with a steamer or warm iron. The only downside is that they only come in six sizes, which could be an issue if your windows aren’t a standard size.

What our tester says: “Of all the machine-washable curtains we tested, these held up the best. Because they have a textured finish, light wrinkles barely showed. They basically came out looking new.”—Stacey L. Nash, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the H.Versailtex soundproof curtains (various sizes and colors) at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Appearance 5/5; Effectiveness 4/5; Ease of Cleaning 3/5; Value 4.5/5

These Deconovo blackout curtains prove there’s no need to sacrifice style just to enjoy the benefits of sound-minimizing curtains. Made of soft, durable polyester, these attractive curtains have a textured weave that mimics fine linen, giving them a luxe look. They’re available in a range of decorator-loved hues and basic neutrals and come in 11 sizes to fit most standard windows.

We tested a light green set of these faux-linen soundproof curtains, and they reduced sound by 5 decibels and blocked out almost all incoming light. They also resisted wrinkles better than most others, but we did have to hand-wash and air-dry them. If necessary, you can smooth any wrinkles that appear using a cool iron, but ours didn’t even come wrinkled from shipping and showed minimal wrinkling after washing.

Get the Deconovo soundproof curtains (various sizes and colors) at Wayfair.

Our Ratings: Appearance 2/5; Effectiveness 5/5; Ease of Cleaning 2/5; Value 4.3/5

Since a home studio has different needs than other rooms, those outfitting this space may want a professional product rather than residential curtains. Designed to dampen sound, minimize unwanted noise, and block light on movie sets, stages, and recording studios, the Filmcraft studio soundproof blanket is a relatively affordable pick that’s as versatile as it is effective. Measuring 80 inches long by 72 inches wide with grommets on all sides for easier hanging, this sound-minimizing curtain also doubles as a protective blanket to cover set pieces and instruments in transit.

We tested this blanket in a bedroom by using clamps to attach it to a curtain rod. It reduced noise by 10 decibels, matching the top score achieved by just two other picks. Though it isn’t as attractive as either of those options, it would work well in a studio or as a packing blanket. For those playing shows or working on sets. Because it’s designed for professional use, it comes only in black, in a single size, and its price rivals some of the soundproof curtains we tested.

Get the Filmcraft soundproof blanket at Amazon or B&H.

We tested the following options, and while they offered some soundproofing, they didn’t perform as well as our top picks.

To test soundproof curtains for possible inclusion on our list, we hung each set in a room with a single window for 3 to 7 days. We used a decibel meter to measure the level of ambient room noise, then had someone play a trumpet outside the window and measured the decibels again.  If the curtains had thermal properties, we evaluated the temperature difference in the morning, afternoon, and evening while the curtains were hanging versus when they were not. If they had blackout features, we observed how much light filtered in throughout the course of the day and whether we could see in the window from outside. When possible, we also washed and dried the curtains according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

We then scored the curtains according to an established rubric that considered appearance, soundproof quality, light blocking, and thermal abilities. We factored in the quality of the fabric and the durability of construction, eliminating products that didn’t meet our standards and assigning awards to ones that did.

Good noise-reducing curtains help absorb sound waves and reduce noise pollution, so they’re ideal for a bedroom, living room, home office, or home theater. Many can even double as blackout curtains or thermal curtains to help reduce natural light pollution and heating or cooling costs.

Shopping for soundproof curtains starts with choosing one of three types: insulation curtains, audio insulation sheets, and industrial blankets.

Insulation curtains look similar to regular window curtains found in most homes and can come in a range of designs as well, from neutral colors to bold patterns. The main difference is that insulation curtains are made with heavier materials that block some noise. Insulation curtains also often function as blackout curtains since the thicker material that insulates the room from sound also works to block sunlight.

Thermal insulation curtains also help lower energy bills. The same thick material that works to absorb sounds can contain thermal energy, adding a layer of insulation that prevents air from entering or escaping through windows.

While audio insulation sheets aren’t technically curtains, they can be hung to function like curtains. Audio insulation sheets are typically designed with grommets to allow them to hang from a curtain rod, making them easier to install than acoustic panels.

Audio insulation sheets can block more sound than insulation curtains and industrial blankets because they are constructed with multiple layers of heavy fabric, which makes them a nearly soundproof fabric. They also function as blackout curtains due to these multiple layers. However, the amount of fabric required to craft audio insulation sheets makes them a more expensive option.

Industrial blankets are primarily intended to protect furniture and other fragile items during the moving process. Because of this, they are made with thick and padded material, which allows them to serve as sound-eliminating curtains. Though you probably don’t want to use them to soundproof an office or other professional space long term, they can serve as excellent temporary soundproof divider curtains.

Some industrial blankets are designed with grommets, which makes them easier to hang. Otherwise, you’ll have to find a way to drape them over windows or rig up a hanging mechanism so that they can help absorb outside sounds. Industrial blankets are one of the most budget-friendly options for soundproofing walls or creating a soundproof doorway curtain to reduce outdoor sounds in your indoor space.

Before purchasing soundproof curtains, check to confirm that the product is available in the appropriate size. Measure the length and width of the window, and look for a curtain that is wide and long enough to sufficiently cover it. Ideally, soundproof curtains should cover a portion of the wall, in addition to the window, especially in small spaces like apartments, to be most effective.

If possible, choose a curtain that is up to three times as wide as the window and 10 or more inches longer. Floor-to-ceiling soundproof curtains can be even more effective at noise reduction. Heavier soundproofing curtains are more effective at absorbing sounds and keeping your space quiet than lighter ones. This is especially true for lower-frequency sounds. If deciding between two soundproof curtains, the heavier option may be the better choice.

The materials used to make soundproof curtains will affect not only the way they look but also how well they block and absorb sounds. More fibrous options, such as velvet curtains, can be more effective at noise reduction. Suede and polyester are also quality options to consider.

Many soundproof curtains on the market are crafted with triple-weave fabric, making them denser and more effective. Thermal soundproof curtains also offer additional insulation as well. Thermal insulation can both help to reduce energy costs and also make the curtains more effective at absorbing sounds. A general rule of thumb to keep in mind when looking for soundproof curtains is that more material usually equals better soundproofing capabilities.

Before hanging a new set of soundproof curtains, consider the curtain rods currently installed to see if they’ll work. Since soundproof curtains are heavier than traditional curtains, make sure the curtain rod can support the weight of heavier curtains, or consider installing new curtain rods.

Depending on their dimensions, soundproof curtains could weigh 8 pounds or more, compared to about 2 pounds for traditional light-filtering curtains. In addition to rod strength, shoppers may also wish to consider buying a wraparound curtain rod. This style of curtain rod is more effective at blocking sounds since it attaches to the wall at a curve and allows the curtain to provide a more complete sound barrier.

The color of the sound-blocking curtains won’t affect their noise reduction, but it will certainly visually affect a living space. Based on personal preferences and needs, consider acoustic curtains that match the aesthetic of the room—such as modern, vintage, or farmhouse, for example—and coordinate with the decor as well.

Finally, consider how easy it will be to install and maintain the soundproof curtains. One of the easiest ways to help soundproof a space is with insulation curtains that have grommets along the top for simple installation from a curtain rod.

Depending on their design, audio insulation sheets and industrial blankets may be more challenging to install. If possible, try to preview the manufacturer’s installation directions before making a purchase. Also, take note of the manufacturer’s care and cleaning instructions for each potential purchase. Machine-washable options are easier to maintain.

Hopefully, you now know more about soundproof curtains and how to choose the best product to reduce noise in your home. If you still have questions like where to buy curtains or how to take care of them, check out the following section for more information.

To increase the noise reduction of your existing curtains, add more layers of fabric. For best results, choose heavy and tightly woven fabrics, as they are more effective at reducing the amount of noise that enters your space. Ideally, the curtains should cover the full length of the wall—both above and below the window—since this will allow them to create a seal to block more sound.

Yes, traditional drapes will block some sound. However, the amount of sound absorption will vary significantly based on their thickness and the quality of the seal they create over a window. For example, heavy velvet curtains soundproof​ better than lightweight cotton ones.

You can soundproof a room in several ways without spending too much money. One idea is to use an industrial blanket, or even just thick regular blankets, to help soundproof windows and the surrounding wall space. The thick material can help to block a lot of noise from entering your space.In addition to purchasing soundproof curtains for door and window openings, there are many other DIY soundproofing tricks you can use to minimize noise. For example, you can place weatherstripping tape around your windows and door frames as well as seal gaps between doors and their thresholds with a rubber doorstop to further soundproof a room.

Yes, as evidenced by our tests, even low-quality soundproofing curtains work. All the soundproofing curtains we recommend reduced noise levels by 5 to 10 decibels, and those that didn’t make our list still brought them down by 2 to 3 decibels.

For soundproof curtains, look for dense, heavyweight fabrics like velvet or polyester. Multi-layered acoustic fabrics with thermal linings also make excellent soundproof curtains.

Yes, soundproof curtains can reduce your energy bill by providing thermal insulation and improving temperature control in your space.

Yes, if external noise is disrupting people’s sleep, soundproof curtains can help them sleep better by creating quieter spaces that allow for deeper, uninterrupted sleep.

#7970. Fall Fertilizing: How to Prepare Your Lawn, Shrubs, Trees, and Perennials for a Restorative Winter Sleep

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

In addition to fall being a great time to get new plants in the ground, it can also be an ideal season to fertilize your lawn, trees, shrubs, and perennials. But you have to do it correctly: During these cooler months, plants are slipping into dormancy and not actively growing. Depending on how severe or mild your winter is, they can be anywhere between completely dormant to growing very, very slowly. If you fertilize right, you’ll be giving them the best send-off to their winter sleep.

Before you start, you may want to get in touch with your local cooperative extension. They can help you get a soil test (you can’t help your plants if you don’t know what they need). And they can tell you the first frost date for your area (for practical purposes, fertilizing should be done before the first frost). They know your climate best and can give you advice specific to your location.

Note: We don’t recommend using synthetic fertilizers because of the large environmental impacts associated with them, including water contamination from run off and decimation of soil microbes. Restoring soil health naturally should always be the first option.

Here’s what you need to know about fertilizing (naturally) in the fall.

The best and easiest way to fertilize is to do one last mow with a mulching mower and leave the clippings on the lawn. Mulching the clippings back into the lawn can provide up to 50% of the needed nutrients for the grass. To make up the rest of what your lawn needs, there are two low-cost and environmentally sustainable ways to fertilize. First, you can aerate the lawn and top dress with compost. Second, if you have fallen leaves, mulch them into the lawn as well. Just remember to rake them around so they aren’t too thick. It is a smart idea to keep the nutrients created on your property, on your property. (See Ask the Expert: Doug Tallamy Explains Why (and How to) Leave the Leaves.)

A more expensive, less eco-conscious option is to use organic lawn fertilizer. While organic fertilizers are certainly better than chemical fertilizers, there are still manufacturing and transportation costs to the environment. If you go this route, follow the directions exactly. More is not better.

A closed loop is the best type of fertilizer. Keep the leaves from the trees under them. They have everything the trees need—for free. They help on so many levels. They act as mulch and keep the moisture in the soil, which in turn helps the microbes that break down the leaves, making their nutrients available to the trees. The leaves also become winter homes for good bugs. Just be sure to keep the root flare exposed; piling the leaves up the trunk can cause can cause the bark to rot. No trees on your property? Organic compost is your next best choice.

For shrubs that were healthy over the growing season, a leaf well around the base will be enough. If they didn’t do well over the summer, they may need a bit of help. Aerate the soil and add some compost and water well.

If you want to add store-bought organic fertilizer to your tree or shrub, you may want to consider consulting with an arborist first. It’s easy to over-fertilize and cause damage. Leave it to the professionals.

Yes, leaves again. Really. And compost. Both the leaves and the compost break down slowly. Nobody is in a rush here, it’s winter and nothing is growing. The idea is that the nutrients will be ready and in a form the plant can use once it wakes up in the spring. If you’re concerned about burying your plants too deep in leaves, lightly cover what remains of your almost dormant plants, but pack the leaves thickly around them.

There are no other real options. If you use synthetic fertilizer while they are going into dormancy, they could come out of dormancy early during an extended warm spell—and then when a cold snap follows, the new growth may be killed. This can weaken the plant, causing it to fail to thrive in the spring or even die.

Our gardens are part of a larger ecosystem, so it’s important to prioritize soil health and natural methods over synthetic fertilizers. Aeration of compacted soil and addition of organic matter will have a better and a longer-lasting effect on plant health.

N.B.: This post was first published November 2023.

Remove These 7 Flower Thugs Before They Self-Seed Everywhere – Or You’ll Be Digging Them Up Next Year

These 7 Flower Seeds to Sow in Fall Are the Best Investment You'll Make for Next Year's Garden

What Coneflowers Need in October for Better Blooms Next Year – Plus One Bonus for the Birds

November can feel like the end of things, but if you put these cottage garden and prairie favorites in the ground this month, you can enjoy beautiful early flowering displays

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November often feels like the end of the growing season in many backyards. Annual and perennial borders have likely died back for the year, and deciduous trees and shrubs stand have lost their leaves. Yet while the air is getting fresher, you can still work a little magic in your cooling soil. Because as it turns out, this month is a prime time for sowing some classic hardy flower seeds.

Many pretty cottage garden favorites, native prairie wildflowers, and pollinator staples actually need a winter chill to thrive. In nature, wild flower seeds drop from seed heads in late fall, settle into the cool earth, and take part in a natural winter cycle known as cold stratification. Exposure to freezing and thawing breaks down the tough seed jackets of key annual and perennial flower types, prompting the embryo to awaken as soon as spring conditions become favorable.

Sowing these flower seeds in November gives them a big head start. Seeds planted now establish strong roots. This means healthier conditions in spring, with sturdier stems, superior drought resistance, and prolific displays that can bloom a month ahead of spring-sown counterparts. By taking advantage of these planting conditions now, you lay the groundwork for an effortless explosion of color next season.

Keep in mind your USDA hardiness zone, your local climate, and weather conditions before deciding on specific plants and a sowing strategy. Successfully sowing flowers in November comes down to matching your plant variety with the right late-season sowing technique. There are a few primary approaches you can try with these flowers, depending on your region and weather. In mild winter climates (zones 7-10), you can try fall sowing (directly outdoors) so seeds germinate before winter, overwintering as frost-hardy rosettes that bloom in April.

In colder northern climates (zones 3-6), there is also dormant sowing. This is where seeds are sown directly into garden beds once the ground is cold enough to prevent immediate germination. Soil temperatures consistently below 45°F (7°C) allow seeds to sit dormant until early spring. For native perennial flowers or regions with erratic thaws, the best approach is winter sowing. This means sowing in outdoor containers and placing in a protected area, like an unheated cold frame, to shield seeds from rodents and heavy downpours while still providing natural chilling.

Before sowing, ground preparation is vital. Check soil temperatures before you start sowing with a good soil probe. Budget-friendly Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter, available from Amazon gives a reliable read on current moisture and temperature levels. Then clear away thick, suffocating leaves, remove weeds, and lightly rake the top inch (2.5cm) of soil into a fine, crumbly tilth. Pay attention to seed packet instructions regarding sowing depth, as this can have a big effect on germination. Some larger seeds may require burying an inch deep, while fine wildflower seeds need light to germinate and need to be surface-sown with just a whisper of sand or light compost.

Water the seedbed gently with a fine mist to settle the soil without dislodging the seeds, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Mark each row clearly with durable weatherproof tags, and cover vulnerable beds with breathable floating row covers, mesh, or clean straw to deter birds. Whether sowing directly in the soil or indoors, these gorgeous flowering picks are all good to go this month…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Sweet peas (Lathyrus odoratus) are the quintessential cottage border bloomers. They are celebrated for their intoxicating scents and ruffled hues, which can cascade across trellises from late spring through early summer. These vintage darlings thrive in cool weather. Sowing sweet peas in November allows the seeds to develop deep roots while temperatures are low. This leads to more prolific flowering displays, with longer, sturdier stems. If you fancy a floriferous blend of lavender, violet and maroon blooms, buy Sweet Pea Burgundy Mix Sweet Peas from Eden Brothers.

In milder climates (zones 7-10), you can direct-sow sweet peas along sunny, well-draining trellises. In colder zones (3–6), sow seeds indoors in deep root-trainer tubes or biodegradable pots, and keep in an unheated greenhouse, sheltered porch, or cold frame. Sweet pea seeds have hard shells, so nick these with a nail file (or soak in room-temperature water for 12 hours prior to planting) to speed up moisture absorption. Plant seeds an inch (2.5cm) deep in rich, organic-rich soil, and pinch the central tips once seedlings develop 3 sets of true leaves for bushier plants.

With their luminous, silky petals, California poppies (Eschscholzia californica) bring effortless cheer to borders, gravel gardens, and sunny slopes. These tough-as-nails wildflowers thrive in sandy or rocky soils, making them ideal for challenging areas where other ornamentals struggle. However, because they have brittle taproots that resent disturbance, they should be direct-sown where they are intended to bloom. Buy Marde Ross & Co California Dreaming California Poppy Seed Mix from Amazon for a near-neon flush of tangerine, melon and magenta blooms.

You can sow seeds now in regions with milder winters (zones 7-10). In these areas, fall rains will trigger late-fall germination, establishing fern-like foliage that bursts into bloom by April. To sow California poppies, scatter them over the soil in an area that drains well and has full sun. Lightly rake the seeds into the soil so they are barely covered, as poppy seeds require light to germinate. If you have colder or very wet winters, it’s best to wait until spring to sow these seeds.

Offering the vertical grandeur of delphiniums without the fussy growing requirements, annual larkspur (Consolida ajacis) produces epic flowering spires in shades of royal purple, lavender, rose, and white. This cottage garden classic is a cool-season annual that is ideal for November sowing. In fact, waiting until spring often results in poor, erratic germination, as seeds need a period of stratification to break dormancy. For a shock of saturated purple-blue spires, buy QIS Dark Blue Larkspur Seeds from Eden Brothers.

Direct-sow in a rich, sunny, well-drained bed. Cover very lightly with an eighth of an inch of fine compost or sand. Winter rain and freezing nights should satisfy the seed's chilling requirements, triggering early emergence in spring. Fall-sown larkspur often blooms up to a month earlier than spring-sown seeds, beating the summer heatwaves that can cause these cool-season annuals to fade. If your winters are very cold, try winter sowing in containers.

Also known as cornflowers, bachelor’s buttons (Centaurea cyanus) are cherished vintage annuals. Their blue ruffled blooms erupt in late spring and summer to create a dazzling contrast with cottage perennials and ornamental grasses (though you can get varieties in shades of pink, purple and white). Also cold tolerant, they are naturally adapted to late-season sowing. Sowing in November helps it to grow strong roots that can withstand hotter summer days far longer than spring-started plants.

Sow in a bright, sunny border with average to poor, well-draining garden soil. Sow at roughly a quarter-inch (0.6cm) deep, firming the soil gently. For the best results, ensure the area with seeds doesn’t erode or get waterlogged over winter. In mild winter regions, seeds will sprout within a few weeks; in northern climates, they will sleep until early March, flowering from late spring all the way to July. Buy SVI Store’s Bachelor Button Mix Seeds from Amazon for a lively mixture of floral heirloom tones.

Black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia hirta) are prairie icons that light up borders from early summer well into fall. With their sunny yellow petals and chocolate-brown cones, these pollinator-friendly perennials and biennials are often bought as transplants. Hardy in zones 3-9, they are super tough. However, their seeds possess dormancy inhibitors that can lead to patchy germination in spring soil. November sowing solves this problem naturally. By scattering now, you allow the rhythm of winter rains, snow cover, and sub-freezing nights to break dormancy smoothly.

Clear away heavy mulch and scatter seeds thinly over the surface. They require light to germinate, so press them into the soil without burying them. While fall-sown plants spend their first spring developing roots and crowns, many will reward you with late-summer blooms in the first year. Buy Harris Seeds’ Rudbeckia Goldilocks Seeds from Walmart for a ruffled twist on the dazzling classic. Just keep in mind that many varieties benefit from cold exposure, but not all, so know your type before you sow.

With their delicate, two-toned blooms and graceful spurs, columbines (Aquilegia spp.) bring woodland romance and grace to borders, cottage beds, and rockeries. Native across North America and Europe, Aquilegia species are hardy down to zone 3. Seeds require 4-6 weeks of cold, damp stratification, making November sowing the easiest, most reliable way to propagate them. Buy Blue Star Columbine Seeds from Eden Brothers for a vivid bounty of iconic violet-blue and white blooms.

Select a site that receives gentle morning sun and dappled afternoon shade with rich, well-draining soil. Some varieties require sunlight to trigger germination, so check the seed packet. Scatter seeds onto the soil surface and press lightly into the earth, but don’t cover with soil. If you live in an area with winter gales or heavy rains, you can winter-sow columbines into ventilated plastic jugs in a shaded outdoor spot. Seedlings will emerge in spring, providing pretty nectar for returning hummingbirds.

Purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) is a perennial staple in the sustainable, pollinator-friendly yard. Featuring daisy-like blooms and spiky cones, echinacea feeds native bees and butterflies in summer, while offering seed cones for goldfinches in fall. Seeds have evolved to weather harsh winters before germinating, making November a great time for sowing. Buy Purple Coneflower Heirloom Seeds by the Kviter Store from Amazon for a generous supply of purple drifts.

Broadcast seeds in a sunny spot with well-drained, average soil. Echinacea seeds need minimal light filtering through to sprout, so rake them into the earth no more than an eighth of an inch deep, firming the soil. Winter's freeze-thaw cycles settle the seeds, softening their husks so that strong roots push down early in spring. While coneflowers focus heavily on root establishment in the first year, November-sown echinacea tend to bloom reliably by the second season.

Your gardening season doesn’t have to be over in November. Taking a little time this month to start off some pretty cottage garden and pollinator favorites is such a rewarding investment in future backyard bloomers. By partnering with winter’s cold cycles rather than fighting them, you give these key annuals and perennials a real head start on early spring beauty. Using seeds is also a cost-effective way to get more flowers. If some don’t germinate or establish, you haven’t lost a lot of money. So grab a few seed packets, prep your beds, and get planting. It’s time to start looking forward to an effortless run of blooms well ahead of the neighbors.

#7967. The Best Screw Extractors to Remove Stripped Fasteners, Tested

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Few things can bring a building project or repair effort to a grinding halt like a stripped screw or bolt, which is why keeping a screw extractor at the ready is key. These handy tools consist of a drill bit that grinds a hole into the head of a screw and a threaded extractor that bites into this hole, gripping the screw so you can remove it with a drill or ratchet.

There are many types and brands of screw extractors on the market, but few have the mettle to do the job properly. We put five screw extractor kits to the test by using them to remove various sizes of bolts and screws. With its effective design and affordable price, the Alden Grabit Pro Bolt and Screw Extractor Kit proved to be the best of the bunch. Read on to learn more about our test results for the Alden and other screw extractors, and find out what factors to keep in mind when shopping for the best screw extractor for your workshop.

Bottom line: Choosing the right screw extractor depends on your needs, with the Alden Grabit Pro Kit standing out for its effectiveness and value.

The products below represent some of the top screw extractors on the market. This includes small sets designed for occasional use and large sets for pros and avid DIYers who regularly deal with damaged screws and bolts.

Our Ratings: Performance 4/5; Durability 5/5; Value 5/5

Not only is this kit from Alden one of the cheapest of the bunch, it also happens to be the easiest to use and most effective at removing stripped screws. The kit’s design eliminates the guesswork of trying to match drill bits with extractors sizes—each of the four bit sizes is conveniently double-sided with the drill bit on one side and the threaded extractor on the other.

During testing, each extractor gripped nicely to the insides of the stripped-out holds, allowing us to remove screws easily. In fact, the Alden removed screws that two other screw extractor sets we tested failed to remove. Of all the kits we tested, this one most consistently gripped and removed screws.

Since this screw extractor set only comes with four bit sizes, it is somewhat limited. Still, those bit sizes are the most common you’ll find. The kit includes a small carrying case that keeps these bits organized, so they’re easy to find when needed. We also like the fact that this kit is small. This makes it easier to throw in a tool box or tool belt pocket so it’s at your side when you encounter a dreaded stripped screw.

Get the Alden Grabit Pro screw extractor at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Performance 4.3/5; Durability 4/5; Value 4/5

This compact screw remover and extractor set includes five extractors and drill bit sizes. Each extractor and bit is conveniently paired in a storage box, so there’s no confusion as to which bit goes with which extractor.

While we liked the paired design of this set, we experienced mixed results during testing. The larger sizes worked well for removing bolts. The bits drilled nicely into the screw and bolts heads, and the spiral shape of the removers bit well into the drilled holes.

Unfortunately, we didn’t have very good results with the smaller drill bits and extractors. We couldn’t get the extractors to bite in the drilled head on stripped-out 3-inch decking screws despite several attempts using various sizes of drill bit and matching extractor. While we were ultimately able to back the screws out, we had to do so using very slow speeds so the extractor wouldn’t slip and strip out the pilot hole.

Although we would certainly recommend this set for removing bolts and larger screws, we’d consider other options for smaller stripped-out screws.

Get the Irwin 10-piece screw extractor at Amazon or Acme Tools.

Our Ratings: Performance 3.7/5; Durability 4/5; Value 4.5/5

We’ve typically found Bosch’s power tools and accessories to be of good quality while remaining somewhat more affordable than other power tool brands. This screw extractor kit from Bosch was, for the most part, no exception. It performed fairly well with bolts and smaller screws with a better-than-average success rate when compared with other sets.

Durability was also good but not great. All of the extractors feel as if they would last a long time. Our only concern was with the two smaller drill bit sizes, which feel as if they could potentially snap. While we didn’t experience any broken bits, this was a common complaint with online reviewers.

We like the handy carrying case, which is compact and holds each bit securely. We only wish it was easier to read the sizes on the case. Overall, though, this is a good screw extractor set that’s affordably priced and compact enough to fit in a tool bag or belt.

Get the Bosch screw extractor at The Home Depot.

Our Ratings: Performance 4.3/5; Durability 5/5; Value 4/5

With some 35 pieces, Topec’s screw extractor kit gives you plenty of options for removing all types of fasteners, ranging from small screws to large bolts.

In terms of performance, Topec’s effectiveness tilts to large fasteners. The bits and extractors perform best on larger screw heads and bolts. While we found some success removing bits with its spiral screw extractors, these multispline extractors, when used with a drill and bit driver, garnered the best results. The tighter threading of the splines just seemed to bite better into drilled-out holes than the spiral extractors.

While we liked the broad range of bits this kit offers, we didn’t like the fact that Topec doesn’t group the bits with the extractors. This leaves you to make those matches on your own, which can be a challenge, especially if you use the kit only occasionally.

This design makes the kit a tougher pick for those who don’t have a lot of experience using this type of tool. Given that and this kit’s size, the Topec extractor set is best suited for home mechanics who find themselves facing off against stripped-out screw heads and sheared-off bolt heads of varying sizes on a fairly regular basis.

Our Ratings: Performance 4/5; Durability 5/5; Value 4/5

This is no ordinary set of combination pliers. A closer look at its jaws reveals that it’s designed with one purpose in mind: to remove stripped screws. The aptly named Vampliers have fanglike serrated teeth and a concave opening in the jaws that fit around the contours of a screw head, making it an excellent tool for stripped screws.

The serrated teeth bit nicely into screw heads during testing, allowing us to turn the screws without having to put a death grip on the handle. The rubberized grip makes the handles fairly comfortable to hold. We also liked the fact that we could grip screw heads either by holding the teeth perpendicular to the screw for maximum grip or vertically over the top of the screw for heads just barely poking above the wood surface. Of course, the Vampliers are only useful if there’s something to bite into; they won’t work for embedded screw heads.

The Vampliers is an expensive stripped screw removal tool, especially for anyone who already has a pair of vice-grip pliers in their tool arsenal. Still, they’re worth the investment if you find yourself dealing with stripped-out or sheared-off screw heads on a regular basis.

Get the Vampliers screw extractor at Amazon.

While we didn’t test the products below, they still make the grade based on their impressive specs and extensive positive customer reviews.

This five-piece bolt extraction set from Irwin is a simple yet effective bolt removal tool. Each size extractor has a reverse spiral design that bites into the bolt head, making it easier to remove bolts that have been painted over, rounded-off bolts heads, and frozen bolts. The extraction kit for bolts comes with five sizes to suit bolts ranging in size from ⅜ inch and 10 millimeter (mm) to ⅝ inch and 16mm. And if that’s not enough, Irwin also makes a five-piece expansion set with additional sizes. The bolt extractor bits work with 1/2-inch ratchets, impact wrenches, flat wrenches, and locking pliers, and all five pieces fit into a hard plastic case that’s small enough to fit into a tool box or bucket.

Extracting large stripped-out bolts and screws can be a tough job. With its large extractors, this set is up to the challenge. It boasts 25 extractors that run in 1/32-inch increments from ⅛ inch all the way up to a hefty ⅞-inch extractor. Each extractor features microplaned reverse threads designed to thread into drilled-out holes to remove stripped screws or bolts with rounded-off or sheared-off heads.

Its hexagonal head fits into standard sockets for optimal torque. Socket sizes are etched into the metal, making identifying each extractor easy. The extractors consist of chrome molybdenum steel that is hard enough to extract these larger bolts, and all 25 pieces fit into a molded carrying case.

Get the Neiko screw and bolt extractor at Amazon or Walmart.

Removing tiny damaged screws from electronics such as laptop computers isn’t doable with a standard screw extraction kit. The bits are simply too large. With its ability to remove machine screws as small as a 1 rating, which is just 0.0781 inches in diameter, this small screw extractor kit is an excellent solution for extracting smaller stripped machine screws.

In addition to the 0.0781-inch size, it also includes 2, 3, and 4 machine screw sizes. Each bit is double-sided with a drill bit on one end and a threaded adapter on the other. They consist of durable high-speed steel that is heat tempered twice for maximum hardness. A plastic carrying case conveniently keeps all four bits organized so they’re easy to find when needed.

Get the Alden Grabit Micro bolt extractor at Amazon.

We assembled our list of the top screw extractors through a mix of research and hands-on testing. After comparing the specs and scouring reviews for some two dozen different screw extractors, we narrowed down the list to eight models, and then proceeded to test the top five sets.

We tested each on a variety of fasteners, including small and large screws and bolts, keeping in mind that screw extracting is challenging. No screw extracting kit will have a 100 percent success rate. Keeping that in mind, we assigned points to each kit based on how effective it was at removing fasteners and how easy it was to use. We also considered the range of extractor sizes, awarding points for those capable of handling a broader range of screw and bolt sizes. We considered the durability of each kit. Finally, we factored in performance and durability along with price to determine the value of each kit.

Screw extractors come in different types to suit the different sizes of damaged fasteners you can’t remove with a screwdriver. Read on to learn more about each type and crucial factors, including gripping power and the material one will want to consider when choosing the best screw extractor.

Screw heads come in a wide variety of sizes, so it’s important to pay attention to what sizes the screw extractor can accommodate. Most sets include sizes ranging from 0.125 inch up to 0.625 inch. Larger sets have extractors as large as 0.875 inch and are capable of removing large bolts on vehicles and industrial machines. Other sets can remove tiny machine screws found in electronics, such as laptop computers, with extractors as small as 0.0781 inch. While a small kit with four or five extractor sizes is adequate for most, it makes sense for pros or DIYers to invest in a set that can cover a broad range of sizes.

Different types of screw extractors use different strategies for gripping a stripped or rusted screw or bolt head. Some drill into the head and use reverse threads to bite into and grip the head, while others grab the head by fitting over it. Although the latter generally creates more gripping power, this style of extractor is limited to instances where the bolt or screw head is jutting out of the material enough to allow the tool to grip it.

The material type also affects gripping power. Drill bits and extractors made of high-quality steel alloys do a better job of boring into and gripping fasteners and last longer than those that use cheaper materials.

Since screw extractors must burrow into metal screws in order to work, they need to consist of hard metal. Most screw extractors are made of high-speed steel, the same steel alloy used in many drill bits and saw blades. This type of steel is harder than other alloys and is capable of enduring high temperatures without softening, a key characteristic for drilling into the heads of metal fasteners.

If it’s in the budget, extractors made of cobalt steel are even better, but they’re also pricier. Cobalt steel is harder than high-speed steel and holds up better to the high temperatures created by metal cutting into metal. Cobalt steel also has a higher tensile strength, which makes it a better choice for extractors with a narrower flute of 0.125 inch or less. Stay away from extractors that consist of softer alloys, as they will not be hard enough to do the job.

Screw extractors have features that make them easier to use and ensure that the right drill bit is used with the right extractor. Those that work in conjunction with a drill bit must match the bit size to be effective. This type of extractor should have the compatible drill bit size etched onto its side to avoid confusion.

Double-sided extractors are some of the most convenient models as they feature the drill bit and extractor on a single reversible shank, eliminating the need to hunt for a compatible drill bit. Simply drill the hole with one side, then flip the shank to apply the extractor.

Some kits use magnetic extension bit holders that can hold either the drill or extractor bit. This allows the user to quickly swap between them, speeding the screw-removal process along.

Since screw and bolt extractor kits can include 30 pieces or more, most come with handy carrying cases that keep all the pieces organized so they can be found when needed.

Most screw extractor tools are easy to use, even for beginners. Here are a few valuable tips for using a screw extractor.

If you have additional questions about how to use a screw extractor, read on for answers to some common queries about these handy tools.

The drill bit is a crucial part of the extractor that is used to bore a hole in the head of the damaged bolt or screw, creating a place for the extractor to penetrate and grip the screw head so you can remove it.

There really is no standard length for a screw extractor. In fact, short and long extractors work equally well at removing damaged screws and bolts. It’s more important to choose the correct- diameter drill bit and extractor to suit the damaged fastener.

To determine the proper extractor size, begin by choosing the proper drill bit size. The drill bit should be about half the diameter of the screw head. For example, to remove a 0.375-inch screw, begin by drilling a hole in the head with a 3/16-inch drill bit. Once the hole is drilled, use an extractor that’s slightly smaller than the drill bit—most kits conveniently match the bits on the kit to the extractor. The slightly smaller extractor should fit inside the hole but still be tight enough that its threads can lock into the hole’s contours.

Screw extractors are reverse threaded. This means that you’ll need to set your drill/driver or impact driver in reverse to remove the fastener. Keep in mind that the drill bits in screw extractor sets are also usually (though not always) reverse threaded, meaning you’ll need to set your drill in reverse when drilling the pilot hole.

A straight flute extractor is a smooth tapered bar. After drilling a pilot hole in the screw head, you have to hammer the straight extractor into the screw head, then use a pair of pliers to twist the extractor counterclockwise to remove the screw. A spiral screw extractor doesn’t require any hammering. It has threads that bite into the pilot hole, allowing you to remove the damaged screw with a wrench or drill.

#7965. Gardening 101: Aster

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

It is a mildly sad sight at the end of the summer when many plants lose their luster, with flowers fading and leaves looking a bit burned, as if they forgot their sunscreen. But late summer and early autumn is when perennial asters can save the day, and the garden.

Coming up: the most colorful season at Old Court Nurseries in England, a small family-run operation specializing since 1906 in propagating its own Michaelmas daisies (and many other varieties of asters). Photographer Britt Willoughby Dyer visited the nurseries’ Picton Garden at the height of the season:

Asters have a deep history in Greek mythology. According to legend, the goddess Astrea created asters with her tears. The story goes that she was so distraught at how few stars appeared in the dark sky that she started crying, and as her tears fell they turned into star-shaped asters on the ground. Aptly named for the ancient Greek and Latin word for star (because of its long, radiating petals), asters are a star of the late-summer garden.

As other perennials are starting to slow down, asters are winding up to add hints of necessary color. Asters come in a range of colors, including pink, purple, red, and white.

With more than 600 species in the Aster genus, it also shares the same family as the daisy. Found wild in North America and southern Europe, asters are mainly perennials but a few are annuals and biennials. The two main groups of asters are the New England aster (Aster novae-angliae) and the New York asters (Aster novi-belgii).

While there is a galaxy of asters to choose among, a favorite is Aster frikatii ‘Monch’ for its long bloom time; it grows to a dramatic height of up to three feet and bears large lavender-blue flowers.

The downside to asters is they can be tricky when it comes to water. They tend to drop their lower leaves if not kept well-watered in the hotter months. Also, aster plants have a tendency to eventually die out in the center, making them a great candidate to rejuvenate by dividing and replanting in new clumps every two to three years.

Another issue is powdery mildew. If your garden is plagued with mildew in the fall and your asters are afflicted with this punishment, consider planting mildew-free varieties, such as the low-growing variety Aster dumosus. Another solution is to make sure asters have good air circulation around them and plenty of sun.

For more growing tips, see Asters: A Field Guide to Planting, Care & Design. For more late-summer ideas to perk up a garden, our Garden Design 101 guides can help.
