#7948. 15 Things Nobody Tells You About Pawpaws

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

As soon as late summer edges toward fall in New York, I begin to lick my pawpaw-loving lips. As this native North American fruit gains mainstream recognition it has become easier to source both the fresh fruit as well as pawpaw saplings. Despite the rising tide of awareness, many people are still unfamiliar with them and have yet to taste a fresh pawpaw. And if you have lusted after the perfumed fruit but have not met one, there are few things about these green-mango lookalikes you may not know.

The pawpaw under discussion is the native North American fruit belonging to the genus Asimina. The cold-hardy common pawpaw is A. triloba, but there are over a dozen other species, with regional distributions that cleave to the eastern and Mid-Western parts of the United States, from southern Canada down to Florida.

In regions and countries with Commonwealth and British colonial histories (think Australia, England, India, South Africa, the West Indies, and more) the common name “pawpaw” refers to what anyone from the Americas calls papaya. Soft-skinned and subtropical, small or football-sized, that pawpaw, Carica papaya, has yellow to deep rose flesh and is filled in the center with little black, peppery seeds. It is available in many grocery stores, year-round.

The botanical genus name Asimina is derived from the Shawnee word for pawpaw: ha’simini. For the Shawnee, September is the month of the pawpaw moon, ha’siminikiisfwa, according to Joel Barnes, Archives Director for the Shawnee Tribe (via a West Virginia Public Radio interview in a 2020).

Until the 19th century, before they were forcibly removed by the US government, the Shawnee’s ancestral lands were in pawpaw-rich Appalachia, including current southeast Ohio.

The three-day Ohio Pawpaw Festival in southeast Ohio in September is a celebration of everything pawpaw. There are pawpaw tastings, and dozens of pawpaw dishes to choose from. Chris Chmiel is one of the founders of the festival and the co-owner (with Michelle Gorman, his wife) of Integration Acres, which has sold the fresh fruit and frozen purée, and other native wild things to the public since 1996. (The first pawpaws I tasted were shipped from Ohio’s woodlands to my Brooklyn front door in 2016.)

On 18 September, 1806, William Clark wrote, in the detailed journal that Thomas Jefferson dictated the expedition keep, that “…our party entirely out of provisions Subsisting on poppaws…the party appear perfectly contented and tell us that they can live very well on the pappaws [sic].”

There are many similar entries (reading the journal is equal parts recoil and wonder; but it is a compelling chronicle of plants encountered).

The aroma of pawpaws is strong—they will perfume a room. Their texture when ripe is creamy. Different cultivars vary in flavor: Some pawpaws taste like a kaleidoscope of passionfruit and pineapple, lychee, and mango. Many tasters mention banana; personally, I detect none, but perhaps it is the pawpaw’s soft consistency that inspires the comparison. Others taste like caramel, lightly scorched. Think crème brûlée, with tropical overtones. A fruit may taste intense, or mild. The little slippery sac around each large seed is slightly bitter, as is the flesh closest to the skin.

Unless they are very close to ripe on the branch, pawpaws do not ripen well once picked (they are not like avocados). Visiting your local tree/s after a windstorm or heavy rain is a great way to find windfalls. Their skin may bruise or discolor, but this seldom means that the fruit itself is damaged. Rather, it’s a sign of ripeness.

Pawpaws are  close cousins of custard apple (cherimoya) and soursops. All these large-seeded, soft-fleshed, deeply aromatic fruit belong to the family Annonaceae. The pawpaw is the cold-hardiest among them.

There’s no reason why you would, but don’t chew up and swallow pawpaw seeds. Eating the skin has the same effect.

While the evidence is anecdotal, there is enough chatter in online forums to suggest that some people react badly to eating pawpaws. The result is dramatic diarrhea and, sometimes, nausea. Eat pawpaws in moderation (I cut myself off at three in one sitting. Is that moderate?). Also, some pawpaw purveyors, like Integration Acres, recommend against drying the pulp for use in fruit leather, since it can cause gastrointestinal distress. The reasons for this are not understood (yet).

Some researchers posit that eating pawpaws regularly could be detrimental to the eater. The seeds and pulp of pawpaws contain acetogenins, including annonacin, which is toxic to cortical neurons. Could regular pawpaw ingestion cause neurotoxins to build up over time? A connection has been drawn between pawpaws and their cousins, custard apples, which are popular in the Caribbean, where clusters of Parkinson’s in Guadalupe have been documented, possibly linked to a diet where the custard apples feature regularly. (Annonacin was also thought to play a role in cancer-cell death. That published paper has since been retracted.)

The common pawpaw is hardy from USDA growing zones 5 through 8 (according to Cornell).  It’s the tropical-tasting fruit many cool-climate gardeners can grow. Bradley Farms in New Paltz, New York (zone 5), brings pawpaws to greenmarkets in October. While pawpaws in the wild tend to grow in clonal colonies in the woods and on woodland edges, pawpaw trees will thrive in full sun as long as they have ample moisture in summer. They like hot, humid summers and cold winters.

Sowing pawpaw seed is most successful when the seeds are planted before they dry out. Even three days of drying can reduce germination rates to 20%, according to the University of Kentucky. (If you can’t plant them at once, keep them in a baggy with potting soil until you can). Sowing them in fall (right after you eat them) allows them to cold-stratify naturally, outdoors.

If you’re mosying around a pawpaw patch and are tempted to remove a sapling, think twice:  Pawpaws have long taproots and respond poorly to being yanked out.  Unless you have emerald-green thumbs, either grow them from seed or find a nursery that sells pawpaw trees. More and more do.

N.B.: This post was first published October 2023.

Zipping tender shrubs into plant covers keeps them cozy over winter, and here's everything you need to know to choose the right one for your zone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A plant frost jacket is such a simple, straightforward way to keep plants alive and well over winter, and modern designs with drawstring bases and ventilating zips make it easier than ever to use them. When winterizing a garden, zippered plant jackets don’t only protect tender beauties like banana plants and tree ferns but can help to stop sensitive souls like olive trees from dropping their leaves in a cold snap, shield citrus trees from the occasional frost if you garden in zone 9, and prevent palms from rotting.

Fleece plant covers are also incredibly useful to cocoon early-blooming shrubs like camellia and magnolia if a frost hits just as they’re setting their buds, so you can save the flower show. Young fruit trees, too, can benefit from this extra layer to stop their thin bark splitting in freezing winter conditions, and a plant cover can shield all sorts of other plants from damage caused by snow, sleet and strong winds.

So, if you're getting ready to winterize plants as you prepare your garden for the onset of cold weather, plant jackets should be part of your plan. Not all fleece plant covers are created equal, however, so if you want them to actually work, you need to take a close look at their weight rating. The material used to make frost jackets comes in different weights and, just like comforters offer various levels of warmth, that directly impacts how well it will protect plants in winter, but also the more sunshine it'll block.

Horticultural fleece is a non-woven material typically made from polypropylene, and its weight determines how much protection it offers your plant, measured in grams per square meter (gsm) or ounces per square yard (oz/sq yd). Check the label or online description to find the rating. Any good-quality frost jacket will state the rating and the higher the number, the more insulation it will provide but also block more sunlight.

Armed with this knowledge, you can choose the exact right level of protection for whatever plant you’re winterizing in your USDA zone. While you need to ensure your plant is getting the right level of cold protection, you also need to cater for its sunlight needs.

Because these plants are dormant through winter in colder zones, they don’t need sunlight so you can safely use an ultra heavy-weight fleece to protect them. The fleece alone won’t be enough to protect banana plants (Musa basjoo) and tree ferns (Dicksonia antarctica) from the deep chill of colder zones but are still useful as a cover once you’ve packed layers of insulating straw around the plant. Not only will the fleece form a great barrier against wind and rain but it’ll keep the straw in place and that wrapped plant looking tidy.

Made from 95gsm or 2.8oz/sq yd non-woven material, these plant covers have rounded tops for a good fit and come in green, beige or white in four sizes: 31" x 25", 47" x 39", 71" x 47" and 94" x 79".

Because deciduous shrubs drop their leaves in fall, they don’t need any sunlight over winter to survive so you can safely zip them up in a heavy or ultra heavy-weight plant jacket, depending on the level of protection needed in your zone. This thicker material will also keep snow from weighing down and snapping brittle winter branches. Do choose a design with a zipper as well as a base drawstring so you can regularly open up the zip on milder days to let air circulate.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

In 60gsm or 1.77oz/sq yd non-woven fabric, these zippered plant jackets are made of a minimum 50% recycled material and come in four sizes: 23" x 23", 39" x 31", 71" x 47" and 83" x 71".

Hardy shrubs that flower early in the spring such as camellias and magnolias are typically tough enough to survive most winters without a jacket, but their flowerbuds are quickly killed by a late frost or cold snap. Throw on a medium- or heavy-weight plant jacket overnight to save those new buds from the frost.

Evergreen plants such as conifers still need sunlight and fresh air to survive through winter, so a medium-weight fleece is your best bet for general winterizing if your aim is to shield a hardy plant from snow, hail and wind damage. If you’re planning on leaving it on permanently through winter, use a medium-duty fleece for more tender evergreen olive and citrus trees and certain palms, too.

However, if you live in a colder climate you’ll need the increased protection of a heavy- or ultra heavy-weight fleece for these more tender plants. Either use this as an extra layer to throw on over the top of the permanent medium-weight layer in severe weather or, if you use this as the mainstay cover, you’ll need to keep unzipping it to allow sunshine and air in during milder daytime temperatures.

Most medium-duty fleeces are designed without a zipper but that’s not a problem: because the thinner material lets more air and sunlight through, they can safely be left in place.

Made of 32gsm or 0.95oz/sq yd breathable material, this medium-weight plant cover has a drawstring base and is available in three sizes: 32" x 32", 55" x 48" and 72" x 72".

No fleece jacket can generate heat, it can only insulate from the cold, so how you use it has a huge impact on how effectively it protects your plant in winter. Choose a design with both a drawstring and a zip as this not only makes the jacket quick and easy to pop on, but allows you to fit it closely and avoids the wind ripping it off.

Wherever possible, peg the plant jacket to the ground to catch any heat rising upwards. Soil holds onto considerable warmth from the sun, so make use of this natural radiator. Use bricks or stones to weigh the jacket base down, or peg it to the ground with landscape fabric pegs, choosing a product with gaskets to prevent the fabric tearing like these Galvanized Landscape Pins from Amazon.

Similarly, if you’re winterizing a plant in a container, use a frost jacket that’s big enough to fit around the pot, too, as this will protect the roots as well as trap any heat from the soil. Roots in planters are very vulnerable to freezing temperatures so consider wrapping the pot with bubble wrap first.

To prevent moisture building up under the cover and causing mold, make sure you buy a jacket marked as breathable, and open the zip on mild days to allow air to circulate.

While you don’t want to squash a plant into a cover, it’s a wise idea to fit the jacket around the plant to prevent it flapping in the wind and metal greenhouse clamps such as these from Amazon are invaluable to gather loose material or clip a jacket to existing plant supports.

Measuring 8’ x 8’ to fit bigger shrubs and trees, this ultra heavy-weight 80gsm or 2.4oz/yd cover comes with ties and stakes so it can be pinned securely to the ground in exposed gardens.

These ultra heavy-weight zippered covers are made from 75gsm or 2.2oz/sq yd patterned fabric and are available in a green or grey print in sizes 32"x24", 47"x32", 71"x47" and 83"x71".

Shaped for wide, bushy shrubs, this heavy-weight plant cover made of 50gsm or 1.5oz/sq yd fabric measures a generous 7' x 7' and is also available in an 8' square size.

#7943. Renovation Diaries: The House Envelope and Other Lessons in Efficiency

Editor’s note: This is the latest in a series of posts by Sally Kohn— journalist and CNN political commentator, TED talk giver, and design aficionado—chronicling her adventures in remodeling.

Let’s level set. I live in a 1780s barn that was turned into a house in the 1950s, and as far as I can tell the windows and the siding haven’t been changed since. The fact is, many parts of our money pit farmhouse need updating. Some, like the 1950s asphalt roof built directly on top of a much older shake shingle roof, we replaced last year. Other things we’re still waiting on, like the vintage 1950s bathroom tile with vintage crumbling grout. But since we can’t close many of our windows without pushing on them from the outside, and we have an inexplicable leak behind our very ancient siding, we put off the inevitable long enough. It is time for some grand-scale renovations.

Stay tuned for some of the other things we’ll be changing, including a kitchen refresh. But first up, if we’re going to go to all the trouble—and, ahem, expense—of replacing all of our siding and windows, can we make our old home more environmentally responsible in terms of both materials and energy efficiency? Let’s find out.

My guide on this journey is Shannon Pendleton, principal of Sanderson Sustainable Design and co-host of Passive House Accelerator. In addition to being a friend and neighbor, Shannon is a leading expert on how to make homes more sustainable and energy efficient. And while those concepts might immediately make you think of solar panels and the like, Shannon explains that in energy efficiency, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. In other words, using green energy to power your home is great. But designing your home to need less energy in the first place is even better.

But with apologies to Shannon, when she explained the science of the “building envelope,” all I could think about is that envelope feels like the wrong word. Maybe it should be “building envelop”—as in, how enveloped is your building. Because your “building envelop” is what stops the outside environment from getting in and the inside environment from getting out. That means everything from bugs and dust to wind to heat and cold.

So I’m making two big changes to my “building envelop,” both of which create an opportunity for more energy efficiency. Let’s start with the siding. We have very old, very stained, very falling-apart cedar. I could just replace it with cedar, maybe even sustainably harvested cedar. But the fact is, our old cedar is cupping and splitting. Yes, more maintenance would help, but that’s hard to do with second-story wood. Also I’m lazy. Alternatively, I could have gone with some plastic product or chemically treated wood but, like I said, we care about the environment and also want to preserve the look and feel of our historic home. So we’re going with Thermory siding.

Thermory takes sustainably forested wood—in our case, we’re using pine—and puts it through an intense heat-treating process that makes the wood more stable and rot-resistant. It’s an updated twist on the Japanese shou sugi ban process, where wood is charred to make it water and rot resistant. Thermory is that, without the blackening (though they actually do have a product that mirrors the shou sugi ban look, but with the added benefits of Thermory’s advanced thermal modification). In other words, Thermory gives us everything we like about natural wood plus all these added benefits.

Using a more stable rot-resistant siding definitely envelops our house better (take that, flying squirrels), but the energy efficiency upgrades come from what will be behind the siding. Our contractor—the wonderful, lovable, fantastic-to-work-with John Gemmi and his company, Gemmi Construction—were already planning to weather-seal behind the siding, and of course put new insulation behind that where we find any lacking. But Shannon suggested installing “a rain screen, a continuous air barrier, and continuous exterior insulation” to give us the most enveloped envelope possible. Ultimately, we settled on Zip R sheathing, which does all three of those things in one system. So that’s our plan.

As for the windows, well…. The most energy-efficient option is triple-pane glass, but in our case, since we’re replacing a gajillion windows, we just couldn’t make it work in our budget. We have two walls of windows in our great room, most of which are currently fixed panes that we’re excited to replace with operable awning windows. We looked into doing triple-pane for just those windows, but that would have made the windows too heavy to open. So yes, we’re choosing a little less efficiency there but counting on the fact that having new windows that don’t require a screwdriver and grunts to close will nevertheless up our efficiency. Plus, thanks to Ambiance Design, we’re adding retractable Duette Honeycomb shades over those large window walls, which will give us some extra energy efficiency on super hot days.

Niece Lumber helped us pick out Lincoln Windows, a family run U.S.-manufactured brand with two advantages. First, we could get retractable screens which we’re very excited about. And second, they offer custom colors on their exteriors. You’ll have to stay tuned to figure out what color choice we’ve made. It’s gonna be…dramatic.

Work on the siding and window part of the renovation is starting soon. I’ll be posting updates on my Instagram (@sallykohn), plus more updates along the way here as we get into our kitchen renovations, including the most sustainable and cool countertop and our very locally made and custom color stove. Watch this space!

#7942. 12 Proven Solutions for Sealing in the Heat This Winter

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 26, 2026 11:35 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Winter drafts find every weak spot in your house, even if it’s a well-heated one. Warmth slips out through glass first, but small gaps around doors, a pull-down attic stairway, a garage door, and even the walls of a water heater tank can all let heat escape. Tracking down those weak spots is the first step toward keeping your home comfortable and using less electricity to do it.

The following list of proven solutions for sealing in the heat this winter includes everything from simple weatherstripping and draft stoppers to smart controls for managing your heating needs. It mixes affordable DIY supplies, decorating upgrades, and high-tech tools, and it includes several products the BobVila.com team has personally tested. There’s a fix here to suit nearly any space, and a few that would make a great gift for the handy homeowner on your list.

Get the Home Decorators Collection cellular shades at The Home Depot.

When it comes to sealing in the heat, it helps to start by seeing where it’s escaping—and the Topdon TC005 thermal camera makes those cold spots visible. Named best overall in our thermal cameras guide,it has a 3.5-inch display for examining temperature patterns, laser distance measurement for reference points, and 64GB of storage for documenting findings. App and PC connectivity support further analysis, while its 8-hour battery and built-in LED light make home inspections easier.

What our tester says: “I was impressed with the TopDon thermal camera’s ability to detect\ the lowest temperatures in its images. It makes it possible to pinpoint where heat loss is occurring.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Review tester and writer

Get the Topdon thermal camera at Amazon or Walmart.

As the top pick in our thermal curtains guide, these Best Home Fashion blackout curtains feature an extra-thick triple-weave polyester to keep warmth in. A wide design offers generous window coverage to keep drafts out, and antique-bronze grommets add a decorative touch. Because they’re also machine washable, they’re an easy-care fix for a chilly living room or bedroom.

Get the Best Home Fashion thermal curtains (various sizes and colors) at Amazon or The Home Depot.

With a bit of weatherstripping, small gaps around doors and windows don’t have to mean piling up under blankets and quilts—and thanks to its notable durability and simple installation, Yotache’s self-adhesive foam tape was an easy choice for Best Insulation Tape in our window insulation kits guide. This pick is available in a range of sizes, including a 2-pack with 26 feet total, which is enough for a couple of small windows or doors.

Get the Yotache foam weatherstripping at Amazon.

Our testing team’s favorite in our door draft stoppers guide, the Maxtid Adjustable Door Draft Stopper, installs in mere minutes—without tools or much effort. The adjustable design fits different door widths throughout your home, and the adhesive backing helps the stopper stay in place. There’s also a hook-and-loop fastening system that lets you detach the sleeve for quick cleanups.

What our tester says: “Despite some online reviews saying this was difficult to install, it took me all of 5 minutes and was very straightforward. At first I thought it would be unattractive, but once it was installed, I barely noticed it.”—Amber Guetebier, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Maxtid door draft stopper at Amazon or Walmart.

Runner-Up in our tests of the best window insulation kits, the Duck Brand Max Strength Window Kit uses thick, puncture-resistant shrink film to block winter drafts and keep warm air in, helping you save energy. The film comes in one easy-to-install roll, so there’s no need to measure in advance: simply apply it, then cut it to size. And because it’s see-through, you get to keep your view while enjoying a draft-free home.

Get the Duck Brand window insulation kit at Amazon or Target.

With its ability to add an insulating layer to a compatible garage door without requiring special tools, the Reach Barrier 3009 kit earned the top award in our lineup of the best garage door insulation kits. Its eight easy-to-cut panels trap air between reflective polyethylene layers to help retain warmth in winter and deflect heat in summer, and in our tests, they also noticeably reduced noise.

Read our full review: Reach Barrier Garage Door Insulation Kit

What our tester says: “This kit is accessible for DIYers of any skill level and installs quickly. Plus, it’s lightweight enough to adhere to the door with stickers and to line the door without straining your garage door opener.” —Kathleen Corlett, Editor in Chief

Get the Reach Barrier garage door insulation kit at Amazon or The Home Depot.

Pull-down attic stairs are convenient, but the opening can break up an otherwise insulated attic floor. The Owens Corning attic stairway insulator closes off airflow between the attic and the main floor with R-10 fiberglass insulation and tough, highly reflective foil. The cover comes fully assembled and installs easily over existing insulation, helping improve energy efficiency and indoor comfort.

Get the Owens Corning attic stairway insulator at Lowe’s or The Home Depot.

When you’ve already paid to heat the water in your water heater, it’s a real shame to have that warmth leak back out through the tank walls. As the best overall pick on our water heater blankets guide, the Frost King SP60 wraps your tank in 3 inches of foil-faced fiberglass rated R-10 insulation, helping you save on energy bills. It fits water heaters up to 60 gallons and allows you to leave openings for vents, valves, and access panels.

Get the Frost King blanket at Amazon or Walmart.

As our top-ranked smart ceiling fan guide, the Dreo CLF712S offers reversible airflow that pushes warm air collected near the ceiling back down into your living space. Six speeds range from a gentle breeze to high winds, dimmable and colorful accent lighting add ambience, and in-app customization and automation make this fan a truly smart addition to your home.

Read our full review: Dreo Smart Ceiling Fan

What our tester says: “Even before powering it on, I could tell the Dreo had a more premium design than many of the other fans I had been working with.”—Paul Rankin, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Dreo smart ceiling fan at Amazon or Dreo.

The GE Advanced Silicone 2 sealant, rated best for windows and doors in our exterior caulk guide, is a low-cost, high-impact fix for persistent drafts. The clear formula seals fixed joints around windows, doors, and trim, helping keep heat in and cold out. And since it’s also easy to apply and quick to dry, the job goes fast.

What our tester says: “This flexible caulk’s formula doesn’t just withstand expansion and contraction, it’s also mold- and mildew-resistant, which makes it perfect for caulking windows, doors, siding, attics, molding, and vents.”—Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the GE window and door sealant at The Home Depot or Walmart.

Topping our best smart thermostats guide, the fourth-generation Google Nest thermostat learns your temperature preferences and suggests schedule adjustments to help you save energy and stay comfortable. Its Adaptive Eco feature accounts for outdoor temperatures while you’re away, and the included room sensor helps manage hot and cold spots in the home. There’s even an app that lets you control it from anywhere, provides filter-change reminders based on actual use, and sends alerts if it detects potential heating or cooling issues.

Get the Google Nest thermostat at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

#7941. Campbell House: A Restoration-First Renovation by Nuud Studio

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

Two years ago, we shared the sensitively renewed “bush modernist” home of architect Brad Mitchell and interior designer Kerli Valk—a thoughtful renovation that won a 2023 Australian Interior Design Awards Commendation and a 2023 Houses Award for Sustainability. Now the couple, founders of Melbourne-based Nüüd Studio, have produced another award-winning design by following the same successful formula: maximize natural light, create functional flow, focus on exquisite joinery. And, above all else, where possible, make the most of what’s already there.

“One of the most effective ways to manage a budget is to work with the existing character and materials of a building rather than trying to contradict them,” says Kerli. Here, she expounds on the idea.

“When we first saw the property, much of the interior was a combination of pine lining boards, bagged brick, and whitewashed timber ceilings. At the time it felt quite dark and dated, and understandably it was difficult for the clients to imagine how those elements could form part of a new, more contemporary interior.

“Rather than removing them, we looked at how color, texture, and light could change the way they were perceived. The existing ceilings were left largely untouched, the brick walls were celebrated rather than concealed, and the pine-clad walls were painted.

“Retaining these elements was probably one of the largest savings in the project, but it also gave the finished interior much more character. We are often more interested in transforming what is already there than replacing it. Sometimes a relatively light intervention—a change in color, texture or the way light reaches a surface—can completely alter how an existing material is experienced.”

Photography by Sean Fennessey, courtesy of Nüüd Studio.

Backyard birds and other wildlife need a little extra help finding food, water, and shelter as the seasons change. That’s why we’ve teamed up with our friends at Birdfy to celebrate the nature lovers who go above and beyond to make their outdoor spaces a welcoming haven for local wildlife.

#7938. Heartleaf Skullcap: A Deer-Resistant Native Perennial

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Here, Amy Galloway Medley shares heartleaf skullcap, one of her favorite underappreciated native plants.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

One of my favorite native species right now is heartleaf skullcap. The fuzzy, heart-shaped leaves are beautiful, and they produce an oil that makes the plant very deer resistant. It looks fantastic planted in masses in a perennial border, with spikes of blue-purple flowers that are similar to those of salvias (Salvia spp. and cvs., Zones 5–11) and that attract hummingbirds.

Some claim that heartleaf skullcap is aggressive, but I find it doesn’t over-compete or crowd anything if you use it for filling those trouble areas where nothing else will grow. In central Texas, most of our native plants prefer full, scorching sun, but this is one that thrives and blooms in dry shade. It’s also impressively cold hardy and makes a wonderful container plant.

Learn more from Amy about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Amy Galloway Medley is the lead horticulturist at Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center at the University of Texas at Austin.

#7937. Off Hours: How Landscape Design Star Cleve West Survives His Day Job

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

What does a top garden designer do to relax? He gardens, of course—but not exactly where you’d expect. Cleve West, winner of seven Chelsea Flower Show RHS Gold Medals, spends his free time tending to a plot that couldn’t be more different from the conceptual spaces he creates for clients. Not especially private and the opposite of chic, his patch is in a West London community garden (in the UK it is called an allotment) and has been his personal project for a decade.

Cleve’s 2011 book, Our Plot, part memoir, part manual, part state-of-the-world discourse, takes us through the highs and lows of allotment life. Meanwhile, we’ve been invited for lunch:

Cleve West is the Gary Cooper of the garden design world. Modest, sincere, assured, he is admired by all. Did I mention that he can cook? Besides growing vegetables, fruit, and flowers, Cleve does a surprising amount of entertaining in the allotment that he shares with his partner, Christine Eatwell.

They use a variety of garden-side cooking contraptions: a grill, a gas-fired oven, and a hand-built pizza oven. “Many hours are spent not growing vegetables,” admits Cleve, shown here with his grill, picked up in Normandy, and the impressive pizza oven, which has a brick base, mud and sawdust dome, and bottles placed in the middle to stop the heat from going down.

“Some people think that the word ‘design’ is a little too pretentious and would rather their garden ‘evolve’ over the years,” says Cleve. “But how you arrange your plot, whether you draw it on paper or not, is design.” His intriguing wild tangle—I mean design—contains a rotation of vegetables including squash, beans, leaks, artichoke, onions, and gladioli by the shed.

Cleve’s client-based designs are characterized by sculptural forms and so, too, is his allotment. Wigwams made from coppiced hazel are finished off with heavy duty chains instead of insubstantial twine. They support beans and gourds, and last for about a season.

Recycle, improvise, and modify. This is the heart of the British community garden ethos. “If I had control over all the allotments, I would ban pre-fabricated sheds,” says Cleve. “I’d urge people to make their own in the name of local distinctiveness and individuality.”

Cooking at the plot intensifies the enjoyment of fresh food. Basic ingredients—seasoning, spices, oil, and vinegar—are kept in one of the sheds, but key elements, such as pizza dough, are made at home and carried in. True, cooking and entertaining without electricity and hot water involves extra work, but chopping and frying onions is far preferable out of doors than in.

Feeling inspired? Here’s Cleve’s recipe for a simple relish made on a barbecue or makeshift grill. He promises that allotment cooking “doesn’t get much easier.” Pair with naan or pita bread for a quick lunch.

Put the eggplant and green tomatoes on the barbecue or open fire and char them until they are black and “all squidgy” inside. Then cut along the middle and scoop out the contents of both eggplants and tomatoes. Mash, add the rest of the ingredients, mix, and eat!

N.B.: This post was first published July 2013. It has been updated with new links and information. For an update on Cleve’s allotment, read his recent blog post.

#7936. This Old-School DIY Reduces Drafts Inside the House (and It Looks Pretty Cool, Too)

Published Oct 26, 2026 4:50 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Some home design features have been around for generations, such as grandfather clocks, wingback chairs, and wraparound porches. Often found in drafty homes and hung only in doorways, the portiere curtain is another example dating back to the Aesthetic Movement of the late 19th century. It is named for the French word meaning “porter” or “doorkeeper.” Portieres are heavy, functional door curtains designed to block drafts, divide spaces, or close off hallways without requiring permanent walls.

As portiere curtains make a comeback, explore how to incorporate this older feature into your home so you can enjoy the many benefits they provide.

To effectively insulate a room, portiere curtains are crafted from thick, substantial fabrics like rich velvet rather than sheer materials. Hang the portiere on a rod mounted directly above the door so it can be pushed neatly against the wall when not in use. You can also use rings inside the doorframe to ensure smooth opening and closing from both sides.

Because both sides remain visible, they are typically hung within the doorway frame so mounting looks the same from both sides. It’s also usually constructed with decorative fabrics on both faces or finished with deep hems to conceal any backing, ensuring a polished look from every angle.

Back before heating systems existed, portiere curtains were installed to help keep warmth in a room. Even today, they can still help reduce drafts by providing a physical barrier of fabric to limit the flow of air from one room into another or from entering a doorway due to its draughty condition, says Goorha. The heavier the fabric and/or more densely woven, the better the curtain will be at limiting airflow since there is less opportunity for air to move through.

“To maximize effectiveness, hang the curtain above the door opening so that sufficient fabric hangs down and covers the door opening without much space between the side edges and the floor edge,” she advises.

Most carved pumpkins tend to get binned or left rotting on the curb once the candles burn out. Yet that leftover gourdish grin is packed with benefits for your soil, future plants, and wildlife

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first few days of November bring a familiar sorry sight, as pumpkins start piling up beside the trash cans, a few of them still grinning. Millions end up in landfills every year, where they break down without much air and give off greenhouse gases. That's a poor end for leftover Halloween pumpkins. In a garden, all that soft tissue could be breaking down into organic matter and feeding soil life – and that’s just the start.

If you took the time to grow pumpkins for Halloween, you know how much space, moisture, and fertilizer a single vine demands. All summer long, its leaves absorbed sunlight and pumped nutrients directly into its swollen fruit. Letting those nutrients leave your yard in a trash bag deprives your yard of valuable goodness that could be benefiting vegetable beds, feeding organisms and helping beneficial creatures. Even a carved pumpkin can have a second life as long as it hasn't been painted or coated.

Giving your post-Halloween gourds a productive second act is simple, fun, and satisfying. The only rule is that your fruit needs to be clean and free of contaminants. Any sections coated in craft paints, glitter, chemical sealants, or fake snow must be removed and tossed into the trash. Pull out any burnt candle stubs, melted wax, and battery-powered tea lights, and you are ready to put this fall bounty to work!

Turning post-holiday pumpkins into garden assets is a real no-brainer. Standard carving pumpkin varieties like Howden and Jack O' Lantern work especially well for the soil, because their flesh is tender and relatively easy to slice. Thicker, denser culinary and heirloom varieties (such as ribbed Cinderella, dusty-blue Jarrahdale, or warty Marina di Chioggia) offer firmer rinds that hold their shape for weeks, making them ideal where shape and rigidity are useful.

These fall projects work across every USDA hardiness zone, though local temperatures will determine how quickly your gourd decomposes. In cold northern regions (zones 3-5), freezing nights preserve carved pumpkins on porches longer, but freeze-thaw cycles eventually cause cell walls to collapse into watery slop, making early November the best time to act. In warm southern places (zones 8-10), elevated daytime temperatures accelerate mold and fruit flies, requiring immediate conversion into ground-based or wildlife-specific benefits.

Before tackling these projects, you need the right hand tools. A heavy-duty hori-hori knife is an excellent investment if you don’t have one, and can be used to simplify all kinds of cutting work. The Nisaku Hori-Hori from Amazon is great value and makes slicing through thick rinds a joy, and levers drainage holes through thick base walls without snapping. So find out exactly why your grinning pumpkin still has lots of goodness to give…

Tossing an intact pumpkin onto your compost heap can lead to disappointment. Its waxy rind acts like a raincoat, and depending on the variety and the weather, it could sit there for a long time with its skin intact. It needs breaking up first. Take a sharp spade or round-point shovel, and break the fruit down into fist-sized chunks to expose the flesh to soil bacteria and fungi.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Because the tissue is roughly 90% water, this green compost source needs plenty of dry browns mixed in. Balance every bucket of chopped pumpkin with two buckets of carbon-rich browns, such as shredded leaves, straw, or torn cardboard to keep the pile aerated. Turn the heap now and then. If space is tight, a single-chamber tumbler like the Vivosun Outdoor Dual Chamber Tumbling Composter, available from Amazon speeds up heat decomposition in a more compact way.

If your compost heap is overflowing, try direct trench composting in an empty veg bed. Dig a trench 18-24 inches (45-61cm) deep, in a bed reserved for heavy-feeding spring crops like sweet corn, squash, or tomatoes. Fill the bottom with chopped chunks and stomp them down. Backfill with 12 inches (30cm) of clean soil. Don’t go shallower, or neighborhood raccoons may smell it and dig it back up. Loose, well-drained soil can break it down in 2-3 months, but if you have heavy clay soil, you may still hit chunks of pumpkin a year from now, so be patient.

A healthy, mature Halloween pumpkin contains hundreds of plump seeds loaded with goodness. If your pumpkin grew with vibrant color and a firm rind, these seeds are prime candidates for saving for next year. Strain the tangled seed mass in a colander and massage it under a stream of cold running tap water to strip away the pulp. Spread the cleaned seeds in a single layer over non-stick parchment paper, a fine metal screen, or a ceramic plate. Let them dry in a warm, well-ventilated room out of direct sunlight for 2-3 weeks.

To test for dryness, try bending one: if it flexes, it still retains moisture, but if it snaps in half, your seeds are ready to store. Slide your dried seeds into breathable kraft paper seed envelopes. Pour them into paper seed envelopes, like the Seed Packet Kraft Envelopes, available from Walmart in packs of 100. Write the variety and date on the front, and store in a cool, dark drawer. Word to the wise, though: modern carving pumpkins are typically hybrids that won’t go true to type. Also, bees can cross-pollinate squash varieties across neighborhood zucchinis, so next spring’s seedlings may produce some wacky, unpredictable gourds.

Songbirds burn through vital fat stores as November temperatures drop, and a firm pumpkin makes a wonderful natural feeding bowl (although it’s best to stick to uncarved porch pumpkins for this project). Cut your pumpkin in half across the middle, or slice the top third off. Using a sturdy spoon or hori-hori to scrape out the inner pulp and seeds, until the interior walls are clean. Poke 3-4 half-inch (1.25cm) drainage holes through the base using a large screwdriver.

Punch 3 evenly spaced holes along the thick top rim, thread some sturdy jute twine through, and hang the bowl from a sturdy tree limb or pergola beam. Alternatively, set the flat shell on a low wall, tree stump, or deck railing. Fill with black-oil sunflower seeds or a good seed blend, such as Pennington Wild Bird Food from The Home Depot. You can also use some of your rinsed and dried pumpkin seeds as extra treats. These nutritious kitchen scraps make a nourishing treat for cardinals, blue jays and titmice. Just inspect every few days: when the inner walls turn squishy or develop fuzz, take the feeder down and consign it to the compost heap.

If you have a solid (again, uncarved) ornamental pumpkin on your porch, you can turn it into a temporary planter. Carve a generous opening around the stem and scoop out the pulp and seeds. Using a long screwdriver, puncture 4-5 generous drainage holes through the bottom crust. If you need a good screwdriver, Black Canyon’s Phillips Extended Length Screwdriver with Soft Grip Ergonomic Handle from Walmart is an efficient way to punch through thick rinds. Elevate the pumpkin on some stone or a trivet for drainage, as sitting water will rot the base rapidly.

Fill the lower half of the pumpkin with light, free-draining potting soil, then tuck in your choice of cold-tolerant fall ornamentals. Some great options include dwarf flowering kales, ruffled ornamental cabbages, winter violas, pansies, and trailing English ivy. These cold-hardy choices will look fresh and colorful for 2-4 weeks. With wet soil sitting inside it, the pumpkin starts softening from the inside out, and a few freeze-thaw nights will hurry it along. When yours starts to sag, move the plants to a bed or regular pot, and compost the gourd.

Slugs and garden snails are a persistent menace in fall, but at night they seek shelter in dark, damp, sheltered crevices to conserve moisture. A curved chunk of pumpkin rind provides a perfect natural decoy. Take sections of rind, including leftover pieces from carving or scraps that have softened too much for bird feeders. Place them skin-side up on the soil, beside vulnerable vegetable rows, hosta crowns, or mulched borders. The sweet scent of decaying squash flesh will attract slugs from several feet away, luring them under the hollowed domes.

Early the following morning, flip the rinds over. You should find dozens of slugs, snails, and earwigs clinging to the flesh. Scrape them off into a bucket of warm soapy water, or feed them to backyard chickens. Reset the traps for several nights in a row. Every slug removed now is one fewer laying eggs. Once the rind collapses, compost it. Dust a little Harris Food Grade Diatomaceous Earth Powder, available from Amazon, around your traps to stop slugs escaping back into your beds.

This last one is a lovely eco-friendly bonus for anyone keen to support overwintering beneficial insects in their yard. As fall frosts intensify, beneficial predatory insects and pollinators seek sheltered crevices. Ground beetles, centipedes, roving rove beetles, lacewings, lady bugs, and solitary native bees are valuable allies in the organic garden, consuming thousands of aphids, slug eggs, and weed seeds. You can turn a hollowed pumpkin shell into a cozy winter sanctuary. Take an uncarved or cleanly carved pumpkin. Slice a wide entryway near the base (or prop the shell upside-down on a couple of flat stones to leave an open gap underneath).

Stuff the cavity with natural textural materials that create micro-tunnels and air pockets. Use bundles of dry hollow plant stems, bamboo canes, small pine cones, crumpled dry leaves, and coarse straw. You can buy Bell Nursery Mini Straw Bales from The Home Depot which can also be used as mulch for strawberries and other overwintering plants. Tuck your bug hotel beneath a thick hedge, under a quiet shrub border, or along a perennial bed out of wind and rain. The shell will slowly soften, insulating the center. By spring, it will return harmlessly to the soil, leaving your beneficial guardians safely in the mulch bed, ready to go to work.

Before you drag your hollowed Halloween pumpkins down to the street corner, hopefully these ideas show you that they could be working hard for your yard. These seasonal gourds are far more than short-lived porch decorations. By turning into a rich soil ingredient, feeding wild birds, constructing cozy shelters for beneficial beetles and stocking up on seeds to plant next year’s pumpkins, you keep valuable resources out of landfills and grab a head start on next year's growth. Once winter sets in, those leftover gourds may already be enriching your soil: a true win-win!

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7933. Wild Bleeding Heart: A Hardworking and Adaptable Beauty

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Here, Melissa Starkey shares about wild bleeding heart, one of her favorite underappreciated native plants to grow.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

This plant is extremely close to my heart because I remember seeing it growing wild in Pennsylvania when I was a child. A great alternative to nonnative common bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis and cvs., Zones 3–9), it produces its best flush of heart-shaped flowers in spring but keeps blooming through the entire growing season, even as late as November here at Mt. Cuba Center. Wild bleeding heart also has fernlike foliage, which has a kind of blush tinge.

But all its aesthetic qualities aside, wild bleeding heart is incredibly hardworking and adaptable. It can grow in partial shade and makes an excellent woodland plant. This plant also does quite well out in the sun; it grows naturally on rocky, sunny outcrops. I have seen it growing right out of rocks in the wild. While it does adapt well, its unique flowers require larger pollinators, like bumblebees, that are strong enough to force themselves through its tight petals.

Wild bleeding heart is a bit smaller than common bleeding heart, but it does not go dormant like its nonnative relatives, giving you three seasons of interest. If pink flowers aren’t to your taste, there is a white cultivar available called ‘Alba’ (D. eximia ‘Alba’, Zones 3–9).

Learn more from Melissa about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Melissa Starkey is the marketing and communications manager and an instructor at Mt. Cuba Center, a botanical garden in Hockessin, Delaware.

Dicentra photo courtesy of Mt. Cuba Center.

#7931. The Best Fire Starters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

By Glenda Taylor, Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tony Carrick, Donna Boyle Schwartz

Published Oct 27, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Fire starters make it easy for anyone to start a roaring fire. Rather than having to wrestle with damp wood or crumpled-up newspapers to get the first flames going, users can employ a fire starter to achieve this with a single match or the flick of a lighter. The catch is that these outdoor living aids aren’t all created equal.

Some fire starters stand out for their ability to help ignite a fire rapidly and effortlessly, while others are difficult to light or won’t stay lit long enough to ignite a wood fire. We wanted to know which ones were worth buying, so we tested them in our own fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, and fire pits, eventually choosing the Superior Trading Co. All-Natural Fire Starter as our favorite for its nontoxic ingredients and effective performance. Ahead, we’ll cover how the following products earned a place in our lineup of the best fire starters.

Bottom line: Discover the best fire starters of 2026, tested for performance, ease of use, and environmental impact, with options for every need and budget.

In total, we tested 15 different fire starters: 12 small accelerant products, and three ferro rods that could fit into a pocket on a camping or hiking trip. Our main goal was to determine which fire starters performed the best in their relative categories. We didn’t test matches or lighters, but we did use them to light the accelerant fire starters. Not every product we tested made the cut for this guide. Each of the products below earned a spot by being a top performer in our hands-on testing.

These Superior Trading Co. fire starters are safe, easy to use, and effective. We found that just one pod was typically all we needed to get a log fire lit and burning. Made from wood shavings and food-grade wax, the pods are odorless, nontoxic, and environmentally safe, making them ideal for everything from indoor fireplaces to camping bonfires.

It took about 4 seconds for the pod to catch fire when we lit it with a single match. It started burning slowly, but within 5 minutes, the flames were about 8 inches tall, and the pod continued burning for about 15 minutes, which was plenty of time for the logs to catch fire.

The manufacturer lists these fire starters as waterproof, so we dropped a couple in a glass of water before testing them. We couldn’t get them to light immediately, but that was understandable. Once they dried out, they lit quickly and burned well. We used them in a fireplace and a charcoal grill. We placed one Superior Trading Co. fire-starter pod under the charcoal basket in our grill and lit it. By the time the flame from the pod burned down, the charcoal was lit.

Get the Superior Trading Co. fire starters at Amazon or Superior Trading Co.

Forget about newspapers and kindling—we were able to get a real wood fire going using just one small Lightning Nugget. It took three matches to light the nugget, but once lit, it burned brightly with a hot flame about 6 inches high for a little more than 10 minutes.

The nuggets are made from a blended composition of all-natural, recycled, and nontoxic flammable materials, including pitchwood sawdust and paraffin wax. Pitchwood is a type of pine that contains natural resins that are flammable.

When burned, these nuggets give off a slight pinewood scent, making them suitable for fireplaces and campfires. We were hoping for more of an aroma, but it was pretty weak. Each box comes with 50 nuggets, and since it takes just one nugget to light most fires, one box goes a long way. They’re not suitable for use in grills, however, since they are scented.

Get the Lightning Nuggets fire starters at Amazon, Ace Hardware, or Tractor Supply Co.

Buyers don’t have to spend a lot to get quality fire starters. With 24 fire starter squares in a box, this option from Rutland is one of the more affordable fire-starting options.

We placed a couple of Rutland fire starter squares beneath logs in our fireplace. They lit quickly—within 1 or 2 seconds of touching them with a lit match. The flames rapidly engulfed the squares and continued burning for about 8 minutes, which was more than enough time to ignite the logs in the fireplace.

The fire starter squares are made from recycled wood chips, paper fiber, and wax. Although the manufacturer claims they’ll light when wet, we couldn’t get them to light after we dropped them in a glass of water and then took them out. After about 15 minutes, however, they were dry enough to light.

These are nontoxic fire starters, and we couldn’t detect any odor as they burned, making them suitable for starting charcoal fires for grilling food. It took two Rutland squares to get the charcoal in our grill started; the first one burned out before the charcoal caught, so we slipped a second one under the charcoal basket and lit it. The briquettes caught fire a few minutes after that.

Get the Rutland fire starters at Tractor Supply Co.

Nature offers excellent fire starters, but gathering traditional materials such as birch bark, tinder fungus, or cattail fluff is not always practical. One of the best natural fire starters, fatwood, comes from naturally resin-saturated pinewood. These fatwood fire starter sticks from Better Wood Products catch fire quickly, even when wet, and burn longer and hotter than factory-made fire starters. Our 10-pound bundle of fatwood contained 160 sticks, each measuring 8.25 inches long and about .5 inches in diameter.

After submerging two sticks in a bucket of water for 5 minutes, we pulled them out, shook off the water, and held a lit match against them. Within 5 seconds, both sticks were ablaze like giant matchsticks. They appeared to burn more intensely than typical wood shavings or compressed fiber and wax fire starters. Compared with those, these fatwood starters produced a larger flame with more heat—enough that we could feel it from 3 feet away. We were also impressed by the 14-minute burn time, but the downside was an excessive amount of smoke and pungent pine aroma.

Possibly the most intriguing quality of a fatwood fire starter is its versatility. The seller recommends lighting two sticks at a time with a match as an easy way to get a fire going with dry, seasoned firewood. We experimented with smaller amounts and managed to start one with just half a stick. Another time, we made a nest of fine fatwood shavings and lit it with sparks off of the ferro rod. However you light it, this stuff just works.

Get the Better Wood Products fire starters at Amazon.

Getting back to basics by creating a fire with friction no longer means using flint and steel; today’s outdoors enthusiasts trust ferrocerium alloy to supply the sparks. In skilled hands, a quality ferro rod and some dry tinder are all it takes to build up a roaring fire in no time. We preferred the Exotac FireRod XL over competing models, not least because of the massive shower of sparks it produced. We also appreciated its precision-machined aluminum handle with a watertight tinder chamber and the fact that the rod can be unthreaded from the body and replaced with a new one if needed. It did not come with a striker, but the spine of a fixed blade or lock-back folding knife served that role perfectly.

Before the ferro rod could make sparks, we had to scrape away some of the black surface coating. We then dropped it in the water bucket to find out if the tinder chamber was truly watertight. It was. Next, we dried our hands, opened the tinder chamber, and pulled out one of the three included cotton fiber tinder pieces. We loosened the fibers and placed the tinder in a bundle of dry pine needles shaped like a bird’s nest. The very first strike sparked into the tinder and ignited it, which then lit the pine needle nest. We built the fire up with kindling from there.

We’ve tried smaller ferro rods, such as spring-loaded UST BlastMatch, but the FireRod XL’s large rod and chunky handle made it easier to use with gloves, and it produced a larger spark shower to light the tinder. Three of the six fires we started with the FireRod XL only required a single strike. We also appreciated the built-in waterproof tinder chamber inside the handle, as this allowed it to serve as a complete fire-making kit at all times. On the downside, the precision-machined aluminum handle seems to be a costly addition, as the price was multiple times more than that of a similarly sized drilled ferro rod on a lanyard.

Get the Exotac fire starter at Amazon, Target, or Exotac.

These all-natural fire starters blend recycled pine “wood wool” (which is a fancy way of saying slivers of wood cut from logs) and stearin wax (a wax made from plant and animal materials) with no added chemicals. That makes GreenSpark’s fire starters a clean and eco-friendly way to get a fire going. We tested them to start a campfire and to create a traditional log fire in the fireplace.

To get the campfire going, we placed three GreenSpark fire starter squares on top of some small logs and lit them with a lighter. It took 3 or 4 seconds for the starters to catch. Once they were burning well, we added some small pieces of kindling and more logs. The GreenSpark squares sent up flames about 6 inches high and burned for around 8 to 9 minutes. That was plenty of time to ignite the larger logs we put on the fire.

The test in the fireplace had similar results, and we enjoyed a roaring fire there. These fire starters are billed as waterproof, so we dropped them in a glass of water and then retrieved them. We couldn’t light them immediately after we took them out of the water, but as soon as the moisture on the surface dissipated—which took about 10 minutes—we were able to light them again.

They contain all-natural ingredients, so the GreenSpark squares are also suitable for use in grills for cooking food.

Get the GreenSpark fire starters at Amazon.

Nothing lifts the mood in camp faster than a roaring campfire. Black Beard’s fire starter “ropes” are ideal for fire pits because they can be stored indefinitely, are completely weatherproof, and offer enough burn time to coax even wet firewood ablaze.

We tested a three-pack of “ropes” (which is how these come packaged) using several methods, and while a lighter and matches were the most straightforward approach, we also had success using the ferro rod. For our timed test, we cut a 1-inch section from one rope, lit an end, and stood it up like a little candle. It burned strong for 11 minutes.

Next, we cut another piece of the same size, dunked it in a bucket of water for a minute, shook it off, and lodged it beneath a mix of damp, seasoned kindling and greenwood logs that had recently been cut. Success. The residual water sizzled on the fire starter for a few moments as it began to burn. Within 5 minutes the kindling directly above the fire starter had dried and begun to catch fire. After 10 minutes, the kindling was well lit, the greenwood logs were beginning to char and smoke, and we had enough of a fire to build on.

The resulting fire was very smoky—not because of the Black Beard fire starter, but rather because of the uncured firewood. We performed this experiment to find out if the fire starter produced adequate heat long enough to actually dry out damp wood in the bottom of a damp fire pit, and it did.

Get the Black Beard fire starters at Amazon or Walmart.

When charcoal chimneys first became popular, newspapers were much more widely read—and sometimes, burned. Those who get their news online and don’t want to start the barbecue with a trash fire will be glad to learn about these quick-light fire starters from Kingsford. These simple bundles of wood shavings and paraffin wax light easily, burn for a long time, and won’t pollute food fires with questionable chemicals.

When it comes to grilling, Kingsford has been a household name for a long time, so we weren’t surprised that its hardwood fire starters ended up being one of the top performers. The average burn time with these was an impressive 13 minutes. Even after we dunked them in water, they lit within seconds and burned hot once ignited. We only needed one fire starter to get the fire going in our charcoal chimney, but some folks who are less patient may prefer to use two or three.

With an average cost of about $0.31 per fire starter ($9.99 for a pack of 32), this was one of the most affordable options. The only complaint we had was that the packaging fell apart in transit while the fire starters were being shipped to us, so we had to store them in our own plastic zipper bag.

Get the Kingsford fire starters at Amazon.

When it comes to fire starters for camping, ease of use, weather resistance, and burn time are critical factors. Compact packaging is also important. UCO’s Sweetfire fire starters combine the easy strike-starting of a match with the burn time of a waxed fiber fire starter. They come in boxes of 20.

Using this fire starter was just like using a match. We slid open the box, tore off one of the fire starters, and struck it on the side of the box. The “match head” was about four times the size of a conventional match, so it provided more than enough of a flame to get started. The individual fire starters measure 1 inch wide at the base, 2 inches from base to tip, and .5 inches thick—relatively small compared to the competition.

The burn time was pretty good at just under 10 minutes. That was more than enough time to start a fire under ideal conditions, and it worked fine in damp, drizzly conditions as well. It also performed well in our dunk test, starting on the first strike after a 5-second submersion. However, we suspect that the box with the built-in strikers could be a weak link if it absorbs too much moisture. This is a great choice for camp, but be sure to pack them in a zipper bag just in case.

Get the UCO fire starters at Amazon or Public Lands.

When the unexpected happens, a little preparation can make the difference between a rough day and an absolute disaster. Pull Start Fire was designed to start and burn for 30 minutes in all kinds of weather, and it can be lit without matches, lighters, or other devices. Just unwrap it, remove a tab, anchor it to a log, and pull a string. We’ve tried it, and it really was that simple.

This was by far the most expensive fire starter we tested on a per-fire basis. But it was also the easiest to operate in difficult conditions, such as one-handed, with hands in gloves, in high winds and rain, and so on. Each Pull Start Fire was sealed individually and, according to the manufacturer, has an indefinite shelf life. We held it underwater for 60 seconds and the cellophane wrapper didn’t leak. Then we opened the wrapper and followed the directions to start the fire.

This fire starter burns aggressively at first, like a roadside emergency flare, until the materials inside the inner packaging catch fire. In our test, it burned for 32 minutes with no additional fuel. On the second try, we placed it beneath a pile of moist but moderately cured 3-inch-thick firewood logs with no kindling. As the Pull Start Fire burned, it dried the wood directly above it. Within 10 minutes some of the damp logs began to burn, and after 20 minutes they were well engulfed. Bottom line, if we were the character in Jack London’s story To Build a Fire, we would rather have a couple of Pull Start Fires than a pack of matches.

Get the Pull Start Fire fire starters at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Lehman’s.

The fire starters that earned a spot in our lineup are all relatively inexpensive, and most are made from natural ingredients. For those who want something that not only ignites and burns reliably but looks good, too, consider making pine cone fire starters.

Making pine cone starters is fairly simple. It requires melting beeswax in the top of a double boiler and then dipping the cones two or three times until they have a nice wax layer. For fun, try rolling them in Epsom salt after the final dip while they’re still warm to lend them a frosty look. For scented pine cone fire starters, add natural essential oils to the melted wax, such as pine or cinnamon.

We considered a variety of factors when deciding which fire starters to test. We selected starters that would burn long enough to ignite wood or charcoal without needing to add other burnable materials, such as wadded-up paper or cardboard. A fire starter should also be easy to use, so we chose options that light easily with a match or lighter—with the exception of the ferro rods we tested, which function a bit differently.

During our testing, we followed the manufacturers’ instructions, placing one or two fire starters as suggested and using them to start the recommended fire types. For many of the tests, we used a traditional fireplace, but we also used a fire pit, a chiminea, and a wood-burning stove if the directions recommended using the fire starters with those appliances. We also tested a few fire starters to see how well they worked for lighting charcoal—but only if they were listed as safe to use for grilling food.

If a fire starter was advertised as waterproof, we dropped it in a glass of water and then attempted to light it. We determined that many waterproof fire starters aren’t genuinely waterproof but rather water-resistant. In other words, they needed a little time to dry out before lighting.

We timed how long it took for a fire starter to catch fire from a match or lighter, how tall its flames were, and how long it burned before extinguishing. We discovered a fire starter needed to remain lit for 5 to 9 minutes, at minimum, to fully ignite the rest of the wood and logs in a fireplace.

The only fire starter we tested differently was the ferro rod, which is intended to ignite finely textured, highly flammable tinder via sparks. We tested it on cotton-fiber tinder that was included with the rod, and then we built up the fire with progressively larger twigs and kindling.

During the testing phase, we awarded points based on how well each fire starter performed the tasks. After testing, we added and averaged the scores and compared packaging, prices, dimensions, and other factors to categorize the products for different applications.

Aside from considering the various types of fire starters, there are other features that shoppers will want to consider, such as ease of use and convenience. While any fire starter will make starting a fire easier than using tinder, not all fire starters are suitable for all types of fires.

In general, fire starters fall into two camps: flame/spark producers or accelerants. Shoppers already know about lighters and matches, but they might not be familiar with other types of flame/spark producers, such as ferro rods.

Accelerants are usually what buyers are usually looking for when shopping for fire starters, and these products are used in conjunction with typical fire-building materials, such as seasoned logs. An accelerant fire starter is placed beneath the other materials and then ignited with a match, lighter, ferro rod, or other flame/spark producers. Here’s the rundown on all of them.

A lighter consists of a metal or plastic container filled with a flammable liquid or compressed gas. A lighter lights by simultaneously creating a spark with the flint wheel while releasing a controlled amount of the fuel with a button. Unlike other methods, a lighter creates an actual flame, making it significantly easier to start a fire.

Matches are the tried-and-true method of starting a fire. Like a lighter, a match creates an actual flame rather than a spark, making it an easier way to start a fire. However, many matches are susceptible to water damage.

A ferro rod is a pencil-shaped piece of ferrocerium alloy. When a steel or carbide striker is scraped or struck against the rod, tiny shavings of ferrocerium oxidize and ignite as a result of the friction, burning at a high temperature of more than 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit.

Flint and steel consist of a steel striker and a piece of natural flint. When the two are struck together, they produce heated pieces of steel in the form of sparks that ignite a piece of cloth or tinder, starting the fire.

A magnesium fire starter typically consists of a small block of soft magnesium with a ferro rod embedded into one edge. The magnesium, which burns at an intense 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit, is an accelerant that works with the tinder to quickly build a fire. With a knife or the striker that came with the kit, scrape a quarter-size pile of magnesium into the tinder pile, then use the embedded ferro rod and striker to light the tinder. This will ignite the magnesium fragments, which will help set fire to twigs and kindling.

Accelerants are the most popular fire-starter products, and we tested a number of these. Nuggets and squares consisting of flammable oils, wax, and recycled paper and wood are the easiest to use; however, they require a flame ignition source, such as a match or a lighter. Once lit, these fire starters typically create tall, hot flames that light the materials above them.

As handy as fire starters may be, their usefulness is, to a degree, dependent on their convenience. Look for fire starters that are lightweight and compact, ranging from 1 to 6 inches in length. Typically sold in cases of 12 or 24, these pocket-size pouches, pods, or cubes can be stored in plain sight or easily tucked out of sight. Small, lightweight, neatly packed products are also more portable.

Most fire starters consist of wax, oil, and dense recycled wood, which holds up well in wet weather. Some fire starters are waterproof—drop a ferro rod in water, for example, and it won’t be affected. Just dry it off and it will still throw a spark that can ignite dry material. Fire starters also tend to burn at high temperatures of 800 degrees Fahrenheit or more, which allows them to better withstand windy and damp conditions.

Fire starters are meant to simplify the sometimes painstaking process of starting a fire by providing a persistent flame that can ignite nearby kindling. To do so, the fire starter must burn long enough to establish the fire. The longer the burn time, the more likely users can achieve a robust blaze. Our tests determined that most burn for an average of 3 to 15 minutes.

Earlier types of fire starters were typically infused with flammable compounds, which gave them a chemical smell. But the best fire starters in this day and age are nearly odorless. Many people appreciate the less noxious types of fire starters. However, fire starters that contain natural essential oils can lend a pleasing scent to the product that enhances the user’s experience without being toxic.

The best fire starters tend to be made of environmentally friendly materials, be it wood waste (sawdust or shavings), natural nontoxic wax, recycled paper, or waste textile fibers. Using fire starters typically results in faster and more complete ignition, which reduces airborne soot and smoke. Don’t miss our DIY fire-starter option above to find out how to make eco-friendly fire-starting accelerants from pine cones and beeswax.

A key to using a fire starter effectively is understanding how to arrange logs and kindling for the fire. Ahead, learn about how to build a fire correctly and use a fire starter to light it quickly.

To use a fire starter, begin by setting up your wood. If building a wood fire, you’ll need some kindling, which will ignite more quickly than full-size logs. Place the fire starter under the kindling or charcoal, leaving room so that you can reach the fire starter with a match or lighter. Light the fire starter and wait as it begins to burn and ignite the kindling.

To start a fire in a fire pit, gather wood, kindling, and a fire starter. Stack small pieces of kindling on top of one another, about four layers high, until you’ve formed a shape resembling a log cabin. Place the fire starter in the middle of your log cabin, pile kindling loosely in the middle, and then light the fire starter.

Begin by placing a layer of kindling and two or three small pieces of firewood on the fireplace grate, then place your fire starter in the space beneath the grate. Lighting the fire starter will ignite the kindling above it, which will, in turn, ignite the logs. Add larger logs as needed to keep the fire burning.

Fire starters are made up of materials that include recycled wood fibers, paper, oil, and wax that do not expire; hence, most fire starters do not have a shelf life. They may be attractive to insects, rodents, or other pests, so it is best to store them in airtight containers. Also, since heat may degrade the waxes and oils that are often used in these products, be sure to store them away from excessive heat.

Glenda Taylor is a product tester and writer specializing in the construction, remodeling, and real estate industries. She and her husband own a general contracting company, and Taylor is experienced in both residential and commercial building applications. She tests a wide range of power tools as well as other home improvement, household, and lawn-and-garden products.
