There is no easier way to make new plants for free than by taking hardwood cuttings from deciduous shrubs in late fall. Try it yourself and see!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November doesn't have to mean the end of the gardening season, as late fall is the perfect time to multiply your backyard shrubs for free. Taking hardwood cuttings sounds complicated but it’s as simple as poking sticks into pots of soil and waiting for them to grow. Yes, really! November is the very best time for this propagation method as stems of deciduous shrubs are full of stored energy ready to go into winter so you'll get great results, even if you're a beginner gardener or it's your first time trying.

Many of our favorite garden shrubs can be multiplied by taking cuttings in late fall, from roses to butterfly bush, dogwood to mock orange, so add this enjoyable task to your fall gardening checklist. Whether you’ve got a new garden to fill on a budget or you’re planting up a fresh area, or you want to propagate some plants to sell at a yard sale next year, you'll get free shrubs without spending a dime at the garden center. Or perhaps you’ve been eyeing up a pretty shrub in a friend’s garden and want it growing in your yard, too!

Clone these deciduous shrubs now and they’ll root over winter, ready to be planted in spring. Ready to have a go? Here’s exactly how to take hardwood cuttings, step by step.

Timing is everything when you propagate plants, and late fall is peak time for growing free shrubs from hardwood cuttings. In November, deciduous shrubs will be about to enter dormancy so they’ll have stored up plenty of energy in their stems and the bare outer bark is tough and weather-resistant. To catch the optimum moment, wait until your shrub has just dropped its leaves or, in a mild autumn, lost a good three quarters of its foliage.

Look for stems that grew this year, as these are going to be far keener to throw out fresh roots than older growth. Choose stems from the outer, sunniest side of the shrub, too, as these will have stored more energy. Stems that are about the width of a standard pencil are ideal, and remember these are hardwood cuttings: you need stems that are mature enough to snap rather than softly bend if you tried to fold them in half.

You’re going to need straight-ish stem sections, and cut plenty as not even expert gardeners get a 100% success rate from hardwood cuttings.

Make the base cut just below a bud or leaf node, straight across the stem. Make this cut close to the node – ⅛ inch below is perfect – as there's a high concentration of rooting cells and hormones in the stem here. Make the top cut about ¼ inch above a bud or leaf node, at a 45° angle. This little bit of extra room allows the stem to heal over without damaging the node. Ideally, you want 2-3 nodes in between the top and bottom nodes (so 5 in total). For most shrubs, that means your stem sections will be 6-12 inches long.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

While the top cut is angled to encourage rain to run off rather than pool on the step tip, the base cut is horizontal simply so it’s easy to tell which end of your cutting is which. Use your pruners to trim off any remaining foliage (don’t tear leaves off as this can damage the stem).

Rooting your cuttings in deep containers rather than the ground makes it easy to provide the sharp drainage and shelter needed for stems to root rather than rot. You can either use one pot per cutting or put multiple cuttings into a bigger container.

Use an all-purpose potting soil without any added fertilizer or synthetic moisture retainers such as Organic Mechanics Premium Blend Potting Soil, available from Amazon, and mix in a similar volume of horticultural grit, sand or perlite such as this from Walmart to open up that soil some more.

Water the mix and leave the pots to sit for 15 minutes to drain.

Use a stick or pencil to poke holes into the potting mix, making them deep enough to swallow two-thirds of the stem length. If you're using a larger container to hold multiple cuttings, space the holes about 2 inches apart. Then pop the stems, base cut downwards, into the holes and use your fingers to gently close the soil around them. There’s no need to water.

Some shrubs have a high-enough concentration of natural auxins – the hormones that foster rooting – that they'll root just fine, all by themselves. Twig dogwood, forsythia, butterfly bush and spirea all fall into this category. Some shrubs need a little help, however. Roses are still reliable rooters, but encouraging them with a rooting powder that stimulates their natural hormones brings a higher success rate. Simply dip the base of the stem into a rooting hormone like Garden Safe Take Root, available from Amazon, and tap off any excess before popping it into the hole.

A few, like mock orange and viburnum, need an even bigger nudge, and that’s easy to deliver by slicing off a narrow inch-long strip of bark at the stem's base before dipping it into the rooting powder, and popping it into the hole. This ‘scoring’ cuts through the tough outer bark to expose the green cambium layer beneath, which is where the cells that will become roots are concentrated. Scoring also triggers auxins to be sent straight to the damaged area.

Stand your pots of cuttings in a sheltered spot where they’re shielded from the worst of the winter rain and cold. Position them up against a south-facing wall of your house and they’ll be protected from cold northerly winds and benefit from the heat escaping your home. An unheated greenhouse, conservatory or sunroom is another good option, as is a bright porch. You could also cover your cuttings with lightweight horticultural fleece such as this AgFabric Plant Blanket from The Home Depot to keep them cozy, pushing canes around the pot so the fabric doesn’t sit directly on the stems.

The stems will use very little water so only irrigate occasionally when the top inch or two of the soil is dry, which will only be once a month or so. By spring, you’ll see fresh green leaves on the cuttings that have rooted. If you're growing multiple cuttings in one big pot, move them into their own container at this point.

Shrub dogwoods or twig dogwoods are super-easy to propagate from hardwood cuttings in late fall, and grow fast for quick results. Why not raise enough to create a wildlife-friendly hedge with a flurry of fragrant spring-summer flowers followed by fall berries? Or create a vibrant display of winter stems for you to enjoy? Cornus has a high concentration of natural rooting compounds so you’ll enjoy a near 100% success rate from hardwood cuttings.

This bulletproof shrub is one of the earliest to bloom in spring, bursting into a cheery show of bright yellow flowers in March. Once mature, Forsythia is drought-tolerant, cold-hardy and incredibly low maintenance, and even copes with urban pollution, making it a welcome gift for beginner gardeners or new home owners. Forsythia's easy-going nature also makes this one of the easiest shrubs to propagate from hardwood cuttings.

Buddleia earned its common name for good reason, putting on a bountiful summer buffet for pollinators from July to October. Butterfly bush is an enthusiastic, fast grower so it’s a useful shrub to quickly make a new garden look more mature, or fill an empty yard corner. Do check that the Buddleia you’re taking cuttings from is a newer, non-invasive butterfly bush variety first though. There is no easier shrub to take hardwood cuttings from as this is a plant that’s naturally programmed to grow, grow, grow!

Spirea is a low-maintenance must-have, bringing fabulous flowers and fall foliage colors in a size to suit every garden. This deciduous shrub responds really well to clipping so you can use it to create a stylish low hedge for free by taking November cuttings. Spirea is a foolproof shrub to start with if you're propagating this way for the first time.

You can never have too many roses in a garden and these shrubs are expensive to buy, so propagating from cuttings will fill your yard with scented flowers for free. The ‘backyard rule’ means you can propagate even named, patented Rosa for your own use, but restrictions apply if you’re planning on selling the resulting plants. While your new rose plant will probably try to flower in its first summer, pinch off any flower buds to focus its energy on growing roots and stems.

Philadelphus brings an aromatic blend of jasmine and citrus to your garden from May to June, so adding a few more mock orange shrubs to your yard will boost its perfume as well as flower power. Mock orange shrubs have tough bark so carefully scrape an inch-long strip off both sides of the stem base and dip into rooting powder to stimulate root growth, and don't worry if cuttings take their time to show spring growth.

The viburnum family includes so many garden-worthy deciduous shrubs such as snowball bush (Viburnum opulus) and the Arrowwood viburnum (Viburnum dentatum) that are straightforward to propagate from hardwood cuttings. Viburnum go into deep winter dormancy however, so also need a boost to root. Score by removing an inch-long strip of bark from the base (one side is plenty) and dip into rooting powder to trigger the stem into action.

Clean cuts made with sharp pruner blades significantly increase your chances of success as crushing stems with blunt pruners damages the plant tissue and creates jagged surfaces where fungal spores can settle.

Wipe isopropyl alcohol over pruner blades to disinfect before cutting stems or scoring, to make sure you’re not transferring any fungal spores or bacteria that might cause rotting rather than rooting.

Winter stems can look identical so be sure to label those sticks clearly so you know what your plants are in spring. These hook-ring tags are useful if you’re rooting cuttings of different varieties in one big pot.

You see, you really are growing free plants by sticking stems into soil, so add this to your list of November gardening jobs. You can put a heap of cuttings into the same pot to propagate plenty of plants without spending a fortune on compost, too. Looking after hardwood cuttings takes minimal time over winter, and it’s so satisfying to spot bare stems bursting into leaf in spring. And just wait till you discover how much more you love a favorite plant when you’ve propagated it yourself!

If you want to propagate plants that are growing outside of your garden, do be aware of the legalities of taking plant cuttings from public spaces and get permission from the landowner.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

Recently spotted and noted: a fun, new iteration of Ravenhill Studio’s sheet-metal Peek lights. Turns out, their mastermind is a 9-year-old. Well, kind of.

We recently asked Marjory Garrison, who co-owns the L.A.-based lighting studio with her husband, Brendan Ravenhill, for the origin story behind the Peek Sconce Switch Colorblock collection:

“We’d worked on developing the Ravenhill Studio In Color palette for more than a year, and when we finally settled on colors, our son Ashley immediately wanted to mix and match parts into a colorblock fixture. Our design specialist Anya Gupta enthusiastically indulged him, helping him put together a Peek Sconce Switch in what he came to call ‘Color Explosion‘ (his version also has a color changing bulb),” she explains. “Luckily it’s a plug-in fixture, since Ashley hasn’t committed to where he wants it permanently.”

Here’s a peek at the newest members of the Peek Sconce Switch family.

#7908. The Real Reason Your Kitchen Smells (and What to Buy to Fix It)

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 27, 2026 2:26 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Your kitchen is supposed to be a place where you can gather to enjoy meals with family and friends. But if you walk into the room and are turned off by unpleasant smells, you may quickly lose your appetite. There are lots of reasons why your kitchen may be stinky. We spoke to a couple of cleaning experts to find out the most common sources of kitchen smells and how best to address them.

The sink itself is a common source of undesirable odors in the kitchen. “Many people regularly wipe down their countertops but neglect to clean the sink, which is constantly coated in food remains and liquids of all sorts,” says Ben Pullman, founder of Cubby Bear Cleaning in Chicago, Illinois. The best way to tackle this issue, says Pullman, is to simply clean the sink with some dish soap and a sponge after you’re done doing the dishes.

In addition, avoid throwing food scraps directly into the sink, recommends Arthuza Rabelo, a cleaning professional from Cleanzen Cleaning Services based in Boston, Massachusetts. “It’s better to use a sink strainer that catches small food particles and prevents them from going down the drain, as food scraps can accumulate in the pipes, cause blockages, and eventually produce unpleasant smells,” she says.

Finally, check the area under your sink as well, Rabelo adds. “Water damage in this area can cause a musty smell, similar to the odor of a damp cabinet floor,” she explains. If left unaddressed, it can also lead to mold or mildew growth and damage to the cabinet. “Make it a habit to inspect this area regularly so you can catch leaks early and prevent more serious damage, beyond just the unpleasant smell.” If you notice a leak, consult a professional as soon as possible.

Long-lasting, rust-proof stainless steel sink strainer with a double-layer design.

Although the trash can is one of the most obvious culprits of a smelly kitchen, there are steps to take to easily avoid this from happening. “The odor can come from the trash itself or the bin, which tends to get caked with residue over time,” says Pullman.

The best ways to combat this issue include taking your trash out more frequently, including as soon as it is full; replacing the garbage bag regularly; and cleaning the bin itself with a disinfecting wipe. Make sure to wipe down the inside of the bin as well as the lid, says Pullman. Also, avoid mixing biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste, as decomposing food can produce a strong odor that spreads throughout the kitchen, adds Rabelo.

Lysol Disinfecting Wipes are pre-moistened disposable wipes for cleaning, disinfecting, and sanitizing every surface in your home.

If there’s a new smell emanating from your kitchen, you’ll want to check all appliances to see if any of them are the cause. “Refrigerators, ovens, and other kitchen appliances are often sources of unpleasant smells,” notes Rabelo.

First, open the refrigerator to see if the stink is coming from inside. Expired, rotting food is often the cause of smells, says Pullman. “The best way to prevent it is to leave an open container of baking soda in the fridge at all times since it absorbs odors,” he adds. Aside from that, store food in sealed containers, regularly discard expired and old food, and wipe down the shelves and drawers of the fridge monthly, or even more frequently, with an all-purpose cleaner.

Next, check your microwave. “Especially if you’re heating up food without a cover, food tends to splatter in the microwave and even if it’s not a lot at once, over time it really builds up and starts to smell,” warns Pullman. “The best way to clean this is just using an all-purpose cleaner and a paper towel.”

Dishwashers can also pick up unwanted scents over time as a result of food particles getting trapped in the filter. After emptying the dishwasher, use a damp microfiber cloth to wipe off any debris on the floor and sides of the dishwasher’s interior. Next, fill a glass cup or bowl with about 1 cup of distilled white vinegar, and place it on the top rack of your dishwasher between the prongs used to separate glasses. Run the dishwasher through a single cycle on the hottest setting possible. Once the cycle is complete, leave the door open for about an hour to let the dishwasher air out completely.

Iberia Distilled White Vinegar has 5% acidity that can be used as a natural, eco-friendly cleanser for everyday tasks like wiping glass and counters.

The garbage disposal is another big one, as grinding food waste inevitably leaves the disposal smelling from time to time, says Pullman. Leftover food particles and soap residue often get stuck down in these areas or on the blades where bacteria can develop and produce a foul smell.

His favorite way to clean this is by cutting a lemon wedge, throwing it in the disposal, and grinding it up. “This works really well for most maintenance cleaning. If it requires more elbow grease, you can use some Bar Keeper’s Friend. Let it sit in there for 10 to 15 minutes, and then rinse and grind with hot water,” Pullman suggests. It’s a good idea to clean your garbage disposal on a weekly basis to prevent future stenches.

Concentrated powder cleanser that eliminates stubborn rust stains, cuts through grease, restores burnt pots and pans, and removes hard water deposits.

Grease and oil buildup from cooking can also start to smell. “When we cook, oil and sauces often splatter around the cooking area and gradually build up on nearby surfaces, especially the walls,” explains Rabelo. “Even if the smell isn’t too strong at first, this buildup can be one of the reasons your kitchen develops an unpleasant or unusual odor.”

He recommends making it a habit to wipe down the stove after each use, once it has cooled down. “Use a cloth with a little dishwashing liquid to clean the stove and surrounding areas, then wipe again with a damp cloth and finish with a dry one.” You can also prevent this from happening by using a splatter screen that has a carbon lining to absorb odors. Running your kitchen ventilation system will help manage the odor as well.

This gadget keeps stovetops and countertops clean when frying, while also controlling odor with its activated carbon filter.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

Back in 2010, the founders of Fantastic Frank sized up standard real estate broker fare and vowed to do things better. The approach paid off: the Stockholm-based firm has since gone global: it now has offices in, among other places, Berlin, Lisbon, Mexico City, and NYC. Masters at showing other people’s quarters, the company recently had to figure out a fresh guise for itself when it prepared to move into new headquarters in Stockholm. ASKA, an emerging Swedish firm led by architect Polina Sandström, was hired to transform a hodgepodge of spaces in a historic building into Fantastic Frank’s showcase. Wanting to preserve existing, characterful elements while unifying the office, Sandström made masterful use of the firm’s old office furniture, a tightly orchestrated materials palette, and, most notably, a beguiling shade of pistachio. #7906. 10 “Must Do” Home Projects for November

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Updated Oct 27, 2026 3:58 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

For many of us, November marks the beginning of a season filled with house guests, nonstop holiday cooking, and cozy nights indoors. It’s also the last chance for cold-region dwellers to finish last-minute outdoor maintenance and garden projects. Get ready for whatever this month brings by taking on these timely tasks.

Installing a programmable thermostat puts savings on automatic: It’s another task you won’t have to remember to do yourself. The U.S. Department of Energy estimates that homeowners can save about 10 percent on their heating costs by turning their thermostats down 7 to 10 degrees for eight hours a day. If you work outside the home, automatically setting your thermostat to a lower temperature while you’re gone should be a no-brainer. The Google Nest Learning Thermostat, the Best Overall pick in our tested guide to the best programmable thermostats, can be controlled via Alexa, Google Assistant, or the thermostat’s dial interface. Nest learns quickly when you’re home (and want the heat on) and when you’re away (and don’t), and builds an ideal winter thermostat schedule accordingly.

BobVila.com’s Amazon storefront is your one-stop shop for links to products we recommend in ideas articles, DIYs, and Buyer’s Guides.Find BobVila.com’s November Must-Dos Shopping List on Amazon.

If your home is on a septic system, this month is prime time to give it a little TLC. Dropping a septic tank treatment product into your toilet is an easy, effective DIY. We also like getting our septic tanks pumped in November, to ensure that there are no issues (remember that scene in Meet the Parents?) when we’re hosting company and our toilets are working overtime. In some areas, septic waste disposal fees increase on January 1, which gives you added incentive to take care of the task before the New Year.

Americans are getting ready to put their ovens and stovetops to work this month. Here’s an important reminder as you start your holiday prep: More cooking fires occur on Thanksgiving than on any other day of the year. Make sure you’re ready for whatever comes your way by keeping a fire extinguisher close at hand the kitchen, and letting the cooks know where it’s kept. Be sure to check the pressure of your current units, and replace old or damaged fire extinguishers.

The First Alert Kitchen5 weighs just under 1.5 pounds of dry chemical BC powder—typically enough to put out a small grease fire. Read the review.

There’s some debate over when to hang the Christmas lights, but many of us waste no time and flip the switch on Thanksgiving weekend. One of the best reasons to hang lights in November is that the (slightly) warmer weather makes this outside job easier to do. Whenever you choose to light up the yard, check all cords for fraying, and dispose of any damaged strings. Plug the lights into ground fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs) to reduce the risk of electrical fires, and turn them off before you go to sleep. We like the idea of hanging Govee’s outdoor strip lights, which you can leave up year-round and change the colors and patterns to suit different holidays. Our tested guide to the best Christmas lights has some other great choices, too.

When they are exposed to extreme temperatures, under- or non-insulated pipes, especially those that run along an exterior wall or an unheated garage, can freeze and cause major problems. To protect your pipes, first ensure that your walls are adequately insulated. You may also consider wrapping specialized heating cables or heating tape around water pipes that run along exterior walls. Heating tape can be plugged into an outlet, which will heat the water in your pipes to prevent freezing and bursting. Avoid installing heating tape inside walls, ceiling, or floors, where it can pose a fire hazard.

Gathering the family around the fireplace is one of the good things about cold weather. Before you strike a match, make sure you have plenty of firewood on hand for the season. Seasoned hardwood, like oak or ash, is generally the best wood for burning in the fireplace.

If you’ll be playing host to friends and family this season, now’s the time to get the guest bedroom in good shape. A fresh coat of paint or new bedding can make the space more inviting and won’t break the bank. Don’t have a spare bedroom? Alternative guest bed ideas, like cots, air mattresses, or pull-out sofas, can quickly turn any room into a bedroom.

Given the extra time you and your family will be spending in the kitchen through the end of the year, odds are higher that your countertops will see more spills, stains, and scratches than usual. The best ways to protect these surfaces depend on their composition: While materials like quartz and laminate only need regular cleaning with an all-purpose spray, countertops made of butcher block, marble, and granite should be sealed in order to resist stains (and warping, in the case of butcher block).

Once your countertops are protected, move on to cleaning your cutting boards: Plastic boards can be sanitized in the dishwasher; clean wood cutting boards with vinegar or, if stained, salt and half a lemon. Condition wood cutting boards with a food-safe mineral oil.

Your water heater is probably installed in an unheated environment, like a basement or a garage. Insulating your appliance is an absolute must to prevent it from losing heat. Choose an insulating water heater blanket that’s the right size for your tank, and follow the manufacturer’s instructions for installation. This quick task could save you 4 to 9 percent in water heating costs, and pay for itself in about a year.

Frost King’s water heater blanket is nonflammable, 3 inches thick, and provides an insulation value of R-10. Read the review.

Your kitchen will likely be getting a lot of use over the Thanksgiving holiday, which is why now is the time to minimize the risk of grease fires. Make sure to clean your stove drip pans and the stove top itself; go ahead and clean the oven, too, and whip up a nontoxic, fume-free mix of baking soda, water, and vinegar. Don’t use the self-clean function on your oven right before the big day: Self-cleaning puts strain on your appliance and could result in a maintenance call, or worse.

Why settle for decorations that only last a few weeks? Create beautiful seasonal containers that can brighten your entrance well into winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Holiday porch pots are a cheerful way to decorate your home's entrance for the festive season. These outdoor winter arrangements look beautiful and welcoming when placed near front doors, steps, or entryways to greet guests during the holidays.

As October ends, the holiday season approaches. Families make Thanksgiving plans, starting a season that lasts right through the new year. This is the ideal time to start putting together natural holiday decorations that bring bright colors and greenery to your home's entrance.

If you are ready to jump into a creative gardening project for winter, we’ve got the ideas to get you started. The basic idea is to combine beautiful plants and greenery to make spectacular seasonal containers. But you should plan to have some fun while you are doing it.

The best plants for DIY holiday porch pots combine appealing structure with festive cut boughs. They should be hardy enough to survive cold weather and add winter curb appeal.

Why not start with an evergreen that nobody else on your block is likely to display? This silver Korean fir cultivar is one of a kind: a curious, fascinating dwarf evergreen with twisted, curled silvery needles. The twisted needles of ‘Ice Breaker’ Korean fir (Abies koreana), available at Nature Hills, have frosted undersides, making it look as if it is perpetually snow-covered. These little beauties grow very slowly, getting to 2 feet tall after 10 years. They are hardy down to -20°F.

It’s easy to find evergreen foliage plants without red berries, but harder to find red berries without evergreen foliage. That’s exactly why winterberry holly (Ilex verticillata) in holiday porch pots is totally intriguing. You can order a best-selling Berry Poppins winterberry holly from Plant Addicts.

These native hollies – growing in eastern Canada through the southern United States – are pretty plants all year long, but they become stunningly beautiful at the dreariest time of the year. They lose their leaves in autumn, leaving only the amazing crop of bright berries to light up your winter pots. They are hardy down to USDA zone 3.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Ornamental cabbages and kales (Brassica oleracea) are cold-hardy foliage plants that provide exceptionally vivid white, pink, red, and purple winter colors for holiday pots. They are technically edible but are not grown for eating. Rather, they are cultivated for their bright, rose-like center rosettes.

Ornamental cabbage and kale plants maintain their bright structure and color well into freezing winter months. For a festive container, they can be combined with winter-hardy pansies, berried twigs, chrysanthemums, or ornamental grasses.

Pick up a four-pack of Song Bird Red Ornamental Kale Plants from Burpee.

You may know these stunning plants as hellebores (Helleborus niger), or as Christmas roses. Whatever you call them, they make fantastic additions to holiday porch pots, with their shining white flowers and strong, dark green leaves. The only issue with hellebores is that they usually don’t bloom until January – past the heart of the holiday porch pot season. But some cultivars bloom just in time for the holidays, such as ‘Christmas Carol Early’, 'Jacob', and 'Snowbells', available at Plant Delights Nursery. The Christmas rose is usually hardy to USDA zone 3.

This dense, naturally round shrub is a perfect little ball of soft green needles. Its small size and low-maintenance nature make Little Gem Norway spruce (Picea abies 'Little Gem') a popular addition to your holiday porch pot. You can order a plant from Magic Valley Gardens at Walmart.

Norway spruce grows slowly, adding only about an inch or two in size every year and topping out at about 3 feet tall and wide. Don’t worry about winter weather – ‘Little Gem’ is hardy down to -40°F. The new growth emerges soft and bright lime, but by Christmas it will be a handsome forest green.

The flowers that give Heuchera its common name of coral bells only appear in spring and summer. By the time the holiday season rolls around, you’ll appreciate this plant's incredible foliage. Coral bells offer a wide range of leaf colors beyond green, including apricot, bronze, pewter, burgundy, and deep purple. The foliage often adds even more enchantment with scalloped, wavy, or veined edges. Select ‘Caramel’ or ‘Peachberry Ice’ cultivars, both available at Plant Addicts, for foliage with rich tones and holiday warmth.

Many trailing “spiller” plants work well in holiday plant pots, but few are better than the classic evergreen trailing English ivy (Hedera helix), available in an ivy variety pack from Plant Addicts. This hardy vine softens the edges of holiday planters and offers all-weather resilience. It stays vibrant throughout the season and works well with flowers or small evergreen shrubs to create a festive feel. The cascading leaves create a rich, full look, balancing upright or mounding holiday plants.

If you’re ready to create gorgeous holiday plant pots of your own, a few practical tips will help. Let’s get down to the basics of how to put it all together.

The base of it all is the pots or containers you select. Choose pots in materials that can handle winter temperatures, like metal, wood, or even plastic. Avoid materials that will crack when the temperatures drop. Get pots that are big enough, but not too big. Generally, front door holiday plant pots should be between 12 and 30 inches in diameter and between 12 and 18 inches deep.

You’ll want to use potting soil in the containers. Leftover summer potting soil works just fine, but it’s best to buy fresh, like Miracle-Gro Organic Outdoor Potting Mix, from Amazon.

Next, you’ll want to put in the plants, and I suggest using a classic thriller, filler, spiller design. Start with the thrillers. These are the tall, eye-catching focal plants that make guests admire the pots. You can use one of the taller plants you have selected – like winterberry holly or ‘Ice Breaker’ fir – or you can use cut boughs after trimming the stems.

Get ready to layer in the fillers. This is the place for medium-height evergreens or foliage plants. Coral bells or ornamental cabbage work well in this role. Alternate textures and shades.

Last, add the spillers, plants with draping or trailing foliage. These go around the bottom edge of the container so that they cascade gracefully over the edges of the container.

Creating your plant pots is fun, but you’ll also have to put in a little effort to keep them going strong through the season.

This starts with care immediately after you set out the pots. Give each of them a deep watering, enough to saturate the entire soil. Excess water should run out of the drainage holes in the bottom of the pot. Make sure that’s the case, or your plants will die of root rot. It helps to add pot feet to elevate the containers off freezing patios.

Don’t worry too much about freezing weather. It is normal for the moisture in the patio pots to freeze. Keep checking the soil and add more water if the top inches are dry. Mist the evergreen branches during dry winter days to rehydrate the foliage. As the weather cools, cluster the containers close to the house wall to shield them from winter winds and create a microclimate.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

7 Kitchen Scraps You Should Save for Backyard Birds This Fall – Give Them a Helping Hand as Temperatures Drop

Squirrels Don’t Like These 3 Types of Bird Seed – Fill Your Feeders and Watch Songbirds Flock In

Do You Have America’s Most Bird-Friendly Backyard? Enter for a Chance to Win a Birdfy Smart Feeder

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Huddled in hedgerows and shedding trees this fall, your backyard birdies need your help. Here are the simple things you can do now to keep them healthy and happy through winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall can be deceptive: for a while, the lingering sunlight might be warm, and there might still be pops of color as late-season annuals stand in defiance. But all it takes is one big cold snap or a nibble of frost for the whole yard to change, literally overnight. The transition from late fall color to the reality of several months of winter can be a shock – and not just for us. As we huddle over morning hot drinks and contemplate the gaps in the yard, imagine how it feels for our feathered chums.

From plump northern cardinals to energetic black-capped chickadees, these shifting conditions present a challenge for bird feeding, shelter, and survival. Tree cover is starting to bleed away as fall leaves spiral to the ground, exposing branches to biting winds, cold rain, and sharp frosts. The juicy bugs of July are history, dogwood berries are being stripped, and crisping soils mean foraging birds have to work twice as hard for every meal. For birdies that only weigh a couple of nickels, getting through the night means burning nearly an entire day’s energy just to stay warm.

So for our pint-sized backyard companions, the big chill isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a fearsome calorie crunch. This narrow window in late fall is your best opportunity to step in with kind, targeted care. These little backyard wins won’t punish your wallet and they don’t demand much time. Just a little thoughtful prep today will keep your feathered neighbors safe, spunky, and singing outside your window all winter.

Preparing your backyard for happy wintering birds is all about timing. Whatever you do, don’t be tempted to put these little fall tasks off too long. I get it: in the whirl of leaf raking, perennial cutting, and hose winterizing, it’s easy to get distracted. But waiting until the first blizzard strikes and the ground freezes is a classic birdcare blunder, and one that tends to result in a yard devoid of birdsong.

Early winter is when resident birds establish foraging routes. By taking action now with these simple steps, you set up your yard as the place to stop mid-route – before the mercury plunges. Your USDA hardiness zone and regional climate have a part to play. In colder northern areas (zones 3-5), the risk of sudden hard freezes requires an earlier focus on high-density fats and ice-free water sources. Warmer zones 7-10 may host nomadic cedar waxwings and lingering eastern bluebirds as well as year-round residents. Yet they tend to share the same priorities: fast fuel, reliable drinks, and a cozy place to ride out a gale.

Before diving into these quick fall tasks, survey your yard. Observe how morning light strikes your patio, identify sheltered spots safe from north winds, and check that feeding and water stations are 10 feet (3m) from protective shrubs and safe staging or waiting branches for timid finches to peek out. Speaking of peeking, if you can’t afford a smart feeder, keep some compact binoculars or a monocular scope on hand to monitor visiting species and track which treats disappear first. The Pankoo 16x52 High Powered Monocular Telescope, available from Amazon, is a great way to enjoy shy songbirds on a budget.

Helping your birds thrive during winter starts now. These timely acts of care require minimal effort, and the payoff for getting your yard dialed in for the season is huge. By setting up your stations for winter, you’ll be rewarded with fluttery visitors even when the snow starts to fall. Here’s how easy it is to create a sanctuary for birds to fly in the face of the big chill…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As late fall chills settle in, backyard birds undergo a dietary pivot. During summer, they could thrive on lean insects and grains. But once night temperatures flirt with freezing, survival tilts towards fats. Burning fuel just to stay warm until breakfast is serious business. Now’s the time for you to swap out cheap summer filler seeds like red milo for lipid-rich options that deliver maximum energy per beakful.

This is the time to load your feeders with black-oil sunflower seeds. Their thin, papery shells are easily cracked by finches and chickadees, and their plump hearts are packed with plant oils. For ground-foraging juncos and sparrows, sprinkle hulled sunflower chips on low platforms so they don’t have to waste energy on dehulling. And hang some rendered suet cakes laced with berries or raw peanuts to nourish blue jays, red-bellied woodpeckers, downy woodpeckers, and nuthatches. C&S Peanut Suet Treat Cakes, available from Amazon, come in great-value packs.

Toss a handful of crunchy, dried mealworms onto a shallow tray to entice visiting eastern bluebirds and hermit thrushes to the party. Just make sure your feeder is able to support these extra nibbles, as well as allowing fall rains to drain freely. An open platform feeder, like the Kingsyard Hanging Platform Bird Feeder Tray from Amazon, can house a healthy fall feast in comfort while reducing the risk of mold.

Some of the simplest (and yet oddly, easily overlooked) fall birdcare measures involve your bird bath. Yes, topping up the seed hoppers and platform feeders is critical, but what’s worse is when the trusty bath is just left to freeze over. For birds, crunching on cold snow isn’t a fun winter pastime but an energy disaster. It drains their internal body heat precisely when they need every drop of warmth to survive.

It’s frustrating, because this is such an easy problem to avoid. At this time of year a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, from Amazon, can pay for itself in terms of bird visits. Alternatively, you can keep water in motion (and so reduce freezing) by adding a rubber duck or ping pong ball to your bird bath. Ensure that the water depth in the bird bath remains shallow, never exceeding a couple of inches (5cm), so that small visitors like American goldfinches and purple finches can drink safely.

Drop in a flat, textured stone so little feet have a non-slip surface. Finally, keep water supplies fresher for longer by adding a copper disc to your bird bath. The Mellbree Bird Bath Copper Cleaning Disc from Amazon is a brilliant way to prevent algae build-up between cleans. Easy!

Sitting on a bare branch in a sharp November breeze is an everyday winter reality for your garden birds, but it is one you can help them with. Backyards are losing their natural windbreaks as deciduous trees drop their leaves, exposing birdies to the elements and also nocturnal prowlers. But you can bolster the availability of natural cover and create layered roosting pockets before deep winter sets in.

Late fall is an ideal time for planting certain key containerized native shrubs, such as Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry, available from Nature Hills, which establishes quickly in late fall, providing dense roosting cover and juicy berries for over 40 bird species. American beautyberry is another excellent bird-friendly native that you can also plant now, as long as you can tuck them in a few weeks before the ground freezes. You can pick up containers of Green Promise Farms’ American Beautyberry Live Plants from Amazon which will establish relatively fast. Remember to mulch with a 3-inch (8cm) ring of shredded bark.

Leaving dense conifers and arborvitae unclipped provides dense inner chambers where northern cardinals, dark-eyed juncos, and mourning doves can huddle. It’s also helpful to stack any thick trimmings you might have accumulated from fall pruning in a quiet border. A loose brush pile is perfect for winter wrens and ground-dwelling sparrows. Finally, you can convert unused wooden nest boxes into roosting cabins by sealing ventilation holes, flipping the front panel so the entrance hole sits at the bottom to trap rising heat, and layering the base with pine shavings.

At this time of year, it only takes a couple of heavy showers or sharp gusts to knock our bird-feeding routines into disarray. Even with the best intentions, we might put off bird feeder or bird bath cleaning, promising we’ll do it at the weekend, only to wind up catching up on box sets in our pyjamas (no judgments). But leaving a greasy ring of wet kernels or hulls stuck to the bottom of a feeder is a recipe for disaster, creating a breeding ground for killers such as Salmonellosis and Aspergillosis. Left unchecked, these can spread through the feathered community in a matter of days.

Establishing a rigorous weekly cleaning rhythm is your best line of disease defense. This can be as simple as a quick Sunday scrub routine (these can be surprisingly therapeutic!). It helps to have feeders that are easy to dismantle and clean in the first place. A good bird feeder option for weekly cleaning is the Woodlink Seed Tube Bird Feeder from Home Depot, with removable base ports that detach in seconds.

Once you have disassembled your seed tubes, hopper troughs, and platform trays, discard damp or caked seed remnants. Scrub tight nooks with an extra-long bottle brush, like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon. Then soak the parts for 10-15 minutes. Using a ratio of nine parts to one, dip in warm water laced with distilled white vinegar. Rinse thoroughly and ensure every component is dry before refilling. Sweep away soggy fallen hulls while you’re at it, to help out ground-foragers like juncos and mourning doves.

In the fall yard, pristine neatness can often be the enemy of wildlife survival. Many of the forager’s final treasures of the season may be tucked beneath curling leaf fall or wedged in that forlorn dangling seed head. Stripping away key perennial skeletons and scooping up fallen foliage deprive backyard birds of vital natural gifts. Such backyard litter costs you nothing to leave, and they keep your birds stocked up in other sleeping nibbles, such as dormant spiders and protein-packed pupae.

So leave perennial seed heads standing, kick a mound of leaves under your hedges, and let nature do the catering. Place a low, wire-mesh ground tray nearby, filled with a sprinkling of sunflower chips and crunchy protein-rich mealworms such as Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart to reward their hard work. If you need a good ground tray feeder, the Mizxxidea Mesh Ground Bird Feeder from Amazon has an ultra-fine mesh base allowing fall rains to drain through cleanly. Blending handy extra feeding stations alongside natural foraging options creates the ideal birdie hangout.

These quick fall tasks are a lovely way of supporting your local birdlife as temperatures plummet, transforming your yard into a safe, high-energy refuge. While some of these fall extras are inexpensive, it’s worth investing in a few key features to help stay one step ahead of biting winds and winter chills. These curated staples will help you protect and nurture your resident songbirds from fall through winter.

Made of solid wood with a steep-pitched roof, this charming shelter offers visitors essential insulation against freezing drafts and rain. The side door makes cleaning simple, creating an ideal roosting cabin for chickadees, titmice, and wrens looking to huddle away from the worst of the winter weather.

This pretty jewel-toned basin is made from durable embossed glass and the textured presentation is kinder on birdie feet. It looks like high-end art, but is durable and rock-steady, although it's more likely to be filled with songbirds than hummers. Very easy to keep clean, and a real talking point for friends.

Crafted with vibrant stained-glass mosaic tiling, this fly-through feeder is great for shielding birds against winds and protecting seeds from drizzle. This pretty feeder's tunnel design also provides 360-degree visibility for skittish finches, chickadees, and nuthatches.

This timely fall intervention is all about making subtle, thoughtful shifts in our birdcare. By swapping in dense, high-calorie foods, maintaining easy-access water, supporting roosting options, cleaning feeders weekly, and leaving some fallen leaves around, you provide vital comfort and protection for vulnerable birds just when they need it most. It’s worth it to watch a puffed-up cardinal chewing on a mealworm, or a towhee poking out of some crunchy leaf litter, knowing that you’re doing your bit to keep nature’s sweetest living colors fluttering in and out of your yard.

She’s taken part in a range of conservation and rewilding projects for the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) and the British Trust for Conservation Volunteers (BTCV) as a way of exploring her horticultural horizons. #7901. Kathy’s Fall Garden

Happy Monday, GPOD! Halloween may be behind us but fall still has plenty to offer in Kathy’s zone 6a garden. I love how she keeps the seasonal decorating simple and lets what’s already happening in the landscape do most of the work. A few pumpkins, a refreshed container, and plants still hanging onto their color are enough to make the whole front garden feel ready for November.

Keeping it sweet and simple this fall! It has been a beautiful fall in Michigan so far. Although I’ve been gardening for more than 40 years, this is my eighth year gardening at our current home in Macomb.

I love these Japanese forest grasses (Hakonechloa macra cvs., Zones 5–9).

I replaced this summer container display earlier than usual, and these plants have been hanging tough since the first week of September.

Just sweet! There has been a multitude of fancy pumpkins for sale this year, more than usual, and I think they are so pretty!

Boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), Fire Chief arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis ‘Congabe’, Zones 5–8), ‘Orange Rocket’ Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii ‘Orange Rocket’, Zones 4–9), and Little Lime® panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘Jane’, Zones 3–8) grow in front of our home.

Already, I’m looking forward to spring when I can plant this new garden arch! I’m thinking clematis (Clematis cvs., Zones 3–9).

Here is Belleza Dark Pink gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri ‘KLEAU04263’, Zones 6–9) and yellow ‘Lady Stratheden’ avens (Geum ‘Lady Stratheden’, Zones 5–9). They are hanging tough so far!

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Kathy! I love the little bed by the driveway. The purple tones of the ajuga carpeting the ground against that bright orange mum and the pumpkins make for such an effortlessly beautiful fall display. And I’m with you on already thinking about spring—I’d love to see what you decide to grow over that new arch!

#7900. The Best Air Mattresses of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

By Glenda Taylor, Beth Cranston, Michelle Larson, Paul Rankin, Alexandra Mantella

Published Oct 28, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Air mattresses enable you to host guests when you don’t have extra beds and make roughing it a little less rough. You still want guests to be comfortable, and you don’t want a sharp object deflating your mattress on a camping trip. That’s why we tested several of the most popular air mattresses for 79 hours, eventually choosing the EnerPlex Air Mattress With Built-in Pump as the best overall option for most users.

From themed toddler beds to beds with headboards, we slept on just about every style we could. This lineup of the best air mattresses offers something for any occasion or use, and more importantly, includes options that provide comfort and durability.

Bottom line: Discover the best air mattresses of 2026, offering comfort, durability, and convenience for every need.

The best air mattress models are comfortable, reliable, and convenient. With a supportive air mattress, you can bring a good night’s sleep to any overnight event, from a camping trip to hosting weekend guests. Get some quality shut-eye with one of our favorite air mattresses.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Comfort 5/5; Durability 5/5; Deflation and Storage 5/5; Portability 4/5

EnerPlex offers flexible purchase options, with three thicknesses for all four of the standard mattress sizes. We tested the 18-inch queen model and couldn’t find much to dislike about it. The built-in pump was very simple to operate (plug it in, twist the knob, flip the switch), and it inflated fully in just 1 minute 30 seconds. Deflation was just as simple and took the same amount of time. We especially liked the large twist knobs, which let the air fly out of there quickly.

The EnerPlex includes a drawstring carry bag, but users may need to take a course in origami to learn how to fold the mattress for it to fit back into the bag properly. It’s certainly snug in there, and if not folded correctly, it’s nearly impossible to get it back inside.

There was little movement transfer when two people were on the bed—quite impressive for an air mattress. Most importantly, the 18-inch-thick mattress also provided a stable and comfortable night’s sleep, maintaining its firmness even overnight.

What our tester says: “Storage aside, once inflated, this bed was among the most comfortable that we tested. The plush quilted top and cushioned supporting coil beams made this feel more like a real mattress.”—Beth Cranston, Product Reviews tester and writer

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Comfort 4/5; Durability 5/5; Deflation and Storage 4.5/5; Portability 5/5

The Intex Durabeam Deluxe Comfort-Plush is a lightweight, fast-inflating air mattress that offers cozy, comfortable support in mere minutes at a great price. This durable bed is available in twin, full, and queen sizes and can support up to 300 pounds for the single bed, and up to 600 pounds for the full and queen. It includes a built-in pump as well as a valve for manual pumps if needed.

This mattress is a step up from the Plus series (see product 9) and in testing, we noticed the difference. While both of these Intex product lines offered incredibly easy setup and great inflation and deflation times, durability, and stability, the Deluxe line was noticeably more comfortable. It provided more cushioned support than the Plus series bed that we tested, and we found it easier to find that sweet spot than we did with the Plus series.

Like the Plus series, the Deluxe was simple to set up. With clear markings on the inflation dial, we barely glanced at the printed directions because it was all so intuitive. It also easily withstood our durability and stability tests, though it did move a bit more than the Plus model during our “leap tests.” It felt so durable, in fact, that we even walked on it a few times and dropped a 30-pound hand weight made of metal and hard plastic on it.

We couldn’t find much to dislike about this comfy air mattress except for the slightly small carry bag. We had to squeeze the Dura-Beam Deluxe in, but this is a minor quibble for such an overall great product at a very reasonable price.

Get the Intex Deluxe Comfort-Plush air mattress (various sizes) at Amazon, The Home Depot, Wayfair, or Intex.

Our Ratings: Setup 4/5; Comfort 4/5; Durability 4/5; Deflation and Storage 4/5; Portability 5/5

While the Coleman air mattress is only 8 inches high when fully inflated, its included portable cot raises the full height of the bed to just over 22 inches—keeping sleepers comfortably off the ground and making it easier for those with mobility issues to get in and out of bed. The mattress zips securely into an attached cover to create a barrier between the user and the plastic Airbed as well as prevent the mattress from sliding off the cot during sleep. The included pump makes for super-quick inflation and helps speed deflation for speedier campsite breakdowns—just remember to bring four D batteries for its operation before heading out into nature.

At 74 inches, this cot isn’t long enough for users over 6 feet, but its width of 40 inches and weight capacity of 300 pounds (twin) or 600 pounds (queen) can accommodate many. The frame and table collapse for easy portability and storage, and with the mattress, bag, and pump, the entire setup weighs just under 30 pounds. The carry bag has a reinforced molded base, which allows it to stand vertically without effort—a unique feature for bagged camping-type equipment.

In testing, we appreciated the useful attachable side table with a cup holder, which was big enough at 12 inches square to keep a water, headlamp, and phone within easy reach.

Get the Coleman Airbed air mattress (various sizes) at Amazon, The Home Depot, Walmart, or Coleman.

Our Ratings: Setup 4/5; Comfort 3/5; Durability 5/5; Deflation and Storage 4/5; Portability 4/5

This toddler travel bed comes in two pieces: an inflatable frame featuring tall, sloped safety bumpers on all four sides and a 3-inch-thick mattress that fits snugly inside. The inflatable bumpers aren’t just a safety feature—we found that they added to the comfort of the bed by functioning as a sort of headboard and footboard. Without a toddler on the testing team, one of our brave team members slept on this little mattress. She said that she “slept peacefully for almost the entire night.”

We think it’s a great option as a transition bed for kids 18 months or older even though it is slightly smaller than a traditional toddler bed. Toddler beds measure 51.63 inches long by 27.25 inches wide; this bed measures 49 inches long by 26 inches wide. Despite the slightly smaller size, this comfortable little bed is also great for any kind of sleepover, whether it’s for a weekend at the grandparents’ or for an extra bed in a hotel room. The lightweight bed weighs just 8 pounds and is easy to move when inflated (via an attached handle) or deflated (in its included bag).

Get the Hiccapop air mattress at Amazon or Hiccapop.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Comfort 4/5; Durability 5/5; Deflation and Storage 4/5; Portability 3/5

This queen-size air mattress from Intex is deluxe! It includes a built-in inflatable headboard that adds to its comfort and makes it feel more like a traditional bed. Its 18-inch height makes it easier to get in and out of while its 600-pound capacity enables it to accommodate a wide range of users. This Intex headboard air mattress features an adjustable knob that inflates and adjusts air pressure to desired firmness. The manufacturer lists inflation time as 5 minutes, but we doubled that and gave it a full 10 minutes to get the corners nice and full.

We really liked that the headboard made it feel more like a real bed and prevented that annoying gap that can appear between the air mattress and the wall. However, the solid 90-degree angle between the headboard and mattress felt a little stiff to sit up against without using a second pillow to soften the angle. Despite that minor inconvenience, we found that both the mattress’s ultra-plush top and headboard helped ensure a more restful sleep.

Get the Intex headboard air mattress at Walmart.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Comfort 4/5; Durability 5/5; Deflation and Storage 3/5; Portability 3/5

The Intex Dura-Beam Deluxe Pillow Rest Air Mattress offers a convenient extra bed with the added comfort of a built-in pillow. Available in twin and queen sizes, this mattress provides durability and comfort, made of PVC and Fiber-Tech materials with a flocked top to keep users comfortable and sheets in place. It also has all-around edge support to provide greater comfort and stability.

Like the other Intex mattresses on this list, we found it incredibly easy to set up. We unfolded the 16.5-inch-thick mattress, plugged in the built-in air pump, turned the pump’s dial to the Inflate setting, and the queen-size mattress fully inflated on its own in just 3.25 minutes, as advertised. Once it was inflated, we liked that the built-in pillow provided enough comfort that we did not need actual pillows. Overnight, we found this mattress to be extremely comfortable—it did not lose any of its shape and support.

Takedown and storage were also quite easy. We just turned the dial to deflate and watched the mattress compress in less than 5 minutes. Then we packed up the pump cord into the onboard cord storage compartment, folded it up, which was a bit of a challenge due to the thick material, and put it back in its bag. Thanks to its durability and portability, this Intex air mattress is a great temporary bed option for virtually any need.

Get the Intex Dura-Beam Plus Deluxe Pillow Rest air mattress (various sizes) at Amazon, The Home Depot, Walmart, or Intex.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Comfort 3/5; Durability 5/5; Deflation and Storage 5/5; Portability 5/5

The Intex Dura-Beam Plus packs a lot of great features into one air mattress. It boasts a built-in electric pump, a valve for a manual pump, a flocked top, a bottom ring for stability, and a raised pillow. It comes in twin and queen sizes, supporting up to 300 pounds and 600 pounds, respectively.

In testing, we appreciated the mattress’s easy setup, durability, stability, and portability, but overall it was just moderately comfortable. Setup took less than 3 minutes, with most of that for inflating our twin-size test model. The built-in pump is clearly labeled for fast, intuitive use, and the power cord fits neatly into a small compartment next to the inflation dial. Once inflated, it held onto its air and firmness, even after stretching for 8 hours, and then again after sleeping on it. This sturdy mattress also barely budged 2 inches when we took a few reserved leaps on it, and its surface easily bounced back even after having more than 205 pounds of hand weights on it.

For sleeping, we found it difficult to get to an ideal firmness; it was generally either too firm or not quite supportive enough. The sleeping surface was also disappointingly much shorter than the full length of the bed (75 inches) by about 7 inches; the bed’s bulges on either end account for the longer total length. However, we did really like the raised pillow.

Still, this durable air mattress is tough to beat and very easy to take just about anywhere, thanks to its light weight and less than 3-minute deflation time.

Get the Intex Dura-Beam Plus Pillow Rest (various sizes) at Amazon, Walmart, or Intex.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Comfort 4/5; Durability 4/5; Deflation and Storage 4/5; Portability 3/5

This comfortable mattress from King Koil (which also manufactures traditional mattresses) features an enhanced air coil system to maintain the mattress’s shape and firmness. It also has a few more added luxuries: edge support, a pillow top, a flocked top, and a built-in air pump.

As advertised, inflating and deflating this mattress took just around a minute and a half, approximately 1 minute and 35 seconds to inflate and nearly the same time to deflate (1 minute and 41 seconds). We also liked the mattress’s 5-foot power cord, which allowed us to place the mattress where we needed to more freely, rather than right next to an outlet. In overnight testing, this air mattress performed well, maintaining its air pressure while individual coils contoured and provided support to the hips, shoulders, and back.

While we liked this mattress overall, it did have a couple of drawbacks. Specifically, the edge support of the mattress did not have as much inflation as the coiled surface, which made it awkward to try to get off the mattress. Plus, the manufacturer states that the pump may temporarily stop working and generate heat if turned on for more than 5 minutes, after which users have to wait for it to cool down to use again. However, we can see why a pump that operates as quickly as this one does would also overheat quickly.

Overall, we found the King Koil to be a reliable, comfortable pick with great total-body support.

Get the King Koil air mattress at Amazon, Walmart, or King Koil.

To help guide our decision-making, we reached out to a spokesperson from the American Chiropractic Association for some insight into the best features to look for in an air mattress. Robert Hayden, a chiropractor who owns a practice in Griffin, Georgia, says a selection of firmness levels, as well as self-inflating options, are must-haves. “As you are selecting an air mattress according to your level of comfort, make sure you feel supported in your back, neck, and extremities.”

We kept this advice in mind before testing began, and we researched more than 20 products from eight brands. We scoured product features and user reviews to find the most comfortable, durable, portable, and easiest-to-use inflatable beds for testing. We also wanted to include a group of mattresses that served a variety of budgets, households, and uses. To do that, we looked at products with extra features, such as headboards, cots, and even fun-shaped mattresses for kids.

After extensive research, we landed on 10 beds for our five-person team to test. We assessed comfort, durability, portability, and overall ease of use over 10 days of testing. We inflated and deflated them several times, slept on them, jumped on them, and carried them around our homes. Then we scored each mattress on each of these considerations and awarded them based on their best uses and features. There isn’t a product on this list that we wouldn’t use again.

Whether you’re gearing up for a camping trip or prepping for a visit from the in-laws, an air mattress is a convenient item to have on hand. When choosing the best air mattress for your needs, consider its size, weight limit, materials, and comfort. Also decide if you want any extra comfort and ease-of-use features, like built-in pillows, self-inflating pumps, or “never-flat” options.

Air mattresses are available in common mattress sizes, from toddler to twin to California king. Shoppers will want to consider the best size for their intended use, the number and frequency of house guests, and their available storage space. A twin-size mattress may be suitable for a quick camping trip while a queen-size mattress may better suit a guest room.

Keep in mind, however, that the actual sleeping surface of an air mattress may vary from the dimensions of the air mattress. Air mattresses sometimes bulge out from the head, foot, and sides, creating longer, wider mattress dimensions, but that extra space is not actually usable for sleeping. Taller users and those who intend to share an air mattress may want to look for one that has sides nearly perpendicular to the top. In this type of design, the mattress dimensions and sleeping surface are nearly the same, so buyers don’t have to guess the size of the sleeping surface.

Mattress thickness is another important feature to consider. Air beds can range from thin 3-inch-thick pads for camping to thick 22-inch mattresses for a guest bedroom. A thinner mattress tends to be more portable, affordable, and quicker to inflate. Thick mattresses offer better cushioning and are easier to get up from, but they often come with a larger price tag and are bulkier and heavier to inflate and store.

Portability is an important feature to consider in an air mattress, especially for travel or outdoor use. Some air mattresses deflate to the size of a water bottle and fit into a small bag, making it simple to take on weekend trips and stow away when finished. Also, shoppers will want to consider weight and how much they’re willing to carry up and down a flight of stairs, on a camping trip, or elsewhere. Air mattresses can weigh anywhere between 5 and 50 pounds.

Even if portability isn’t a priority, packable options are generally more compact and easier to store. Plus, a designated storage bag protects the deflated mattress from coming in contact with any messy or sharp items while in storage.

Air mattresses are commonly made of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) or reinforced urethane plastic or rubber. These durable materials are made to be puncture-resistant to prevent damage from pokes and jabs. A puncture-resistant build is especially important for camping and outdoor use. For these activities, make sure to pick a camping air mattress and not an indoor model. Of course, puncture resistance does not guarantee that a rip or tear won’t happen. For that reason, many air mattress brands also include patches, so users can quickly repair the mattress and continue to sleep on it.

Beyond the mattress material, also consider the mattress surface, both on top and bottom. Flocked air mattresses have a soft, velvety finish on top. This textured surface is more comfortable when bed sheets aren’t close by, like while camping, and can also help keep the best bed sheets on when used at home. Nonslip bottoms can prevent the mattress from sliding around.

The best air mattress options are usually easy to inflate and deflate, although some will take a bit more work than others. Inflation methods include manual pumps, electric pumps, and self-inflating or “never-flat” pumps. An air mattress can include a built-in air pump or require an external pump.

Using a manual hand or foot pump takes the most time and effort, but these mattresses are often cost-friendly. They’re also an excellent choice for camping when users might not have a power source. Electric pumps can inflate a mattress in a matter of minutes but will need a power source, like batteries or an AC outlet.

A relatively recent innovation in air mattress design is automatic “smart” or “never-flat” pumps. These pump systems have sensors that monitor the air pressure inside the mattress. If the air pressure drops, the pump will adjust the air pressure as needed to maintain the mattress’s firmness. These smart pumps come at a higher cost but will help a mattress hold firm for a full night’s rest.

A saggy air mattress is uncomfortable at best and can cause back pain at worst. A supportive air mattress maintains an even firmness and does not wobble or sag with every move. A firm mattress top is even more important when sleeping with a partner. When shopping for larger mattresses for two, look for a model with minimal motion transfer.

Quality air mattresses often include features like strategically designed air chambers, vertical air coils, or a firm mattress top to maintain the mattress shape and offer back support. Check out both the inner and edge support. Active sleepers may prefer a mattress with a raised edge so they don’t roll off during the night.

Some air mattress models also include adjustable firmness levels to add to support and comfort. A pillow top or flocked mattress top can offer a soft surface to sleep on.

Hayden also has some expert advice for different sleeping positions on an air mattress. He suggests side sleeping with the use of a body pillow to help take weight off the spine and pelvis. “Adjust the air pressure so that you can sleep on your side comfortably without undue pressure on the shoulder, hip, and knees.”

An air mattress’s weight capacity varies widely depending on its size and design. Weight capacity can range from 200 to 700 pounds.

Since they’re built for one person, single mattresses tend to have a lower weight capacity at around 200 to 300 pounds. Larger mattresses intended for two people will have a higher weight capacity that’s more than 300 pounds. When choosing the ideal weight capacity, it’s best to leave a bit of wiggle room to guarantee that the mattress will offer full support without drooping.

A quality air mattress can include a range of features that add to comfort and ease of use. Extra features can include built-in headboards, USB ports, washable covers, and included sleeping cots.

With a quality air mattress, you’ll always have a comfortable extra bed at a moment’s notice. Since there are so many options, you may have a few lingering questions. Read on for answers to some of the most frequently asked questions about buying and using a new air mattress.

Air mattresses are generally best for short-term use. Most air mattresses won’t provide the consistent support and temperature regulation benefits of a traditional mattress.

While you shouldn’t use an air mattress every day for the reasons mentioned above, we found the EnerPlex air mattress to be extremely comfortable for an air mattress. Its plush, quilted top; cushioned supporting coil beams; and lack of motion transfer made it feel more like a real mattress.

The Coleman Airbed air mattress also makes a great camping option for those who prefer their mattress off the ground, both for comfort and to protect the mattress from damage from an uneven, unpredictable ground surface.

Air mattresses aren’t meant for everyday use, and daily use will cause extra wear and tear on an air mattress, increasing the risk of punctures or stretching. With proper care, a frequently used air mattress can still last a few years. With infrequent use, like the occasional overnight guest, a high-quality air mattress can last more than a decade.Over the course of his decades-long career, Bob Vila has helped millions of people build, renovate, repair, and live better each day—a tradition that continues today with expert yet accessible home advice. #7898. Sorry Squirrels, This Simple Trick Stops Pests Eating Tulip Bulbs (and it Beats Chicken Wire Every Time)

If you’re planting bulbs in your garden this fall, try this simple but super-effective hack to stop squirrels digging up tasty tulips and ruining the spring show.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Freshly planted spring-flowering bulbs provide an easy feast for hungry garden critters as temperatures drop, and are often eaten before they even get a chance to grow roots. Tulip bulbs are always the first to be sniffed out as they taste sweet and provide the perfect high-calorie meal for chipmunks as well as squirrels. Crocus bulbs, too, are carb-rich favorites on the garden menu in fall.

If you’ve experienced squirrels digging up tulip bulbs, you’ll know what determined diggers they are. Gardeners are just as dogged, however, and popular tricks to protect spring-flowering bulbs include laying steel mesh or chicken wire over the top, disguising the appealing scent of tulip and crocus bulbs by planting unappetising allium bulbs alongside, and using bulb baskets. But there’s a far easier, cheaper and more effective way to stop squirrels eating bulbs, and it helps the bulbs grow well, too.

What’s more, this robust solution protects bulbs from rodents and other underground burrowers like voles, who also love to seek out this nutrient-dense food source in fall.

When you're planting bulbs in fall, the magic ingredient to keep these energy balls safe from squirrels is poultry grit made from crushed oyster shells. The sharp, jagged edges of crushed oyster shells means it's painful for paws to dig through, so it provides an effective barrier that stops critters eating tulip bulbs and even tempting crocus.

What's more, as well as keeping bulbs safe from sharp teeth this natural material improves soil drainage, making bulbs less likely to rot through wet winter weather. Crushed oyster shells also break down very slowly to provide plants with a steady supply of calcium, which supports strong root and stem growth.

Not all chicken grit is created equal when it comes to protecting fall-planted bulbs, however. Make sure you buy chicken grit like Pacific Pearl Oyster Shell Calcium Supplement for Chickens, available from Walmart, that's made purely from oyster shells as many products are cut with cheaper materials like limestone. Choose crushed shells (sometimes sold as chick grit) over flaked shells as this is both sharper on paws and easier for plant roots and shoots to grow through.

When planting bulbs in pots, simply add an inch-thick layer of chicken grit to the soil surface to deter squirrels from digging, where it will also act as a mulch.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Opt for a double layer of poultry grit when planting bulbs in the ground. Add an inch-thick layer of crushed oyster shells to the bottom of the planting hole, and sit the bulbs right on top. This helps to protects bulbs from burrowing pests who typically attack from below, when a landslide of sharp oyster shells will send them scurrying away in search of more easily accessible food. If voles, field mice and pocket gophers are a particular problem in your garden, you can also pack a shallow layer of grit all around the bulb to fully encase it.

Fill the planting trench with soil as normal but add a second inch-thick layer of oyster shell grit an inch or two below the surface. When squirrels or other critters hit this sharp, gravelly layer, they’ll give up digging. This top layer can also help deter raccoons and skunks who don’t eat bulbs but are attracted to freshly-dug soil to look for insects and grubs.

Crushed oyster shells will naturally improve soil drainage and create beneficial pockets of air, loosening up heavy soil. The shells also release calcium as they break down, which plants need to build cell walls.

Adding a heap of oyster shells to your soil can affect its pH levels long-term but this hard material breaks down so slowly, that’s not a problem unless you have soil that’s already very alkaline. While some bulbs like camassia (wild hyacinths) prefer acidic soil, more palatable tulip and crocus bulbs both tolerate mildly alkaline soil just fine. Testing your soil with simple pH test strips like these from Amazon will instantly give you an answer if you suspect your soil is highly alkaline.

There are so many striking spring-flowering bulbs to plant in November, and using this clever trick will keep them safe from hungry animals in fall. Whether you view squirrels as garden pests or like to welcome wildlife into your garden, crushed oyster shells are a natural solution to prevent them digging up freshly planted bulbs in fall. Poultry grit is as economical as it is effective, too, so you get to enjoy those beautiful blooms come spring without spending a fortune.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.
