#7869. 14 Secret Storage Spots for Hiding Valuables in Your Home

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Updated Oct 28, 2026 11:22 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

According to the FBI’s Crime Data Explorer, 505,554 burglaries were reported in the U.S. between October 2025 and October 2026. Given the risk of theft, we often tuck our valuables—passports, jewelry, cash, important documents—in a bedside drawer, or maybe even in a small safe. But thieves know to rifle through drawers, and while safes afford some protection, they can be easy for burglars to spot, and it’s possible to break into them, whether they’re password-protected or key-operated. Knowing this, thieves may simply grab a safe and figure out later how to open it.

Outsmarting burglars by concealing your valuables in these unusual places might be the way to go to keep your things in your possession.

Keeping important items and documents secure inside a water- and fire-resistant safe is a good idea, but small home safes are primary targets for savvy thieves. Even worse, they are often portable enough to be picked up and carried off, which is a good argument for bolting a safe to the floor or a fixed shelf. To help protect valuables from thieves without sacrificing the fire resistance a home safe can provide, consider storing valuables inside the safe and concealing the safe itself inside empty luggage.

Certain valuables, like a physical will or a rainy day fund, may go untouched for weeks, months, or even years, so consider an out-of-the-way place to store these important possessions. One such spot is the space above the kitchen cabinets. In some kitchens, ½-inch gaps between the ceiling and the tops of upper cabinets, easily visible only from a ladder, offer a stealthy place.

First, fill a manila envelope with your valuables. Next, secure the envelope with a pair of broad binder clips to prevent it from sliding all the way into the gap, or fasten a string to the envelope for easy retrieval when necessary. Finally, slide the envelope into the gap.

Hiding valuables in a drawer isn’t likely to protect them against a determined thief. Instead, take advantage of the gap behind a drawer by using tape to secure an envelope filled with important documents, cash, or other valuables to the back of the drawer.

If the drawer pulls out too easily, threatening to expose the concealed envelope, attach the envelope to the underside of the counter, dresser, or bedside table so that even with the drawers fully removed the envelope will remain securely fastened to the furniture and out of sight.

Hanging picture frames, paintings, mirrors, and other wall decor throughout the house offer another opportunity to hide valuables. With a bit of tape and an envelope, any wall hanging can discreetly store important valuables.

While almost any framed wall hanging can help conceal items, a deep wooden frame offers a greater potential for subterfuge. If the frame is deep enough, you can neatly cut the paper backing and slide cash or prized possessions into the narrow gap between the artwork and the frame backing. Very thin items may even fit between a picture and the backing. To find the stashed valuables, would-be thieves would have to choose the right piece of artwork and remove the dust cover on the back of the frame—not easy to do quickly.

Creating secret storage spots out of common household items is a time-honored strategy. If you have a few shelves of books inside your home, consider hollowing a book out to make a small storage compartment inside the pages, making sure that the resulting “safe” looks unremarkable unless it’s removed from the shelf and opened.

An empty can is yet another easy secret storage spot, and one you can DIY. Using a smooth-edge can opener, open the can carefully so the top will fit neatly back into place. Empty the can out and clean it thoroughly. When it’s dry, fill it with valuables, replace the top, and return the can to a pantry or cabinet where it will blend in with the rest of your provisions. You can also purchase can safes festooned with realistic labels for corn, beets, tomatoes, and more.

The Jssmst book safe blends in easily on your bookshelf and is ideal for hiding small items like jewelry and passports. See our full review.

When burglars break into a home in search of valuables, they may not be able to take the time to tear through coats, sweaters, and other clothing hanging in the closet. Consider keeping an envelope of valuables in the pocket of an old jacket. You may want to switch the hiding spot when the seasons change, storing important possessions in winter clothing during the summer and summer clothing in the winter. If you have clothing with hidden pockets that can help conceal valuables, all the better.

Frozen pizzas, leftovers, and ice cream novelties keep many freezers tightly packed and conveniently crowded. One more container in the freezer probably won’t draw the attention of would-be thieves, making it a great place to stow cash and other valuables. Just make sure that both the container and the contents are freezer-safe to prevent damaging your important items.

As with an old book or an empty can, a tennis ball or soccer ball can be modified to create a secret storage spot. Tennis balls retain their shape after being cut, so they don’t look out of the ordinary with a slit halfway through the ball. As long as the opening is wide enough, it should be able to accommodate a roll of cash or small valuables like earrings or a ring.

For larger items, however, consider using a soccer ball. Just cut along one seam of the ball to create an opening that’s big enough to slide in your valuables. Cutting along the seam conceals the opening so the casual observer won’t be likely to notice anything odd about the ball.

A drop ceiling, a common feature in finished basements, laundry rooms, and utility rooms,  consists of panels or tiles that are supported by narrow metal frames. The hollow space above the panels can serve as a concealed storage location for lightweight items of value. Simply lift a panel to access the hollow space above and slide in a small packet, such as an envelope, a bag, or even a small box, to keep it out of sight.

This isn’t a spot for heavy items, which could break through the ceiling tile and fall to the ground below. Also, note which tile you’ve stashed the items behind so you can retrieve them easily later.

It isn’t a good idea to store valuable items in an actual air vent because you can block the flow of air into the home, reducing the efficiency of the heating and cooling system. Instead, consider installing a false air vent over an opening in the wall, specifically to store your valuables. Not many thieves are going to take the time to unscrew and check the air vents throughout the home.

Clocks are an excellent option for storing small, valuable items. Most mantel or wall clocks have open cavities in the back or base, where a few small items can be kept safe. If your clock doesn’t have an open cavity, simply tape valuables to the back of the clock and return it to the wall. As long as the clock itself isn’t worth stealing, your items should be safe in a break-in.

Another possibility is to store your valuables in a pillow or a couch cushion. Tuck flat valuables inside zippered cushion covers, and if your pillows don’t have zippers, just cut an opening in the back and stitch in a zipper (or even a hook-and-loop fastener). Take out some stuffing, insert the valuables, and close up the pillow. (Choose a pillow that is not frequently used, lest a visiting great-aunt stumble upon stacks of cash.)

Instead of throwing out your old canister-style vacuum cleaner when you upgrade to a new model, consider using it as a storage space for your valuables. After cleaning the inside of the canister thoroughly, hide your valuables inside. Store the old vacuum in the basement or closet along with your other cleaning supplies so it doesn’t attract attention or look out of place.

Any window seat or banquette that opens for storage offers a good place to cache your valuables, which you can toss in there with random blankets, board games, or tablecloths. If your window seat doesn’t open, consider transforming it into a storage bench—an accessible project for a handy homeowner. While you’re at it, try another clever DIY for stealthy storage: retrofitting drawers into existing stair treads.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them

From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

#7867. The Fall Yard Reset: What to Cut, Plant, Mulch, and Leave Alone

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 28, 2026 11:57 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As the crisp autumn air moves in and summer perennials begin to fade, transitioning your outdoor space with a thoughtful approach to fall landscaping is the secret to a healthy, vibrant yard next spring. Cooler temperatures might signal that it is time to wind down yard work, but this is actually a critical season for maintenance, offering the ideal conditions for root establishment and garden prep.

Knowing exactly what to do can feel overwhelming, since various plants require entirely different approaches. We spoke to several landscaping experts to find out what kind of care each type of plant needs during this time of year.

Pruning plants can encourage new growth and fruit or flower production, shape a plant, or thin it out for better light and air circulation. Fall is a good time to cut back some perennials that have finished flowering, such as daylilies, hostas, and peonies, especially once their foliage starts dying back, says James de Lacey, owner of Texas Tree Post in Austin, Texas. “You can also remove dead, damaged, or diseased branches from trees and shrubs.” After a damaging frost, homeowners can cut back ornamental grasses to make way for new spring growth as well, adds Judd Fitzgerald, sales manager at Richlawn Company in Platteville, Colorado.

However, de Lacy recommends avoiding heavy pruning of most woody plants in the fall, particularly spring-flowering shrubs like lilacs, azaleas, forsythias, and rhododendrons because you risk cutting off next year’s flower buds.

BobVila.com’s product testers say these pruners perform best in terms of comfort, strength, durability, and ease of use.

Fall is one of the best times to plant deciduous trees like maples, oaks, and birches, along with shrubs, says de Lacey. Conifer ornamental trees are also good candidates for fall planting, adds Fitzgerald. As long as the ground isn’t frozen, plants and trees can keep growing roots through winter. Additionally, the cooler temperatures and naturally moist soil help roots establish without the stress of summer heat.

Fall is also an ideal time to plant spring-flowering bulbs like tulips, daffodils, alliums, and crocuses so they can go through the cold period they need to flower properly, says Jose Lopez, owner and founder of Williams Landscaping Inc. in Chicago, Illinois. “Hardy perennials like coneflowers and black-eyed Susans can also be planted in early fall, provided they have enough time to establish before the ground freezes,” notes de Lacy. However, avoid planting tender annuals or plants that need a long stretch of warm weather to establish when frosts are approaching, warns Lopez.

Anything you planted this year, including trees, shrubs, and perennials, can benefit from mulch for winter protection since the plants’ roots haven’t had much time to establish yet, says Lopez. “A couple inches of mulch on top of the soil can help protect the roots, but keep it pulled back from the trunk and stems,” he advises. “Think of mulch as a blanket, not a mound,” says Lopez. “If you pile it against the bark, it holds moisture and can contribute to rot. That’s the kind of problem we see when spring cleanup comes around.”

Roses and perennials with shallow roots can also need extra insulation, depending on the variety and how exposed the planting area is. Garlic planted in the fall also can benefit from a layer of mulch. If you have containers that need to stay outside, you’ll want to protect the roots inside because the soil in a container can freeze more quickly than the ground, says Lopez.

Some plants in fall landscaping don’t need any attention at all this time of year. You don’t need to prune established, climate-appropriate healthy trees and mature shrubs just because winter is coming. Plus, if there’s already enough mulch around them, there’s no need to add more, says Lopez. Mature maples, oaks, and other hardy deciduous trees can generally be left alone as they enter dormancy, adds de Lacey. Other plants to leave alone include:

#7866. Eric Coomer (of Dominion Voting) Loses Libel Lawsuit over The Deep Rig

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court holds that Coomer didn't prove by "clear and convincing evidence" that defendant knew the statements were false (or at least were likely false).

From Judge Tom Barber (M.D. Fla.) Tuesday in Coomer v. Byrne:

This highly contentious defamation action arises from The Deep Rig, a documentary film concerning alleged fraud in the 2020 presidential election[, which was financed by defendant Patrick Byrne, who also appeared in the film].…. Plaintiff Eric Coomer formerly served as director of product strategy and security for Dominion Voting Systems, a supplier of election hardware and software with its United States headquarters in Colorado. Among other things, the film included statements by non-party Joseph Oltmann claiming that he infiltrated a conference call involving members of Antifa and heard comments from a speaker identified by another anonymous participant on the call as "Eric" and "the Dominion guy."

According to Oltmann, the speaker stated on the call in substance that President Donald J. Trump would not win the election because he had "made sure of it." Oltmann clams he later determined through research and by recognizing Coomer's voice that the speaker had been Coomer. Oltmann further stated that he concluded there was a "high probability" Coomer affected the election. Coomer denies participating in any such call or manipulating the results of the 2020 Presidential election and alleges that Oltmann's story presented in the film was false and defamatory.

Coomer sued, and the court earlier held that he had adequately "alleged sufficient facts to avoid dismissal" and to proceed to discovery. But then Byrne sought summary judgment, arguing that, after discovery, Coomer hadn't introduced evidence to support his claim. And the court concluded that Coomer had indeed not uncovered enough evidence to prove "actual malice" by clear and convincing evidence:

[U]nder Colorado law, where the alleged defamatory statement relates to a matter of public concern, a defamation plaintiff must prove actual malice on the part of the defendant, and must do so by clear and convincing evidence, even if the plaintiff is not a public figure. Coomer has expressly conceded that the statements at issue concern matters of public concern, [and] that Colorado's actual malice standard applies ….

Coomer himself asserts that Byrne believed the 2020 election was rigged immediately after the election. Byrne testified that he believed Oltmann's story and remains highly confident that the gist of Oltmann's story was true. Although the actual malice standard focuses on Byrne's subjective state of mind and beliefs, Byrne's statements as to those beliefs are not necessarily dispositive and Coomer may seek to establish Byrne's subjective lack of belief in the story through circumstantial evidence. The relevant question, then, is whether the evidence Coomer points to is sufficient to support a jury finding, under the clear and convincing evidence standard, that Byrne in fact subjectively disbelieved or had serious doubts about Oltmann's story.

Coomer points to circumstantial evidence that includes the improbable nature of Oltmann's allegations, the lack of independent investigation by Bryne and the lack of corroboration for Oltmann's story, published reports and opinions rebutting claims of election fraud, and Coomer's denials and other suits for defamation filed prior to the publication of the film. It would be reasonable to conclude from a totality of the evidence that, had Byrne acted reasonably, he would have concluded that Oltmann's story was probably false and that Coomer probably did not attempt to tamper with or "rig" the 2020 Presidential election. However, the question for the jury at trial would not be whether Byrne reasonably should have reached that conclusion. It would be whether he did in fact reach that conclusion or at least harbored serious doubts about Oltmann's story or was highly aware it was probably false….

[R]egardless of whether a finding of actual malice might be supportable under the preponderance standard, the evidence is insufficient to support the same conclusion under the much higher clear and convincing standard. Byrne's lack of skepticism, failure to investigate, and disregard for government reports and conclusions by others debunking claims of fraud the 2020 election are equally consistent with negligence and a belief that there was essentially a coverup going on, in line with the grand conspiracy theory portrayed in the film.

Coomer points out that Byrne did not include Oltmann's story in his own book of the same title, but Byrne explained that he wanted to present an argument based on publicly available information, which, unlike a single witness's account of an unrecorded phone call, would be taken seriously as supporting a nationwide investigation. Any inference from the totality of this evidence to a conclusion that Byrne actually disbelieved or seriously doubted Oltmann's story would be weak at best and insufficient to support a finding of actual malice by clear and convincing evidence….

Allowing a jury to infer from evidence that a reasonable person would have doubted Oltmann's story to a conclusion that it is not only possible, but highly probable and free from serious or substantial doubt that Byrne, did, in fact, have serious doubts about it would require the Court to ignore not only the standards just discussed but human nature as well.

The world has always had people with zealously held beliefs who are quite vocal and eager to share their views with anyone who will listen. These people are frequently labeled, pejoratively, as extremists, fanatics, "kooks," "crazies," conspiracy theorists, and the like. They typically have a lot to say on their subjects of interest, and modern technology has given them a powerful microphone to convey their thoughts well beyond the limits of their own communities or personal echo-chambers.

They may make statements that reasonable people consider to be wrong, and sometimes their statements are, in fact, objectively and demonstrably wrong. But those with zealously held beliefs hold firm even when overwhelming objective evidence may be to the contrary. This is because they genuinely and sincerely believe what they say with every fiber of their being, even when objective evidence may suggest otherwise. Many are highly intelligent and sophisticated people, but they never seriously doubt the truth of their statements and remain steadfast in their beliefs no matter what. While these speakers sometimes espouse beliefs and make statements many might consider to be extreme, offensive, irresponsible, and factually wrong, their beliefs are, nonetheless, sincerely held and those speakers believe everything they say is completely true.

Even aside from extreme examples, people in general are hardly paragons of reason and often do not reach or maintain their beliefs by dispassionate assessments of the evidence. They believe what they do, especially on important political, moral and religious issues, as a result of unconscious biases, predispositions, prior emotional, philosophical, and political commitments and intuitions, as well as a disinclination to exert the effort or risk the emotional discomfort involved in exposing themselves to contrary evidence and viewpoints.

As John Kenneth Galbraith observed, "[f]aced with the choice between changing one's mind and proving that there is no need to do so, almost everyone gets busy on the proof." Operating within an echo chamber while believing oneself to be well-informed and reasonable has become increasingly easy to do in the age of slanted news sources and targeted media constantly telling their constituencies what they want to hear.

Of course, people with sincerely or even zealously held beliefs may make statements that are both untrue and inflict serious harm on others. Under the actual malice standard, unless it can be proven that the speaker subjectively believed his or her statements to be untrue, the law imposes no liability. That is a policy choice that might deserve reexamination by the appropriate decision makers—the United States Supreme Court and the Colorado courts. As [this] Court noted in the Trump Media & Tech. Group Corp. v. WP Co. LLC (M.D. Fla. 2026) case, the actual malice standard has been criticized by courts and commentators on a number of grounds, with which [this] Court largely agrees.

In short, if the law did not require "clear and convincing evidence" that the defendant subjectively doubted or disbelieved the published statements, it is likely that Byrne's motion for summary judgment would have been denied, and a jury would have had the opportunity to weigh in on this matter. However, under the law as it currently stands, Coomer's evidence is insufficient to meet these standards and summary judgment for Byrne is therefore required….

Peter Ticktin and David Lawrence Perry II (The Ticktin Law Group) represent Byrne.

NEXT: Cancellation, Defamation, Bankruptcy, Discharge

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Inspired by Margot’s post a while back on the stellar, nontraditional kitchens she spotted on the websites of European real estate firms, I found myself perusing the listings of my favorite U.K. agency, The Modern House, and there, I came across an especially dreamy offering: a rambling two-acre, multi-building property purchased by a pair of artists, Leila El-Kayem and Sophie Mayer, who lovingly transformed the dilapidated Victorian walled garden into a stylish retreat that’s appealingly rough around the edges.

The two creatives (Leila is a conceptual artist and poet; Sophie is a painter) enlisted architecture firm McClean Quinlan to help them transform the garden into a two-bedroom home that taps into the “feral” landscape of the area. “There’s something about walking into an untamed space that gives you permission to become untamed yourself,” Sophie told The Modern House’s Journal. “It reduced us back to an instinctive way of living, and that became very humbling and formative for both of us.”

“We wanted to retain as much as possible of what was already here,” continued Leila. “So we worked with the existing materials to make sure that we honoured what came before us, preserving the romanticism of the ruin. We haven’t knocked anything down. We just tried to keep the integrity of what’s here and slowly repair it.”

#7862. Frost Coming Your Way? What to Do With Veggies in the Garden

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Updated Oct 28, 2026 4:20 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

While some people welcome the cooling that accompanies autumn, gardeners know they have work to do before the coming frost kills off the literal fruits (and veggies) of their labor.

First, find out the typical frost dates for your USDA hardiness zone and learn what temperatures cause frost damage. Then, watch local weather forecasts. Understand the difference between frost and light freeze, and which plants are more susceptible to frost damage.

Start with healthy plants and the right soil. Next, you’ll need to know which plants are tender and which can withstand a light frost and which delicious homegrown fruits and vegetables you’ll need to harvest before it’s too late.

Tender plants are easily damaged by frost or cold weather, requiring protection to survive. Common tender fruits and vegetables include watermelon, squash, pumpkin, cantaloupe and muskmelon, eggplant, cucumber, okra, pepper, beans, tomatoes, and most herbs.

Frost-tolerant plants can withstand brief periods of cold or frost, but beyond very limited periods, would require protection. Examples of frost-tolerant plants include lettuce, cauliflower, endive, peas, carrots, Chinese cabbage, celery, chard, and chicory.

Hardy plants generally have higher levels of sugar in their leaves, which enables them to tolerate lower temperatures. Cool-season crops that can survive a frost or even an early freeze include asparagus, cabbage, kale, spinach, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, collards, potatoes, and onions.

Many crops can be saved from an early frost. Even cool-season crops like lettuce and other leafy greens, carrots, and radishes can benefit from overnight covering to protect the plants from frost and extend the growing season. You can use old sheets or drop cloths (using supports to keep the cover from touching the plants), burlap, row covers made of non-woven polyester, or cloches.

Whichever type of plant cover you choose, make sure it is breathable. Do not use plastic. Ensure air circulation and be sure to remove the covers during the heat of the day, and put them back on in the early evening.If you have a greenhouse, move as many plants as you can inside.

Bio Green’s heater has a digital thermostat, sturdy stainless steel build, and is intended for spaces up to 130 square feet. Read the review.

Adding a 2- to 4-inch layer of mulch, particularly in the afternoon while the soil is warm, can help protect roots from overnight dips in temperature. Material choices to minimize frost damage include wood chips, bark, pine needles, straw, and even shredded leaves (including if they’re moldy). Dark mulch absorbs more of the sun’s warmth, which it releases into the soil around the plants at night.

Mulching the garden also preserves much-needed moisture. In addition, a layer of mulch will prevent perennials from putting out new growth at the end of the season, allowing them to go dormant for the winter.

Moist soil actually holds up to four times more heat than dry soil, and conducts that heat to the soil surface faster, creating a microclimate in which the air above it is 5 degrees warmer. In addition to providing an insulating effect, water helps plants withstand temperature changes better.

For best results, water late in the day because the water vapor creates a microclimate that will help plants stay warm and resist freezing.

When all else fails, harvest what you can. Beans, peas, corn, melons, cucumbers, eggplant, and most greens should be harvested early, since they don’t handle frost well. Be sure to pick tender herbs such as basil and oregano.

Tomatoes and peppers can ripen indoors after harvest. In fact, many fruits, including apples, peaches, pears, grapes, cantaloupe, and persimmon, ripen after picking. Store pumpkins and squash in a dry location for later use.

It can be tough to eat all of the last harvest right away, but there are plenty of ways to preserve your bounty: dry herbs, and can, dry, or freeze fruits and vegetables.

Many fruits can ripen indoors more quickly if they’re kept in a paper bag that is loosely closed at the top. Storing them this way traps ethylene gas that helps ripen fruit. Because rice also traps ethylene gas, fruits can be placed in containers of rice, although this is not recommended for tender fruits such as peaches that can suffer bruising. Taking these steps can typically help fruit ripen within a few days.

Plastic bags are not advised for ripening fruit because they don’t allow for ventilation.

Not all produce has to be harvested at the first sign of frost. Many root vegetables, like beets, carrots, onions, turnips, parsnips, and potatoes can easily survive a light frost. So can kale, artichokes, broccoli, cabbage, radishes, leeks, spinach, Brussels sprouts, and chard. In fact, cold temperatures improve the flavor of crops such as carrots and kale.

Several of these can even survive a hard frost, including broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, collards, kale, kohlrabi, mustard, onions, parsley, peas, radishes, spinach, turnips, leeks, and sorrel.

If frost gets your fruits and vegetables, they may not be edible. Tender plants like peppers, tomatoes, and many fruits may be mushy. Lettuces and other greens often turn dark and limp. Beans, eggplant, and potatoes are also susceptible to frost, and may exhibit crystalized moisture in their cells. Even carrots can become rubbery or limp after a hard frost.

If the produce is past its prime, dispose of it in your compost pile or bin, where it can benefit next year’s garden.

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

Today the Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorized seizures to deny malicious cyber actors access to two hacking tools, “Microscan” and “FishHub,” used to scan and, in some cases, hack, U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure systems and other networks. As alleged in court documents unsealed in the Western District of Pennsylvania, malicious cyber actors working for Integrity Technology Group (Integrity Tech), a company based in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), operated and used the tools. Integrity Tech has contracts with the PRC government.

“The United States will not allow China or its proxies to operate against United States interests with impunity in cyberspace,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “The National Security Division will continue to respond decisively and use every tool at our disposal to disrupt the Flax Typhoon threats, dismantle the infrastructure sustaining them, and protect the critical networks that power our daily lives and on which our Nation’s security depends.”

“These state-sponsored hackers continue to aggressively target and access networks and systems throughout the world in an effort to identify and steal files and otherwise exploit victims’ vulnerabilities,” said U.S. Attorney Troy Rivetti for the Western District of Pennsylvania. “These seizures, our second disruption of Integrity Tech’s massive operations in as many years, send another clear message to cybercriminals from the PRC and elsewhere of the Department’s dedication to defending and maintaining cybersecurity in the United States and abroad.”

“Integrity Technology Group provided China-linked threat actors with capabilities used to conduct widespread vulnerability scanning and, in some cases, intrusions targeting U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure,” said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division. “The PRC relies on contractor and enabling companies to expand the reach and scale of its malicious cyber activity. By exposing and disrupting these enablers, we make it harder for the PRC to target American networks and infrastructure.”

“Today’s seizures underscore the FBI’s unwavering commitment in disrupting PRC state-sponsored cyber criminals who threaten our critical infrastructure and national security,” said Special Agent in Charge Mark Remily of the FBI San Diego Field Office. “FBI San Diego and our law enforcement partners around the world will continue to employ the full force of our investigative authority to protect the American people and safeguard our networks from malicious foreign cyber actors.”

According to court documents, Integrity Tech created and used a botnet of internet-of-things devices infected with a variant of Mirai malware. Among other things, this botnet facilitated Integrity Tech’s computer vulnerability scanning using Microscan. Integrity Tech developed Microscan to conduct reconnaissance, via the botnet and otherwise, of victim computer networks for vulnerabilities that its clients would later exploit. Targets of Microscan vulnerability scanning include a U.S. power company based in South Carolina, a multi-national Non-Governmental Organization, Japanese and Polish airports, Taiwanese critical infrastructure companies in the natural gas and power sectors, and two Taiwanese universities. Integrity Tech accessed Microscan through one of the seized domains, c0cc[.]cc.

A second Integrity Tech tool, FishHub, is alleged to have facilitated the exploitation of computer networks through spear phishing. After an initial network compromise, FishHub downloaded additional malware to the victim network. This malware provided Integrity Tech’s clients with unauthorized remote access to the victim network or searched for specific files and sent them to servers controlled by Integrity Tech. Confirmed victims of FishHub activity included approximately 20 Taiwanese universities. Five of the seized domains helped deliver this malware: 98aicai[.]com, 98aicode[.]com, outlook3650[.]com, youtubecard[.]com, and linkedinns[.]net.

Today’s action marks the Department’s second public technical disruption of Integrity Tech’s hacking infrastructure. In September 2024, the Justice Department announced the court-authorized disruption of Integrity Tech’s Mirai malware botnet which consisted of more than 200,000 consumer devices in the United States and worldwide. In conjunction with the seizures announced today, the FBI, along with other U.S. and foreign-partner agencies, published a cyber security advisory. This advisory provides indicators-of-compromise associated with Integrity Tech intrusion activity and is designed to help network defenders identify and respond to Integrity Tech’s malicious activity.

The FBI San Diego and Baltimore Field Offices are investigating the case, in coordination with the FBI’s Cyber Division.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Brendan McKenna for the Western District of Pennsylvania and Trial Attorney Jacques Singer-Emery of the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section are prosecuting the case. Substantial assistance was provided by Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Sullivan for the District of Maryland and the National Police Agency of Japan.

#7858. Israeli Jews Vote by Economic Status, Even Though Elections Turn on Other Issues

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A fascinating chart from Yedioth Aharanot newspaper shows the voting breakdown of the Jewish electorate in the Israeli election.

People the pollsters deem to be in the bottom 10% in socio-economic status voted 96.7% for Netanyahu's Likud and parties aligned with it. Those in the top 10% voted 80.9% for opposition parties.

What makes this particularly interesting is that the election turned almost entirely on issues that are not economic in the ordinary sense, such as conscripting Haredi Jews, which factions would best resist outside pressure for a Palestinian state, who is best-positioned to finish the wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, and who is to blame for 10/7. Many voters expressed concern to pollsters about the cost of living, but none of the major parties talked much about it.

So to a large and often unappreciated (at least outside Israel) extent, Israeli politics is culture-war politics. Netanyahu and his allies represent voters who are more religiously traditional, less-educated, live on "the periphery," poorer, and, importantly, of recent North African or Middle Eastern descent--Israelis who were treated as outsiders by the Ashkenazi socialists who ran the country until Menahem Begin broke their stranglehold on elections in 1977. Netanyahu's opponents rely on voters who are disproportionately Ashkenazi, better-educated, wealthier, live in Tel Aviv or Haifa, and more secular-minded.

Another interesting aspect of this is that while the religious/secular divide comes up in politicking all the time, Israeli politics mostly avoid explicit ethnic or wealth-based appeals. The de facto leader of the opposition, Gadi Eisenkot, is the son of Moroccan immigrants. Moroccans are a huge part of Netanyahu's base, but Eisenkot's potential to be the first Moroccan (and first non-Ashkenazi) prime minister barely played a role in the campaign, and he did not try to give it one.

I will leave it to those more expert than I on Israeli politics to analyze this further, but it sure seems like a big factor in the election was a visceral fear among groups that feel historically marginalized in Israel that victory by the anti-Netanyahu faction would amount to a loss in status.

Finally, the complaint alleges that, also on or about Oct. 5, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building. #7856. How to Wrap a Tree to Protect it From Winter Damage

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:53 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

It may sound like an odd practice, but wrapping a tree can be worthwhile. Once trees drop their leaves, they no longer benefit from their protective canopy, and hazards can damage young and thin-barked trees, along with some evergreen trees and shrubs. “Cold temperatures, drying winds, ice, and hungry wildlife can injure trees during winter,” says Fred Breglia, ISA, a certified arborist and author of the upcoming book titled Big Trees: A Tour of the World’s Biggest Trees.

And it’s not just the cold that makes trees susceptible to damage. Adding a tree wrap around the trunk can protect the bark from harsh winter sun when leaves no longer shade it. Ahead, learn why tree wrapping helps some trees flourish and survive colds—and how you can wrap trees for winter safely and effectively.

Young trees, like those that have been growing for up to two seasons, are especially susceptible to winter damage. Wrapping immature and thin-barked trees helps prevent trunk damage from sun and freeze-thaw cycles. Some evergreens also benefit from a full-tree wrap for winter or a screen to prevent browning foliage, and other young trees can be saved from animal munching or rubbing damage with a fence wrap.

Rapid temperature changes in winter combine with an empty canopy to expose trees to frost cracks or sunscald. Vertical frost cracks can make a tree more vulnerable to pests or diseases.  Sunscald is even more serious. “Sunlight warms frozen bark, then shade or nightfall causes it to refreeze and die,” says Breglia. Sunscald usually occurs on a trunk’s southwest side, where winter sun is most intense and the bark warms up the most. It can cause a jagged vertical wound along the tree trunk and dry, cracked, sunken, or dead bark.

Trees are more susceptible to sunscald include those less than 2 years old and species with thin bark, such as:

Another type of cold damage is winter browning, or desiccation injury, which “occurs when evergreen needles and rhododendron leaves lose moisture faster than frozen soil can replace it,” says Breglia. He adds that low temperatures, freeze-thaw cycles, sun, and wind can worsen winter damage on evergreens or semi-evergreens. “Browning often occurs on the south or southwest side of conifers, though wind exposure may also damage the north side,” Breglia says.

Trees and shrubs most susceptible to winter browning include broadleaf evergreens, needled evergreens, or those with scale-like leaves, such as:

Deer and other browsers can munch on buds of trees in winter when food is scarce, but they also can bite into tender bark. Even in early fall, bucks look for small tree trunks to rub against as new antlers form and cause itching. “Voles, mice, and rabbits can severely damage young trees and shrubs by eating their bark in winter,” adds Breglia.

As always, young trees are most vulnerable to severe damage, along with some trees that wildlife prefer.

If you have a young tree or a tree or shrub species vulnerable to winter damage, you generally need to learn how to use tree wrap so you can prepare it in fall before the first winter frost. The precise timing varies by region and the type of damage that can occur. For example, if deer visit your landscape, you might need to wrap young trunks by late summer or as soon as you see bucks growing antlers.

For potential vole and mice damage, wrap trunks before the first snowfall. Most young trees will benefit from wrap protection for at least two winter seasons. In all cases, be sure to remove tree wraps by spring and never leave them on all year.

The most common way to wrap a tree trunk for winter tree protection is with a poly or fabric tree wrap or plastic guard. A tree wrap should be breathable and a light color. Breglia says the material should “conform to the trunk but also allow airflow without trapping moisture.”

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Using a small trowel or shovel, gently scrape away any debris or leaves against the trunk and dig about 1 inch below the soil surface all around the trunk. This helps to set your tree wrap taut against the trunk and just below ground level.

Start at the lowest point of trunk exposure and begin to wrap around the trunk, ensuring each pass overlaps by at least ⅓ of the wrap’s width so there is no exposed bark.

If you’re using a plastic guard, widen the opening and place it around the tree, ensuring it sits just below ground level.

Continue to wrap the trunk until you reach the area just below the tree’s lowest branch. When you’re finished wrapping, secure the wrap with heavy-duty tape or twine. Do not staple or puncture the tree.

If using a plastic guard, add another guard above the lower one, cutting it if necessary to end just below the branches. Secure it to the bottom guard per manufacturer directions or with heavy-duty tape.

Check the wrap from time to time to make sure it remains secure at the top and has not loosened or been damaged below.

When the cold weather is over, carefully remove the wrap from the tree.

Although you can loosely wrap an entire shrub or tree in burlap to prevent winter browning, it is best to build a barrier around the plant, typically with stakes. “Use a burlap windbreak placed a few inches from the foliage, or loosely wrap multistemmed evergreens to block drying winter winds without trapping moisture,” says Breglia. If you wrap a tree or shrub in the fabric to protect it from wind or moisture loss, leave a hole at the top to allow sun and air to get in.

If you want to prevent winter wind damage like browning, install a burlap or shade fabric screen around the tree. Here’s how:

As long as your tree wrap is secure and at least 1 inch below ground, it can protect the trunk from most small animal damage. If you only need to protect against animals and not sunscald or browning, consider this method suggested by Breglia:

When wrapping trees for winter, always remember to remove the tree wrap in spring. Each spring, check trees and shrubs for any damage as growth resumes, like discolored needles, split bark, or areas that appear to have been nibbled on or stripped by animals. Breglia also advises watering trees well in spring and summer (and after planting a tree) so they are healthy when entering the winter season.

When properly placed, tree wrap can protect many trees and shrubs from winter damage. The trunks of young and thin-barked trees are particularly vulnerable to frost cracks, sunscald, and animal damage, so covering the trunk can keep a tree from the type of damage that could eventually result in taking the tree down and replanting.

Tree trunks are best wrapped in light-colored breathable fabrics especially designed for tree wrapping or plastic tree guards that surround a trunk. Some gardeners use burlap, but it can result in damage and is best used as a light wrap or screen to protect trees from winter browning or animal damage. Breglia recommends against the use of wound paint or dressing for young trees; paint will not protect trees from animal damage.

Always wait to wrap a tree in fall as it goes dormant and before the first hard frost. If you miss the first frost, wrap the tree as soon as the trunk has dried out to prevent repeated injury. Never wrap or leave wrap on a tree in spring or summer growth phases. And the best time to wrap a tree is when it is young (first 1 to 3 years of growth).

Some trees or shrubs need only temporary winter protection from unusual frosts or storms. A burlap screen or windbreak also can protect trees in winter. Spreading a 2- to 3-inch layer of mulch around the tree, at least the width of its root ball or canopy, can protect tender roots from repeated winter freezing and thawing. Breglia says that anti-dessicant sprays can help prevent drying out of trees and shrubs. Fencing can keep browsing animals away from evergreens.  “Proper placement of winter injury-sensitive plants, such as rhododendrons, boxwood, yew, or arborvitae can reduce the chance of winter damage,” adds Breglia. Finally, healthy trees can best survive winter, so watering and other care steps in spring and summer help protect tender trees in winter.

#7855. The Law and Democrats Allegedly Recruiting Second "Dan Sullivan" to Run in Alaska Senate Race

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Election law expert and UCLA Prof. Rick Hasen (Election Law Blog) has a post about this; an excerpt:

Today's New York Times story, if true, strikes me as a political bombshell: despite public denials of a connection, people associated with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska Mary Peltola and Democratic Party officials recruited the second "Dan Sullivan" to run against the incumbent Republican U.S. Senator from Alaska, Dan S. Sullivan. The hope would be to siphon votes away from Sullivan. (As a political play, I'm skeptical that this would work, given Alaska's ranked choice voting approach would allow ranking both Dan Sullivans as 1 and 2, thereby not helping Peltola.)

But what, if any, are the legal implications of the story (if true)?

To begin with, I don't think it has any bearing at all on the current litigation in which the U.S. Department of Justice seeks to delay certification of the race if Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses on grounds of purported voter confusion. The lawsuit is not going anywhere for any number of reasons, but even assuming DOJ's theory that it can sue to block certification, it is irrelevant as to why voters might face confusion over the two Dan Sullivans. (This has not stopped DOJ from now supporting DSCC intervention so that it can get discovery over a potential "conspiracy"). [Disclosure: I will soon be filing a motion to file an amicus brief on my own behalf supporting the State of Alaska in this case.]

Second, if there is any evidence that anyone lied under oath about the cooperation between Democrats and Dan J. Sullivan, that could be grounds for a perjury prosecution. So far I'm not aware of any such allegation in the case.

Third, this leaves the question whether this could be prosecuted as some kind of conspiracy against voters.

To begin with, it is regular practice for people to support candidates for bad motives: Republicans boosting Greens and Democrats boosting Libertarians. It turns out that Elon Musk alone may have bankrolled left-leaning Cornel West's quest to get on the 2024 presidential eiection ballot. The effort in Alaska is just an extreme version of that. From the Times's story: "Ballot-stacking tactics are common in politics and generally considered legal — and have been employed by both parties in Alaska. But this operation, which has not been reported before, reveals the lengths to which Democrats went to seek advantage in a Senate race that could determine control of the chamber." …

This is a case about someone running for office with impure motives who is lucky enough to have a name that could confuse some voters. The solution to this problem is counterspeech (as in: "Don't vote for J.! Vote for the real Senator Daniel S. Sullivan".)

I don't see how the government could criminalize his running for office for having impure motives. And if it could do so, then it could be a crime every time that the Republican Party backs a Green Party candidate, or Democrats support a MAGA candidate in a primary in the hopes that the candidate would be weaker against a Democrat in the general election. This stuff happens all the time….

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through remote information technology (IT) work for U.S. companies. These actions include an indictment, two arrests, searches of multiple known or suspected “laptop farms” in Texas pursuant to “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” and the seizure of approximately 187 computer devices used by DPRK IT workers.

“North Korea’s rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These schemes threaten the security of the IT systems and data of the deceived U.S. employers and leave countless victims of identity theft. NSD, along with our law enforcement partners, will use every available tool to track down anyone assisting the DPRK and to protect our national security.”

“Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation’s economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful to FBI Cleveland for their incredible work and persistence to put a stop to these bad actors. These charges serve as an urgent alert to all U.S. companies to remain vigilant in their hiring practices.”

“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability. Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security.”

“North Korea continues to deploy remote IT workers using stolen identities to infiltrate American companies and generate revenue for the regime and its weapons programs,” said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division. “Today, the FBI and DOJ announced a series of coordinated actions against this threat, securing charges against 14 individuals, conducting two arrests, seizing nearly 190 devices, and executing operations at more than 40 suspected ‘laptop farms’ across Texas. Close coordination between the private sector and federal law enforcement was central to this operation. To further combat the threat, the FBI has issued a Public Service Announcement with detailed mitigation guidance for U.S. companies.”

Sun Sheng Ming, et al. Indictment and Arrests – Northern District of Ohio

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio announced the arrests of U.S. nationals Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas pursuant to a four-count wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft indictment. The indictment describes a multi-year fraud scheme by Bostelle, Pena, and their co-conspirators to obtain remote IT work with U.S. companies that generated more than $3 million in revenue. The indictment also charges China-based Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang, Jin Long for their roles in the scheme. The identities of two additional defendants remain under seal.

According to the indictment, from 2019 to in or around July 2025, DPRK IT workers applied for and obtained remote positions by using stolen or fabricated identity documents, virtual private networks and proxy infrastructure to appear as though they were U.S. persons working from within the United States. They also relied on U.S.-based facilitators who received and hosted multiple laptop computers — issued by victim U.S. companies — at their residences in the United States (“laptop farms”), housed and configured those devices, installed remote-access software and transferred earnings to DPRK‑controlled accounts.

In total, the scheme impacted more than 70 U.S. company employers and generated approximately $3 million in revenue for IT workers. The revenue is believed to have been sent to sanctioned entities controlled by the DPRK. Victim employers included companies in the health care, communications, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio, sixteen additional states, and the District of Columbia.

The FBI Cleveland Field Office is investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Duncan T. Brown for the Northern District of Ohio and Trial Attorney Neeraj Gupta of the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section are prosecuting the case.

Operation Lonestar Roundup Disrupts Multiple Known or Suspected Laptop Farms in Texas

Between Sept. 21 and Sept. 25, the FBI conducted searches and other law enforcement action at over 40 residences in Texas known to be, or suspected of operating as, laptop farms for DPRK IT workers. Over the course of the entire operation (Operation Lonestar Roundup), the FBI seized approximately 187 laptops and KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) devices that DPRK IT workers and their U.S.-based facilitators used to commit fraud, obtain remote employment, and generate revenue for the North Korean regime’s sanctioned weapons programs. U.S. cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has identified this group of DPRK IT workers and their helpers as “Famous Chollima.”

Investigators discovered that the DPRK operatives allegedly used a network of fraudulent email accounts to facilitate their criminal activity. The following accounts were among those identified as being used in these schemes:

Employers are encouraged to add these accounts to the list of indicators they use to identify and disrupt DPRK IT worker employment.

Today, the FBI published a public service announcement describing the evolving DPRK IT worker threat, including tips on how to detect the threat. Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals. Additionally, CrowdStrike today published a blog post describing its efforts at monitoring customer networks for DPRK IT worker activity and its successful collaboration with the FBI to disrupt this threat.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas, the FBI’s Dallas Field Office, and the FBI’s Cyber Division coordinated Operation Lonestar Roundup. Valuable assistance was provided by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio.

Today’s announcements represent the Department’s latest actions to combat North Korean IT worker schemes as part of a joint NSD and FBI Cyber and Counterintelligence Divisions effort, the DPRK RevGen: Domestic Enabler Initiative. This effort prioritizes targeting and disrupting the DPRK’s illicit revenue generation schemes and its U.S.-based enablers. The Department previously announced other actions pursuant to the initiative, including in June 2025, November 2025, April 2026, and May 2026.

As described in Public Service Announcements published in May 2024, January 2025, July 2025, and today, North Korean remote IT workers posing as legitimate remote IT workers have committed data extortion and exfiltrated the proprietary and sensitive data from U.S. companies. DPRK IT worker schemes typically involve the use of stolen identities, alias emails, social media, online cross-border payment platforms, and online job site accounts, as well as false websites, proxy computers, and witting and unwitting third parties located in the U.S. and elsewhere. North Korean IT workers leverage these third parties, which include U.S.-based individuals, to gain fraudulent employment and access to U.S. company networks to generate this revenue.

Other public advisories about the threats, red flag indicators, and potential mitigation measures for these schemes include a May 2022 advisory released by the FBI, Department of the Treasury, and Department of State; a July 2023 advisory from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence; and guidance issued in October 2023 by the United States and the Republic of Korea (South Korea). As described the May 2022 advisory, North Korean IT workers have been known individually to earn up to $300,000 annually, generating hundreds of millions of dollars collectively each year, on behalf of designated entities, such as the North Korean Ministry of Defense and others directly involved in the DPRK’s weapons programs.

The U.S. Department of State has offered potential rewards for up to $5 million in support of international efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s illicit financial activities, including for cybercrimes, money laundering, and sanctions evasion.

The details in the above-described court documents are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7853. Even "Trumpy Judges" and "Woke Judges" Might Know More Law Than You Do

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I appreciate that many people are skeptical about judges. Indeed, it's good that people take with a grain of salt the statements of government officials, including judges. Judges are human, and humans make mistakes and have prejudices and blind spots.

At the same time, judges are generally quite well-trained lawyers, and know a good deal about what they're writing about. Conventional wisdom holds that federal judges generally are particularly well-qualified (of course, with exceptions, as is true for all institutions). Federal judges also generally employ quite well-qualified law clerks, who do much of the  research and initial opinion drafting.

This means that, for all the risk of error and ideological bias, judges generally (though not always) know what they're talking about in their legal analysis. They tend to particularly know more than non-lawyers, but also often more than lawyers who aren't specialists in the particular field. You might assume that some judge is "woke" or "Trumpy" or what have you, but there's a pretty good chance that the judge's legal analysis is still correct.

This post was prompted by a comment I saw on the Eric Coomer (of Dominion Voting) Loses Libel Lawsuit over The Deep Rig post, though this is just one example of a broader trend. The comment quotes an excerpt from the post's excerpt of the judge's opinion:

In short, if the law did not require "clear and convincing evidence" that the defendant subjectively doubted or disbelieved the published statements, it is likely that Byrne's motion for summary judgment would have been denied, and a jury would have had the opportunity to weigh in on this matter. However, under the law as it currently stands, Coomer's evidence is insufficient to meet these standards and summary judgment for Byrne is therefore required….

The comment then says, "Trumpy judge who apparently didn't bother to read Sullivan, which states" (emphasis added by commenter),

The constitutional guarantees require, we think, a federal rule that prohibits a public official from recovering damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct unless he proves that the statement was made with "actual malice" — that is, with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.

And the comment continues, "Seems like this is ripe for appeal. This Trumpy judge seems to think the current precedent requires that the defendant 'subjectively doubted or disbelieved the published statements,' when Sullivan has a looser standard."

The trouble with the commenter's analysis is that Sullivan was of course not the last word on the subject—as the judge knew. Indeed, if one searches for "subjective" in the judge's opinion, one sees a longish passage citing authority supporting the judge's analysis:

Actual malice requires proof that the defendant published the challenged statement with knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for whether it was false. See id. [Coomer v. Donald J. Trump for President, Inc., 552 P.3d 562, 581 (Colo. App. 2024)]; New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254, 279-80 (1964); St. Amant v. Thompson, 390 U.S. 727, 731 (1968). The test for actual malice is a subjective one. Thus, the issue is not whether "a reasonably prudent [person] would have published, or would have investigated before publishing," but rather whether the defendant "in fact entertained serious doubts as to the truth of [the] publication, or was highly aware of its probable falsity[.]" Coomer, 552 P.3d at 591; Diversified Mgmt., Inc. v. The Denver Post, Inc., 653 P.2d 1103. 1105-10 (Colo. 1982) (en banc); Michel v. NYP Holdings, Inc., 816 F.3d 686, 703 (11th Cir. 2016) ("[W]e ask whether the defendant, instead of acting in good faith, actually entertained serious doubts as to the veracity of the published account, or was highly aware that the account was probably false."); Dershowitz v. Cable News Network, Inc., 153 F.4th 1189, 1193 (11th Cir. 2025) ("[A]ll that matters are the speakers' subjective beliefs about the truth of their own statements.").

St. Amant, cited by the court, indeed states,

[The precedents] are clear that reckless conduct is not measured by whether a reasonably prudent man would have published, or would have investigated before publishing. There must be sufficient evidence to permit the conclusion that the defendant in fact entertained serious doubts as to the truth of his publication. Publishing with such doubts shows reckless disregard for truth or falsity and demonstrates actual malice.

Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (1974) expressly quotes this passage as the Court having "equated reckless disregard of the truth with subjective awareness of probable falsity." The judge in the Coomer / Deep Rig case, whether you view him as "Trumpy" or not, knew the law here, and the commenter (who had elsewhere said he wasn't a lawyer) didn't seem to.

So, again, definitely view judges' work skeptically, and feel free to criticize it. But don't assume that just because you know one precedent in the field you know the law better than the judge. Don't assume that just because you think the judge has some ideological bias, that ideological bias has led the judge into legal error. And if you have some skepticism about the judge's analysis, check the sources that the judge cites in the full opinion; my posts usually just excerpt the opinion, and often don't include citations, but they generally link to the full opinion so readers can consult it directly.

#7852. Creating Voter Confusion About Candidates' Names is Bad - But Exploiting Voter Ignorance About Policy Issues is a Much Bigger Problem

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Democrats' apparent effort to confuse Alaska voters about candidates' names is reprehensible. But politicians' routine lying and exploitation of ignorance about policy issues is much worse.

A recent New York Times article presents evidence that Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters in that state's 2026 Senate election by introducing a second candidate with a name very similar to that of the Republican incumbent, thereby potentially siphoning off some of the latter's voters. The incumbent senator is named Dan S. Sullivan, while the other candidate is Dan J. Sullivan. As the Times reports, some of the facts here are disputable, and it is not entirely clear whether Democratic candidate Mary Peltola knew about this effort or approved of it. But it seems likely that at least some of her staffers and other Democratic operatives were involved.

Before going further, I should emphasize that this effort is worthy of condemnation. Trying to confuse voters into voting for the "wrong" candidate in this way is not how democratic political participation should work. And the fact that other politicians (including Republicans) engage in various electoral "dirty tricks" doesn't justify this one.

Elsewhere, I have explained why these kinds of actions are not illegal, and why the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate result deserves to fail. I stand by that conclusion. Legal scholar Rick Hasen (a leading election law expert) has a helpful recent post explaining why the New York Times revelations do not change anything from a legal point of view. But the fact that this scheme is legal doesn't make it right.

That said, it is important to keep this issue in proper perspective, and especially to recognize that many other types of lies and efforts to exploit voter ignorance are much worse. Confusion caused by candidates with similar names is relatively rare, and it is difficult to find examples where it affected more than a small fraction of voters. I am not aware of even one case where it was decisive to the outcome of an election. But I welcome correction on that latter point.

The Alaska case is unlikely to be an exception to the above generalization. In the first round of the ranked-choice voting election (which narrows down the candidates to the top 4), only 2.5% of voters picked Dan J. Sullivan. Peltola led the incumbent senator by a much larger margin than that (8.1 points). Even if every single person who voted for Dan J. did so because of confusion (which is improbable), that's unlikely to change the result.

Moreover, the Alaska ranked-choice voting system reduces the risk of error. Some of those who vote for the "wrong" Dan Sullivan might rank the "right" one second. After the former gets eliminated, those votes get transferred to the latter. On top of that, as Michael Dorf points out, the Alaska ballot explicit indicates that Dan S. Sullivan is the "incumbent." That further reduces any potential confusion. The widespread publicity this issue has gotten over the last few weeks further reduces the risk of error. Many voters have probably now heard about the two Dan Sullivans and will be on guard against the problem.

It is still theoretically possible that confusion between the two Sullivans will end up having a decisive impact on the election. Some people who voted for Dan J. might not rank the other Sullivan second, or might misunderstand how the RCV system works. And some voters might (understandably) not be very careful about how they mark their ballots, thereby making a mistake despite the various safeguards against it. Still, it seems highly unlikely that such errors will have a decisive impact on the outcome.

Overall, this kind of a thing is relative molehill of a problem. Elections where it makes a decisive difference are likely to be extremely rare, at worst. By contrast, candidate lying about policy issues and exploitation of voter ignorance about them is a veritable mountain. I summarized some of the relevant evidence in an earlier post about the Alaska controversy:

Donald Trump is a particularly egregious example, going all the way back to his first campaign in 2016, and more recently with his lies about the 2020 election and other issues. But more conventional politicians also often resort to lies and deception, even if not to the same degree.  President Obama, for example, famously  lied when he claimed that, under the Affordable Care Act, "if you like your health care plan, you can keep it." That deception won the 2013 Politifact Lie of the Year award. But it still helped Obama get reelected in 2012. I am not sure exploiting voter confusion about names is any worse than exploiting their ignorance about policy issues like crime, immigration, and health care….

Ultimately, both exploitation of voter confusion about names and other deceptions used in campaigns seek to exploit widespread voter ignorance. Because of the combination of "rational ignorance" (lack of incentive to seek out political information) and "rational irrationality" (lack of incentive to engage in unbiased evaluation),  most voters know little about government and public policy, and often do a poor job of evaluating the information they do know. This makes them vulnerable to deception and manipulation, and incentivizes politicians to lie and otherwise distort the truth.

I would add that lies and deceptions about policy issues affect vastly more voters and have vastly bigger impacts on electoral outcomes than confusion about candidates' names. To take just a few recent examples, Trump in 2016 and 2024 and Obama in 2012 probably could not have won without the former. If, in 2024, key swing voters had realized that Trump's policy agenda of tariffs and mass deportations was likely to raise prices (as it predictably went on to do) rather than lower them (as he promised to do), he likely would have lost. Polls showed that prices were the biggest issue in the election for key swing voters. Trump also might well have lost if GOP base voters realized he was lying about the 2020 election, among other issues. In 2012, Obama might have lost if swing voters realized that he was lying when said that, under his signature policy initiative (the Affordable Care Act), "if you like your health care plan, you can keep it."

Effective lies and deceptions about policy issues (often exploiting preexisting voter ignorance and bias, but also deliberately seeking to create more of it) are ubiquitous. And they very often affect electoral outcomes. Even when they don't change the outcome between the candidates who run, they often have an impact on the policies those candidates adopt in the first place. As described more fully in my book Democracy and Political Ignorance, political parties and their strategists know most voters are ignorant, and often deliberately select policy agendas based on the likelihood of successfully exploiting that ignorance. The result is that even the lesser of the evils on offer in a given election (or the less egregious liars) are often still very bad.

From a moral point of view, I don't see any reason to believe lying about policy issues and exploiting voter ignorance about them is any worse than trying to trick voters into selecting the "wrong" candidate out of confusion. In practical terms, the former happens much more often than the latter, and has a far bigger effect).

Cornell law Prof. Michael Dorf recognizes that lies about policy issues are bad, but suggests that efforts to create confusion about candidate names are worse, because the latter are harder to combat with "counter-speech." I think the truth is the exact opposite. People can and do use counter-speech to oppose lies and deceptions about policy issues. But "rationally ignorant" voters will often ignore the counter-speech (not wanting to take the time and effort to study it) or reject evidence that goes against their preexisting biases. Many policy issues require considerable time and effort to understand well.

By contrast, it's much easier to find out there are two candidates with similar names in the election, and to take precautions against accidentally voting for the "wrong" one. Counter-speech to that effect need not be very complicated at all, or take a long time to understand.  In the Alaska case, for example, you just need to remember to vote for Dan S. rather than Dan J. or just know to vote for the one marked "incumbent." And figuring this out does not require going against any partisan or ideological biases.

As I have emphasized in previous writings about voter ignorance, I do not believe we can or should fight it by trying to punish politicians for their lies, or by censoring "misinformation." There is, in fact, no easy solution to the problem. But I assess a range of  options in my 2023 article on "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance, and in Democracy and Political Ignorance. I believe the best approach is to make fewer decisions at the ballot box and more by "voting with your feet," where incentives to seek out information and evaluate it wisely are much better.  In the works linked above, I also argue that we should give consideration to simply paying voters to increase their knowledge levels (e.g. by establishing a "Voter Achievement Test" and offering rewards to high scorers). But I  recognize that any effective approach will take time, and there may be no one fix that is sufficient by itself.

The beginning of wisdom here is to recognize we have a wide-ranging problem of voter ignorance, and to prioritize the most significant types of ignorance and exploitation thereof. On that scale, ignorance about policy issues should rank high, while voter confusion about candidates' names is a very minor problem, by comparison.

UPDATE: I have made minor additions to this post.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.
