#7831. Amicus Brief in OneTaste Criminal Prosecution

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Matt Kezhaya (Kezhaya Law PLC) wrote an amicus brief on my behalf in this case (U.S. v. Cherwitz & Daedone) a few weeks ago—many thanks to him for all his work on it!—and I thought I'd pass it along:

Under the Government's theory of spiritual coercion, people who at one point believed that volunteering for a religious organization is the path to enlightenment or salvation, but who later become disillusioned with their former beliefs, can be found to have been retroactively "coerced" into providing that labor. The same logic could apply to nuns who had felt religious pressure to do the educational or nursing work that their order was known for, or to monks who had felt religious pressure to do agricultural work that supports the monastery. Any religious organization that runs a monastery, convent, or any other institution where adherents are expected to work as part of their religious vocation could likewise face felony prosecutions.

Such a theory of criminal liability violates the Free Exercise Clause because it is not "neutral." Governments depart from neutrality not just when legislators pass laws designed to suppress religion, but also when courts enforce otherwise-neutral laws in ways that suppress religion precisely because of spiritual or religious qualities. Liability in this case turned precisely on the religious nature of the allegedly coercive conduct, and was imposed in the absence of any secular coercion such as violence or the threat of violence.

The sexual subject matter and conduct inherent within OneTaste's beliefs and practices is beside the point. The forced labor statute is not limited to sexual labor. 18 U.S.C. § 1589. Rather, it generally prohibits any "labor" obtained through "threats of serious harm." 18 U.S.C. § 1589(a)(3). Indeed, the "labor" subject of this charge was ordinary, non-sexual administrative work entailed in running a religious organization that features events and communal living.

To be sure, laws that restrict sexual labor will usually be neutral and generally applicable, precisely because they do not turn on any claims of religious or spiritual coercion. If any business, religious or not, offers its employees' sexual services in exchange for money, that might well violate generally applicable bans on prostitution or pandering. Likewise, if any business, religious or not, conditions employment on the employee's performing sexual services, that will usually constitute civilly actionable quid pro quo sexual harassment. And enforcing such laws would not jeopardize ordinary religious labor, precisely because they are focused on a narrow range of secularly-defined behavior that is seen as harmful (the exchange of sex for money or employment) rather than on a theory of spiritual coercion that can apply to a wide range of labor.

But such laws were not used in this case. The essence of this charge was punishing a particular religious group. The Court should vacate the convictions, or at least reverse and remand for a new trial with proper limiting instructions.

[I.] A theory of "spiritual coercion" violates the Free Exercise Clause.

The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment prohibits governments from targeting specific religious beliefs or practices as such. Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993). That prohibition bars more than just legislative enactments expressly targeting religion; it extends to criminal prosecutions that apply facially neutral laws in ways that target disfavored religious beliefs. Fowler v. State of R.I., 345 U.S. 67 (1953).

Of course, as Part III will discuss, "neutral" and "generally applicable" criminal statutes may be applied to religious behavior precisely the same way they are applied to secular behavior; otherwise, each of us would "become a law unto himself." Emp. Div., Dep't of Hum. Res. of Oregon v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872, 885 (1990); see also Reynolds v. United States, 98 U.S. 145, 167 (1878). But this power cannot be used to target religious actions because of their religious or spiritual character.

The threshold inquiry is whether the ideas are, within OneTaste's scheme of things, "religious." See Patrick v. LeFevre, 745 F.2d 153, 158-59 (2d Cir. 1984). Indisputably, Defendants, OneTaste, and adherents of OneTaste (including the so-called victims) all considered the doctrines subject of this criminal trial to be "religious." See A-977 ("We believed that … your path to God was through your orgasm") (emphasis added); see also A-1053 (adherents of OneTaste seek "something more" beyond ordinary existence believe "Our most potent biological drive, Orgasm, is the key to unlocking this power.").

OneTaste's doctrines addressed distinctions between the physical and spiritual realms in a dichotomy between the "third dimension" and the "fourth dimension." See A-694. They addressed issues of worldly suffering and promised both enlightenment and transcendence through ceremonial rites. A-1114 (orgasm "was more about energy," borrowing from "Buddhist principles like the concept of qi"); see also A-1446 ("OneTaste teachings integrate the principles of mindfulness with the practice of orgasm"); A-1089 (OneTaste teachings included sex "as a ritual practice" and "Magic School … where we had sort of like priests and priestesses of orgasm"); see also A-1426-1427 (PowerPoint presentation outlining "Alchemize shadow into power through orgasm" and "Orgasm Magic: Bringing out the elements of magic [and] Put the principles of OM into practice in creating what you want … [including] Rituals and ceremonies"). Specific ceremonies described in the record include a marriage ceremony at A-891, a foot soaking ritual at A-1085, and a shower ritual at A-1152. The central ritual tenet of OneTaste was ritualistic sexual activity is, OMing, or "Orgasmic Meditation," which adherents of OneTaste regard as a mindfulness practice, a "meditation on sensation without a goal," A-577, A-785.

The Government made much of the sexual nature of those beliefs and practices. E.g., A-1229. But it is no business of the government, including the courts, to "prescribe what shall be orthodox in … religion." W. Virginia State Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624, 642 (1943). Because OneTaste and its adherents considered these beliefs and practices to be "religious" within their scheme of things, the Free Exercise Clause protects their beliefs and practices from governmental targeting.

And the Government did not seriously contest OneTaste's religiosity; instead, it acknowledged, and even stressed, the spiritual and religious nature of OneTaste's activities. According to the Government's closing arguments, the essence of the charge was that "the defendants indoctrinated the victims to believe that Nicole Daedone was a guru and that her teachings were the path to enlightenment and spiritual growth." A-1222. Prosecutors took issue that "Nicole Daedone taught that orgasm was God." A-1232. And "[n]early all of them [victims] lived in OneTaste housing and were subjected to these teachings incessantly." A-1234. The complained-of "indoctrination" and "teachings" is the very essence of religion: leading adherents to accept doctrines as spiritual truths. That these supposed victims ordered their lives in accordance with OneTaste's beliefs and practices is evidence of spiritual and religious belief, not of criminally punishable coercion.

Had there been evidence these "victims" were physically coerced into accepting OneTaste's religious doctrines, such physical coercion would certainly have been illegal. But that was not the Government's theory. Each of these so-called victims freely admitted that they voluntarily joined the organization. A-267-268; A-872-873; A-939; A-1152-1153. And they freely admitted that they voluntarily left it. A-882; A-939; A-1107. The "indoctrination" and "teachings" for which Defendants stood trial only describes proselytization, the very essence of religion, which cannot be criminally punished.

Likewise, the prosecution argued that Defendants "disrupted victims' personal relationships and isolated them from their friends and family." A-1222; see also A-1235 (victims "felt like OneTaste was all they had"). More particularly, Defendants did so by encouraging some of their adherents, including these "victims," to live in a commune with other like-minded believers. A-262, 359-60, 775, 893-894, 1004-06. But this disruption likewise stemmed not from physical coercion or threats of violence, of deportation, or of other secular harm. Rather, it stemmed from the adherents' sense of the spiritual value of participating in a particular religious and spiritual community. A-872; A-1008-1009 (Ms. Kandell, particularly, described her time at the commune as "one of the greatest experiences of my life," partly because of "the sense of community" and "the focus of the communal living"); A-1138-1139.

This is a commonplace practice among many religious orders. By definition, any follower of any monastic tradition could be described as having their personal relationships "disrupted" or becoming "isolated" from their less committed friends and family. Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1190. Nor does it say anything that a religion discourages association with non-adherents, as many religious groups do. E.g., Paul v. Watchtower Bible & Tract Soc'y of N.Y., Inc., 819 F.2d 875, 883 (9th Cir. 1987) ("The harms suffered by Paul as a result of her shunning by the Jehovah's Witnesses are clearly not of the type that would justify the imposition of tort liability for religious conduct. No physical assault or battery occurred.").

The Government also invited the jury to convict because Defendants "financially harmed victims by driving them into debt and not paying them for their labor." A-1222. More specifically, the Government stressed that Defendants accepted, and even encouraged, these "victims" to volunteer their services to their chosen religious organization. A‑908‑910; A‑1028‑1030; A‑1095-1103. But these "victims" were not coerced or defrauded into performing these volunteer services; they knew full well that their services would be unpaid, and they still chose to volunteer their efforts. A-947-48; A-1152-53; A872-76. This too is commonplace among religions: Under our constitutional tradition, it is a defining feature of religion that it relies on charitable contributions of money, goods, and services from its adherents. See generally James Madison et al., Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments (reproduced in full at Everson v. Bd. of Ed. of Ewing Twp., 330 U.S. 1, 63–72 (1947)). Indeed, many religions call for participants to tithe 10% of all their secular income. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1180 n. 5. But for First Amendment protections, a hostile jury could punish that practice as extortion because of religious pressure constituting "the threat of social ostracism or eternal damnation, or from the promise of community or of eternal." Id., at 1180.

The crux of the Government's charge was that the Defendants "forced" the purported victims to perform voluntary services through religious indoctrination and, more generally, made them feel reliant on OneTaste. See A-1236 (victims "felt like their whole world was OneTaste. It was their community, their friends, where they worked, and where they lived. And the defendants did all of this by design"). But such feelings of deliberately induced reliance on a religious community are entirely unremarkable in the religious context. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1183 (observing that a common technique among many religions is to "slowly lur[e] people into a community and a belief system that they may eventually find emotionally hard to leave, even if they feel some desire to leave").

Many Christians preach eternal damnation without Christ. Buddhists preach eternal suffering without dharma. Latter-day Saints encourage extensive participation in church callings, missionary service, and a tightly integrated congregational life. Countless religious traditions promise spiritual fulfillment, enlightenment, or eternal happiness through faithful adherence to their beliefs and practices. See Volokh, Addiction, 75 Emory L. J. at 1180, 1190. Many religions cause each of us to act and believe in ways non-adherents of our chosen path would find to be irrational or even "rank heresy." See United States v. Ballard, 322 U.S. 78, 86 (1944).

It is no answer for the Government to charge that these so-called victims felt "compelled" to perform the subject services because that compulsion was the product of religious conviction. If each of us are to be entrusted with the right to enter and exit our chosen religions at will, then each of us must also accept the risk that our chosen religions may cause us to donate time, money, or goods. The Court should find that the Free Exercise Clause prohibits this conviction.

[II.] The trial itself was not religiously "neutral."

Government's enforcement action, even under a facially religion-neutral generally applicable statute, violates the Free Exercise Clause when the enforcement of the statute is itself not "neutral," See Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado C.R. Comm'n, 584 U.S. 617, 634 (2018). In Masterpiece Cakeshop, the government sought to enforce Colorado's public accommodations statute in part because of the religious motivations of a baker. Commissioners departed from neutrality by describing the baker's religious beliefs as "despicable" and characterized them as merely rhetorical. Id., at 635. Even "subtle departures from neutrality" on matters of religion are prohibited, not just when a legislative branch enacts a law but also when the executive branch enforces it. See id., at 638.

Just as in Masterpiece Cakeshop, the record in this case is replete with denigration of this particular religion. Ms. Gupta invited the jury to scrutinize OneTaste's vocabulary and the specific doctrines as evidence of wrongdoing. A-1232. She emphasized the specialized use of words or phrases "TurnON" (which seemed [synonymous] with the yoga phrase "state of flow"), "muggles" (meaning non-adherents of OneTaste), "matrix" (referring to "my fake reality of problems"), and "tumescence" (in the specialized spiritual sense of "bad energy that you were holding onto"), and the dichotomy between the "third dimension" (the "concrete world") and the "fourth dimension" ("the higher plane"), and asserted these words or phrases were being used to "indoctrinate the victims." A-1232, A-1235. This argument directly invited the jury to judge unfamiliar or strange religious concepts as proof of religious illegitimacy, which neither prosecutors nor jurors may do. See Masterpiece Cakeshop, 584 U.S. at 639; Fowler, 345 U.S. at 70.

Religions routinely use specialized phrasing like "saved," "possessed," "called," or "enlightened," which may appear unacceptable or incomprehensible to outsiders. That strangeness does not deprive OneTaste of First Amendment protections and certainly cannot underlie a felony criminal conviction, especially when the phrasing refers to spiritual or transcendental concepts. See Thomas v. Rev. Bd. of Indiana Emp. Sec. Div., 450 U.S. 707, 714 (1981). Quite the opposite: Our natural aversion to other religions is why we have tolerance protections enshrined in the First Amendment to begin with. See Ballard, 322 U.S. at 87; see also Marsh v. Chambers, 468 U.S. 783, 792 (1983).

The prosecutor also described OneTaste as a "sex cult." A-1223, A-1264. That label was inherently pejorative. See United States v. Helbrans, No. S219CR497NSR0102, 2021 WL 4778525, *17 (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 12, 2021) (prohibiting the Government from referring to defendants as being part of a "cult," prohibiting insinuations that "leaders brainwash or force members of the community to behave in or observe their religion in a certain way," and prohibiting "incendiary and irrelevant references" to the religious organization). The prosecutor was using this label as a rhetorical device to persuade jurors that OneTaste's teaching should be regarded with suspicion because they were unconventional. Just like in Masterpiece Cakeshop, this label was employed with the impermissible goal of suggesting the illegitimacy of a particular set of religious beliefs and practices. See 584 U.S. at 635.

The prosecutor argued, "that's not because OMing  was actually spiritual. They connected OMing to spirituality for legal protection, and so people would follow Nicole Daedone's teachings." A-1233; see also A-1381 ("They [Defendants] whittled them [victims] down by … indoctrinating them with so-called spiritual teachings and practices."). But what forms of meditation are "actually" spiritual and what are just "so-called" spiritual is not for secular courts to decide. It is no business of our secular government to "prescribe what shall be orthodox in … religion." Barnette, 319 U.S. at 642. The Government simply cannot put the legitimacy of religious or spiritual ideas on trial. Ballard, 322 U.S. at 86-88. Yet the Government did exactly that by arguing:

It is not okay to teach your employees that their spiritual purpose is to fuck the war out of men and that if they stray from the [path] set by OneTaste and by Nicole Daedone, they will be spiritually ruined.

And while there is a narrow zone in which a properly instructed jury can determine whether people's religious beliefs are sincerely held, United States v. Seeger, 380 U.S. 163, 165 (1965), no such instruction was given to the jury in this case. Quite the contrary, the District Court declined to provide jury instructions that any "alleged threats were covered by the First Amendment." A-1211. The District Court even warned defense counsel against referencing Defendants' First Amendment rights: "I'm not going to let you instruct the jury or even come close to instructing the jury on the First Amendment." A-1212. And the District Court refused to order a mistrial despite that the Government "ask[ed] the jury to hold their spiritual beliefs against them." A-1315-1316 (argument); A-1318 (denial).

The Government's rhetorical devices are a far cry from the neutrality required by Masterpiece Cakeshop. The Government was overtly hostile to Defendants' religion in itself and openly invited the jury to judge the legitimacy of OneTaste's religious doctrines and practices. It is no answer that the jury accepted the Government's invitation because the highest law of the land removes that power from legislator, judge, juror, and prosecutor alike. "If one could be sent to jail because a jury in a hostile environment found those teachings to be false, little indeed would be left of religious freedom." Ballard, 322 U.S. at 87.

[III.] Defendants were not charged with commercial sexual practices.

To be sure, nothing in this argument precludes the application of genuinely neutral laws to regulate commercial sexual behavior. For instance, an organization that sells members' or employees' sexual services for money can still be subject, under Employment Division v. Smith, to neutral and generally applicable bans on prostitution. Such laws can be applied without resorting to arguments about spiritual coercion, or claims that the defendant supposedly "indoctrinat[ed people] to believe that [she] was a guru and that her teachings were the path to enlightenment and spiritual growth." A-1222. It would not matter whether the  defendant "taught that orgasm was God." A-977. Commercial sale of certain services that lead to orgasm would be the crime, with no need to address the spiritual significance of the orgasm itself.

Likewise, if an employee claims that an employer required sexual services as a condition of employment, the employee could sue for quid pro quo sexual harassment, again a matter that is entirely religion-neutral. Indeed, the government could even criminalize such quid pro quo sexual harassment. See Tex. Penal Code Ann. § 39.03 (criminalizing sexual harassment under color of public office).

Unlike with the Government's expansive reading of the coerced labor statute, none of this would threaten religions that have a tradition of monasticism, or of religious labor as a calling. None of this would treat religious or spiritual teachings as "coercion." And none of this would treat such teachings as crimes when they lead people to feel moved, or even spiritually or religiously obligated, to perform certain tasks that are given to them by a spiritual or religious community.

Of course, in this case the Government chose not to prosecute under statutes banning commercial sale of sexual services—perhaps because there was no evidence that money was being exchanged in return for sexual activity. But these laws exist, and deal with genuine commercialization of sex. Likewise, laws banning rape and sexual assault exist, and deal with genuine physical coercion of sexual acts. There is no reason for a concern about possible commercialization of sex to be used to justify an overbroad reading of coerced labor statutes, which would apply far more broadly than just to sex.

Because the Government's theory of coercion rested in part on "indoctrination" into religious and spiritual beliefs and threats of excommunication from a religious and spiritual community, these criminal convictions cannot withstand Free Exercise Clause scrutiny….

NEXT: Discovery Sanctions Recommended in "Are You a Jew? … Are You a Zionist?" Case

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7830. 31 Easy, Festive Ways to Dress Up Your Thanksgiving Table

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

By Caitlin Castelaz, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Updated Oct 30, 2026 2:47 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As you plan the tablescape upon which your Thanksgiving dinner will be presented, look to autumn’s stunning natural bounty and colors for inspiration. Earthy green, orange, and red tones can help set the scene, but natural elements like leaves, flowers, pinecones, and foliage, are what will really deliver the “natural abundance” vibe. The best part? Decor that you bring in from outdoors is compostable and inexpensive, if not free.

If you don’t have a ready supply of real leaves, consider creating some of your own, like DIY Candy does. These were made with stencils and thin sheets of cork (both of which you can purchase at craft supply stores). In addition to adding style, these leaves also serve as handy, decorative trivets. You can also purchase premade cork leaf coasters if you don’t want to make them.

Short on time? According to A Beautiful Mess, a beautiful centerpiece can be assembled quickly from items found in the produce department at the grocery store: Group colorful fruits, like oranges, tangerines and pomegranates. Sprinkle green pistachios and sprigs of fresh rosemary along the middle of the table to create the illusion of a decorative runner. When dinner is over, invite your guests to partake of the fruit and nuts as a post-feast treat, or save the tastiest morsels and place them in your kitchen fruit bowl.

The curves of a pumpkin’s stem makes it a natural choice for tabletop decor. Give your simple squash an unexpected twist, as A Night Owl blog does, by attaching a piece of eucalyptus and a nametag to the stem and fashioning a place card. You can purchase faux eucalyptus stems to use for your DIY decor year after year.

Butternut squash is probably in season now at your local farmers market. Bring this culinary hero to the table by featuring it in a Thanksgiving centerpiece, as blog A Piece of Rainbow does here. When placed in a nest of moss and pinecones, it makes a rustic statement.

This simple yet stunning idea from Cherished Bliss isn’t the typical way of serving Thanksgiving cranberries, but it’s certainly stylish. Float a tea light candle atop a handful of fresh cranberries in a water-filled vase. For extra pizzazz, add a sprig of eucalyptus to the water and dip the base of the vase in metallic paint. Or, skip the extras and let the bright berries shine on their own!

The autumn harvest days spent at the local apple orchard might be behind us, but America’s favorite fruit still has a place in your Thanksgiving festivities. Place apples (always in groups of three) of any variety at different places along your table runner, and fill in with pillar candles and faux or real greenery for a rich display.

If you’re burned out on pumpkin-themed decor and pumpkin spice-flavored everything, take a cue from Cupcakes and Cashmere blogger: Swap out the ubiquitous squash for an unexpected edible. Persimmons, for example, are of a similar size, shape, and color but bring a beauty to the table that is distinctly their own.

Cristina Garay at RemodelaCasa uses pears as a beautiful addition to a natural Thanksgiving tabletop display. Add it to an edible centerpiece or place it atop your guest’s place, on its own or with a name card, as an extra touch of hospitality. If, by lucky coincidence, someone has sent you some Harry & David pears for the holiday, why not put them to work before eating them?

Russet, crimson, mustard, and brown: These colors typify the Thanksgiving tablescape, but that doesn’t mean you can’t think outside the box when it comes to your holiday centerpiece. Follow the lead of the blog It All Started with Paint and paint seasonal squash in the color palette of your choice to marry tradition with contemporary style for a look that captures your personality. Or, purchase a set of painted faux pumpkins to use for your holiday table settings every year.

Nature offers an abundance of color this time of year, so use it to your advantage. At the StoneGable blog, napkins are topped with golden-hued leaves, which you can buy online or pluck from your lawn. The centerpiece of tall and short vases and white pumpkins carry through on the theme.

Design Dazzle’s basket of seasonal bounty may look like a headache to assemble, but many of the makings of this Thanksgiving display can be found in your own garden beds. If you do choose to forage in your backyard for your tabletop display, be sure to shake, wash or brush off the greenery, then let it sit for a couple of days before placing it on the table.

Normally hung on a door this time of year, Indian corn can be a beautiful addition to the Thanksgiving Day table. Here, the corn is placed atop plates, along with a seasonal card, to bring color and life to neutral stoneware.

The squirrels in your backyard already know the secret: Acorns are everywhere at this time of year, so there’s no reason not to bring them to the harvest table. Use them as fillers in glass containers or, if you are ready to recreate this DIY craft from Hello Little Home, make acorn napkin ties like those shown here.

Golden-hued wheat is certainly a symbol of the season and the Thanksgiving table. Create miniature sheaves bound with ribbon, as did the blogger at Carolyn’s Homework, or simply use the wheat to create a casual centerpiece of candles, gourds and fruit.

A pie pumpkin, placed atop a dinner plate, makes a wonderful place marker for the Thanksgiving table. Using a paint marker, write your guests’ names on the front of a pumpkin, and set it carefully at each person’s place. It’s a simple gesture but makes for a natural gift they can take with them when they leave and enjoy again, when added to their own homemade centerpieces.

The traditional holiday bird won’t be the only scene stealer this season, when you add feather and cork place cards to your Thanksgiving table. Feathers, corks, and ribbon can be purchased at your local craft store; bind them together to create the look, then watch the expression on everyone’s faces when they marvel at your crafty tablescape.

Bright and cheery, let a sunflower bloom greet each guest when they sit down at the table. Place one inside a folded napkin atop each guest’s plate. For less formal buffet dinners, float a couple flowers in a bowl of water, then place the bowl on a tray filled with rolls of silverware. When your guests go through the line, they’ll see the sunny arrangement and smile.

For a touch of whimsy, sprinkle a handful of fallen leaves over your tablescape. Not for neat freaks, this fanciful display evokes a walk in the woods. However, if you’re playing host to grandma (who never did quite approve of your slapdash cleaning routine), nix this one from your Thanksgiving idea file.

Branches create a natural centerpiece, and a dramatic statement in this country chic home. If you still have trees and shrubs with autumn-colored leaves, consider pruning a selection to decorate your Thanksgiving Day table. Just remember to keep them a reasonable height for dining, or remove them when the meal is served.

Evoke the beauty of nature, without giving the kids ammo with which to torture their cousins: This Thanksgiving printable from Kiki & Company makes an adorable addition to the kids’ table and lends a little fanciness to the little ones’ big meal.

This modern take on a table runner proves that order and symmetry might be overrated. Ruch and wrinkle your runner just so, and nestle vases of bright flowers and little pumpkins among the folds of the fabric for a perfectly imperfect arrangement.

Even after Halloween, pumpkin-carving season persists. Make these clever little votive holders by hollowing out a mini pumpkin and placing a tea light inside. Leave the outside of the pumpkin natural, or gild it with gold-colored paint. The 36th Avenue has the tutorial.

Sometimes simple is best. This understated table setting pairs a single pinecone with dinner plate and charger for an autumnal display that’s perfect for Thanksgiving.

Pumpkins and gourds make great table decorations at a big fall meal. That includes white pumpkins, too!  Here, a grouping of faux white pumpkins and other natural-hued elements set a distinctive Thanksgiving Day table, but it would look just as nice with naturally white (or painted) pumpkins.

Walnuts and pecans are back on the menu at this time of year, so add them to your Thanksgiving table settings for a festive touch. A handful of walnuts gives a name card a boost on this rustic display.

Illumine the simple beauty of natural (or faux) foliage with an arrangement of white pillar candles of varying heights. When the candles start to drip on the kraft paper tablecloth, you’ll know it’s time for pie.

A wooden charger brings a rustic sensibility to a Thanksgiving table of crystal and silver. You can make your own from wood rounds available at most craft stores. Apply wood stain to the rounds or leave them plain for a touch of woodland whimsy.

Another edible arrangement, this one brings together winter seasonal vegetables and fruit (like cabbage and pomegranates) with other colorful picks like bell peppers, globe grapes, and red radishes. Place your produce in a wooden trough or long basket and fill in with parsley and greenery for a unique centerpiece that you can turn into next week’s salad.

Who says evergreens are only for Christmas? Break out the boughs early and fashion them into a delightful place marker. This one from In Honor of Design is made from a couple sprigs of rosemary tied with string.

Nature and artifice combine in this stunning Thanksgiving tablescape. Clear and copper candle holders are complemented with white pumpkins adorned with stripes copper-colored tape, while a patterned table runner continues the theme.

A study in sturdiness, this table runner from Blooming Homestead is nothing more than a pine board stained an elegant dark brown. When laid atop the Thanksgiving table and topped with pinecones, adornments, and a vase full of wheat, it evokes and warmth and cheer.

Mums are the official flower of fall, so give them a spot at the Thanksgiving table. Place small vases of the blooms all along the length of the table for a short centerpiece that’s easy to peer over but still makes a big—and beautiful—statement.

Flowers don’t always have to be arranged in a vase. San Diego-area florist Native Poppy recommends laying a mini-bouquet of dried flowers at every place setting, which guests could then take home as favors. Fresh-flower bouquets are just as pretty, as are single stems in a seasonal color. Placing flowers at each place setting also eliminates the problem of trying to hold a conversation over a tall centerpiece—and probably costs a lot less than that tall centerpiece, too.

#7828. Quartz May Be On Its Way Out—and Here’s How Kitchen Designers Would Replace It

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:06 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Quartz countertops have long been a favorite choice of homeowners and interior designers alike due to their strength, nonporous nature, modern look, and uniformity. However, recent discoveries and legal challenges regarding the material’s potential health hazards to fabricators have caused quite a stir and are now reshaping the industry.

The main issue is with crystalline silica that’s a natural mineral found in quartz. When particles are inhaled, they can penetrate deep into a person’s lungs, causing damage that can lead to serious respiratory diseases like silicosis, lung cancer, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). And many workers have become ill from breathing in dust containing crystalline silica while fabricating quartz countertops. Australia has already banned many engineered-stone products, while California is pursuing policy rules that would prohibit fabricating engineered stone containing more than 1 percent crystalline silica.

As a result, more and more people are looking for safer countertop options to use in place of quartz. “We have found some homeowners shying away from quartz surfaces,” says Kaycee Conallen, owner of Kaycee Conallen Design Studio in Swarthmore, Pennsylvania. There are many alternatives to quartz countertops, and designers have helped us identify three top options for your new home or next remodel.

Note: There is no evidence indicating a health concern with already installed quartz countertops, so if you already have one, you don’t need to rip it out.

One alternative to quartz countertops is eco-friendly, silica-free alternatives like recycled glass and paper composites. Both eliminate silica risks while providing unique designs ranging from bold, contemporary glass patterns to sleek, solid-color paper finishes.

Recycled glass countertops incorporate post-consumer or post-industrial glass fragments bound in cement or resin, offering distinct visual textures from fine-ground particles to large, jewel-like shards. Notable glass brands include IceStone, Vetrazzo, Curava, GEOS, and Compac Obsidiana Zero. Glass surfaces are effective at resisting cuts, scratches, and heat, though stain-resistance and maintenance depend on whether a resin or cement binder is used.

Paper-based composites work well for those gravitating towards a solid color and solid surface materials, such as PaperStone, Richlite, and Fenix brands. Surprisingly durable, these heavy-duty panels are made from layers of post-consumer recycled paper or paper from FSC-certified forests, which are compressed under heat and pressure with a silica-free and petroleum-free phenolic resin.

While heat resistant to about 350 degrees Fahrenheit, minor scratches and stains may appear, but can be sanded out. “Fenix is a man-made resin and paper combination originally developed in Italy, and we love that it has a beautiful matte finish, feels soft to the touch, and is very durable,” explains Conallen.

“Sintered stone is another strong option for its resistance to heat, scratches, and stains,” notes Blima Ehrentreu, founder and CEO of The Designers Group (TDG) in New York City and other locations. Using a high-tech process, natural minerals like porcelain and glass are combined under immense heat and pressure to replicate metamorphic rock with minimal to zero crystalline silica.

The non-porous nature of sintered stone makes it resistant to staining, scratches, intense heat, and color-fading from UV exposure. Brands that make this type of surface include Lapitec, Dekton, Neolith, Florim, Sapienstone, and Caesarstone, which are actively eliminating or reducing silica content. In addition, many of these surfaces contain recycled content.

Conallen also loves the look of authentic materials like soapstone. “Each slab of stone carries unique characteristics, personality, and porosity,” she explains. Composed mostly of talc, this metamorphic rock is free of crystalline silica and has a distinctive, velvety feel. Soapstone offers design versatility, as it ranges in color from subtle grays and muted greens to charcoal or deep black, sometimes accented by marble-like veining. Not only does it offer a classic, understated elegance to modern spaces, but it is also a sustainable option given its low-energy extraction process, nontoxic nature, and recyclability.

From a functional standpoint, soapstone is very durable. It withstands heat, so you can set hot cookware directly onto the surface without trivets. It’s also nonporous so it doesn’t get damaged by acidic etching, spills, or bacterial growth. The only drawback is that it’s a softer material than most of the other options mentioned, so it can show minor scratches.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them

From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

#7827. New Brennan Center Report on Curbing Executive Power

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Many of their recommendations are well-taken.

The NYU Brennan Center for Justice recently published a valuable report entitled "Seven Solutions to Rein In Abuses of Executive Power." The Brennan Center is well to the left of me. But I agree with the vast majority of their recommendations here. We do indeed have an overgrown executive, and it needs to be pared back. I particularly agree with the excellent section on constraining emergency powers:

With just a signature, presidents can declare a national emergency and unlock special powers contained in more than 130 statutory provisions. These run the gamut from the seemingly trivial to the near-dictatorial, including powers to shut down or take over communications infrastructure, freeze Americans' bank accounts, and control domestic transportation. They are intended for sudden, fast-moving crises that Congress can't address quickly or flexibly enough. But presidents of both parties have stretched the meaning of "emergency" far beyond reason, enabling them to draw from a growing stockpile of statutory authorities with few real safeguards.

There are currently 51 active states of emergency, and the longest-running has lasted 47 years.10 Any emergency that persists for generations is, by definition, not an emergency; it's a problem that can be addressed through ordinary lawmaking. Yet presidents have used emergency powers to bypass Congress and unilaterally advance their policy goals.11

The National Emergencies Act once allowed Congress to terminate emergencies with a simple majority vote and without the president's signature. But the Supreme Court struck down that procedure, known as a legislative veto, in 1983. Today, ending an emergency effectively requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto.

Congress should amend the National Emergencies Act to constrain executive overreach.12 Emergency declarations should expire automatically after 30 days unless Congress approves a one-year extension, renewable annually with Congress's assent. And presidents should be required to share detailed reports on their uses of emergency powers. Proposals along these lines have received widespread bipartisan support, with versions of these reforms overwhelmingly passing out of the relevant House and Senate committees in 2024.13

Additionally, Congress should amend specific emergency statutes whose extensive delegations of power and inadequate safeguards make them susceptible to misuse. Of particular concern is the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the most frequently invoked presidential emergency authority.14 Sanctions imposed under this law can equate to a "financial death sentence" lasting years or decades.15 Although the Supreme Court blocked Trump's effort to use the law to set global tariffs, the potential for other abuses remains.

I completely agree, and have previously advocated similar reforms, myself. Brennan is right that IEEPA should be tightened up. While the Supreme Court did rule (in a case I helped litigate) that IEEPA cannot be used to impose tariffs, it still includes a lot of other dangerous powers.

I would add, as I did in this article, that invocations of emergency powers should be subject to  nondeferential judicial review, to ensure that they are used only in the event of genuine emergencies, not bogus ones. Congress would do well to amend relevant emergency statutes to make clear that such nondeferential judicial review is available.

I also strongly endorse Brennan's recommendations on constraining laws governing the domestic use of the military. The Supreme Court did strike down Trump's attempts to use bogus pretexts for federalizing the National Guard; the Ninth Circuit recently reinforced that ruling by rejecting the administration's broad definition of what qualifies as a "rebellion" justifying federalization. But, as the Brennan report indicates, there is still a lot of potential for abuse, especially when it comes to the Insurrection Act.

I also agree with the Brennan report's advocacy of constitutional amendments eliminating presidential immunity from criminal liability for acts undertaken in office, and barring him from pardoning crimes committed by" members of their inner circle, including immediate family members and senior administration officials" and those "convicted of crimes ordered by the president or committed on the president's behalf."

I doubt that these amendments have much chance of being enacted, given the extreme difficulty of passing any constitutional amendment. On the other hand, the reforms to emergency powers and domestic use of the military can be adopted through ordinary legislation. In some cases, they can also be bolstered by stronger judicial review under existing laws and provisions of the Constitution.

I do have a few disagreements with the report. For example, it is not clear to me that the Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter goes as far as the authors suggest. The decision's scope remains uncertain. Among other things, it's not clear how wide a range of federal agencies it applies to and how to reconcile it with Trump v. Cook, decided on the same day. I also think they may overestimate Slaughter's impact, since most federal agencies are already not independent in the sense that there are legal constraints on the presidents' power to fire their heads.

I would also have liked to see more recognition that curbing excessive executive power requires curbing the scope of federal power generally. It is virtually impossible to have a federal government that regulates almost every aspect of human activity without simultaneously delegating vast - and often dangerous - discretion to the executive.

That said, the vast majority of the Brennan report's recommendations are well-taken. I hope future Democratic administrations and members of Congress act on them.

For those keeping score, it's worth noting that Brennan Center emergency powers expert Elizabeth Goitein, one of the authors of the report, is a long-time critic of abuses of emergency powers under Democratic administrations, as well as Republican ones. For example, she condemned President Biden's attempt to use emergency powers to effectuate massive student loan forgiveness. And so did I.

#7826. Why Wind Is More Dangerous When the Leaves Are Still on Trees

Trees with full canopies catch more wind, while wet soil can weaken their hold. Here’s why fall storms can cause serious tree damage.

Trees are vulnerable to powerful storms, even a single gust of wind. While tree damage can occur any time of the year, wind damage is more dangerous in certain seasons.

Fall can be a key season for wind-related tree damage because deciduous trees may still hold their leaves when storms bring strong winds and heavy rain. That’s why anyone who has dealt with mature trees knows how much more movement a leafy canopy creates during a storm.

The reasons leafy trees face more stress during windy weather, and the role wet soil plays, help explain why some fall storms cause serious tree damage.

Tree professionals sometimes describe a dense canopy as having a windsail effect. Leaves and branches give the wind more surface to push against, placing extra pressure on the tree.

A video from arborist education account @fruitstitute on Instagram compared a thick canopy to a sail catching wind. Research published in the International Society of Arboriculture’s journal on red maples found that the makeup of a tree’s crown affects how much wind load it experiences.

A post shared by Fruitstitute (@fruitstitute)

Trees can reduce some of that pressure naturally. Leaves turn and cluster in the wind, while branches bend and move with gusts.

That doesn’t mean a tree should be heavily thinned before a storm. Pruning needs vary by species and tree condition, so major pruning decisions are best left to a qualified arborist.

Foliage can also increase the amount of wind a canopy catches. For example, an eight-year study of street trees in Rochester, New York, showed that most branch failures happened while the trees were in leaf.

Wet ground can add another risk during a windstorm. After heavy or prolonged rain, saturated soil may hold tree roots less securely. The U.S. Forest Service notes that saturated soil and shallow roots can make trees more vulnerable to being uprooted by wind.

Penn State Extension also notes that trees may begin leaning or uproot when wet soil can’t hold the root system securely. Raised soil around the roots can be one sign of movement. A full canopy catching strong wind while the roots sit in soaked soil can create a difficult combination for a tree.

Fall storms can arrive before deciduous trees have dropped their leaves, leaving a full canopy exposed to strong winds. If rain has already soaked the ground, the tree may also have less support around its roots. The combination can increase the chance of broken branches, leaning, or uprooting.

A tree’s condition still matters. Decay, root damage, weak branches, and earlier storm damage can all affect how well it handles high winds. After a storm, homeowners should stay clear of trees with new leaning, lifted soil, cracked limbs, or hanging branches. Penn State Extension recommends professional assessment when a damaged tree could threaten people or property.

#7822. When Are You Too Old To Move Furniture? Experts Weigh In

Learn how to factor in age, strength and safety before your next furniture-moving attempt.

While it’s nice to be able to tackle projects around the house yourself, it’s also important to know your limits, especially as you get older. Jobs you could easily handle in the past, like climbing a ladder to change a lightbulb, can become riskier with age.

This is especially true when it comes to moving furniture. Lifting and maneuvering heavy pieces can quickly lead to injuries, accidents or worse. But it can be tough to know when you’re too old to move furniture, as it varies from person to person.

Ahead, learn about the risks of moving furniture as you age, how to do it safely if you choose to and when it’s time to call in the pros, with advice from strength coach Zac Armstrong and physical therapist Joshua Holskey.

Moving heavy furniture becomes more hazardous as you age, posing risks like back injuries, joint sprains, pulled muscles, fractures and heart attacks.

According to Armstrong, moving furniture poses the greatest risk of injury to the lower back and shoulders. Improper lifting techniques or attempting to move furniture that is too heavy to control can lead to slipped disks, pinched nerves, pulled muscles or injuries caused by twisting. “Most injuries happen mid-carry, when you twist to avoid dropping something and hurt your back or rotator cuff,” he says.

Lower bone density, loss of muscle mass and poor balance are an unfortunate and all too common part of aging that make moving furniture especially hazardous. A trip and fall can easily lead to broken bones under these circumstances and moving heavy furniture only amplifies these risks.

Moving furniture is strenuous work that increases your heart rate and blood pressure. For older adults with cardiovascular disease, this can lead to serious medical events, including a heart attack. Know the signs of a heart attack, and work slowly to avoid overexertion. When in doubt, call a professional mover.

Before attempting to move heavy furniture, follow these tips to do it safely.

While there is no specific age, you’re too old to move furniture when the risk of injury is greater than the likelihood of success. “Is there an age to stop? No,” Armstrong says. “But there is a strength-and-control test: If you cannot pick the item up smoothly and carry it under full control, it is too heavy for you today — at 45 or at 75.”

If you feel uncertain about your ability to move furniture, err on the side of caution and ask for help or call in a professional. Many moving companies offer in-home furniture moving services.

An electric fireplace can easily add ambience and warmth to a room or a household without the associated fireplace installation costs of a real wood or gas-burning fireplace. When gathering our top picks for this list, we included models with realistic flames and sounds so you can feel like you’re sitting by a real fire, allowing you to relax and soak up the heat. Various factors go into choosing the best electric fireplace for a given space and situation. You might simply be looking for aesthetics and something that feels homey, or you might prefer the look of a fireplace and the warmth of an electric heater.

How an electric fireplace will be used and where it will go will help narrow the selection to the style best suited to an individual user’s needs. For instance, will it go in the living room under a wall-mounted TV, or will it add ambience in the dining room? The buyer’s skill level for installation or assembly is also important, along with any extra features and how realistic it needs to look.

The following considerations will help guide your decision on what makes the best electric fireplace for your particular home.

Easy installation is a big selling point when it comes to electric fireplaces. Most simply plug into a wall outlet. The caveat, however, is that electric fireplaces that produce heat require a dedicated outlet. Due to power strip safety precautions, electric fireplaces can’t plug into an extension cord or surge protector. But many of the best electric fireplace models require very little else in the way of installation.

You’ll likely know where you’d like to place an electric fireplace, and it’s important to note that not every model fits every room. Sleek wall-mounted ones, for example, look better in bedrooms and dining rooms.

The planned location and type of fireplace will help determine the right size. It’s vital to get the exact measurements of the space where the electric fireplace will sit or hang, along with the size of the room. For instance, converting a conventional fireplace into an electric fireplace requires the precise measurements of the existing fireplace in order to find the best electric fireplace insert for the job.

The size of the room also makes a difference if the fireplace is meant to heat the room. In this case, it’s essential to ensure that the electric fireplace isn’t too small or too large for the room. Something big enough to heat a 1,200-square-foot room for a space that’s only 450 square feet might be overkill.

A handful of today’s electric fireplaces are purely for looks; they produce a visual fire effect but no heat. Most models, though, generate warmth in much the same way a space heater does. Some come with thermostats to maintain a steady temperature in the room, while others feature basic heat-level settings.

Keep in mind that electric fireplaces shouldn’t be the room’s only heat source. They cannot replace central heating or an electric wall heater, for example.

Advances in LED light technology in combination with small rolling mirrors create the illusion of genuine flames in modern electric fireplaces. Some models include molded fake logs and embers that glow to enhance the effect. The most realistic electric fireplaces and realistic-looking features tend to be more expensive, but not always.

However, not everyone prioritizes realism in an electric fireplace. Some units offer color selection for the flames, such as gold to match holiday decor, green for a spring look, or even purple or pink flames to match the room’s decor or set a certain mood.

Electric fireplaces don’t burn wood, create smoke, or have actual flames, all of which make them safer than the real thing. Moreover, the glass on most electric fireplaces doesn’t even get hot to the touch, making them safe for children and pets. Unlike their conventional counterparts, electric fireplaces can sit safely on carpet or against a wall. They also pose no risk of carbon monoxide exposure.

In addition, electric fireplaces go through tests and inspections during production and come with safety features like automatic shutoffs set to a predetermined time or heat level. Additional safety features may include a Canadian Standards Association (CSA) seal. This certification ensures that the fireplace meets specific safety standards and regulations, giving users peace of mind knowing that the product has undergone rigorous testing and evaluation.

A few tips to avoid electric fireplace mistakes that could affect safey: Follow the manufacturer’s installation instructions, don’t use extension cords or power strips, don’t place objects on the intake fans or heaters, keep them dry, and keep small children and pets away.

A wall-hanging unit will require hand tools, like a drill and a lever, and enough know-how to anchor the wall bracket securely.

Some mantels require assembly while others don’t, and the same goes for TV stands. No matter what type of fireplace it is, make sure to follow the installation instructions carefully and ask for help if something is unclear.

Many people love the idea of a fireplace in the living room, dining room, or bedroom. They provide a warm place to cuddle up with a good book or the latest movie. Not everyone is keen on the mess, work, and upkeep that come along with all that charm, though. Cleaning up ashes, stocking firewood, and maintaining the chimney are chores. #7820. The Best Ice Melts of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

By Zach Lazzari, Additional research provided by Rebecca Wolken

Published Nov 2, 2026 8:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

When the weather turns chilly, most people pull out heavy coats, rugged boots, and, of course, ice melts. Ice-melting products are an important line of defense against slick, dangerous conditions on driveways, sidewalks, and other surfaces. Without using them, drip lines and low spots can turn into serious home safety hazards.

We researched and tested 10 different ice melt products to see which delivered the best results. Nearly every brand improved walking conditions and had a positive impact on overall traction and safety. Some were more capable of handling the heavy-duty demands of high-traffic residential and commercial areas. Others were safer for pets and the environment, making them great for home use. Since it’s common practice to apply ice melts to areas where pets and kids may walk or play, we also spoke with the medical director of a veterinary emergency group to get their insights.

Based on our expert’s feedback and our hands-on test results, we chose the Natural Rapport The Only Pet-Safe Ice Melt You Need as our top pick. If choosing a pet- and kid-safe option isn’t a priority, our recommendations also include value-focused, liquid, and roof-specific products that will go a long way toward cleaning snow and ice from your property this winter. Read on to learn which features to look for and why the following products are among the best ice melts in their respective categories.

Bottom line: Choose the best ice melt based on your needs, whether it's pet safety, budget, or specific applications like roofs.

While they may not be quite as diverse as snowflakes, ice melts do come in a variety of forms, each with its own distinct features. We tested each product in the following list ourselves to help you choose the best ice melts for your needs.

This Natural Rapport ice melt is one of the safest ice melts for pets, plants, and the environment. It’s less corrosive on metal, wood, and concrete than conventional rock salt, and it is also safer on carpet and other flooring materials, should your furry friends or kids track it into the house.

Many environmentally friendly products melt slowly because they use mild formulas. But we were pleasantly surprised by how fast-acting and long-lasting this ice melt was. Its time-released formula not only started working right away but also kept melting, preventing our sidewalks and driveway from refreezing. The crystals are green, so it was easy to see where we’d applied them, helping to prevent waste. Also, our dogs repeatedly walked over the colorful ice melt with no adverse reactions.

Ultimately, this ice melt took the top award because it offers a combination of performance and environmental friendliness. It has organic compounds to help it break down quickly, and thanks to the inclusion of soil-supporting compounds, it may even enrich the soil to a small degree. We spread some over a patch of grass during testing, so we’re interested to see what happens over time.

Read our full review: Natural Rapport The Only Pet-Safe Ice Melt You Need

What our tester says: “We really loved this ice melt’s shaker container for easy spreading. The larger granules also minimized our need to reapply.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Natural Rapport ice melt at Amazon or Natural Rapport.

Snow Joe is a leader in snow removal products, and it has formulated a fantastic ice melt product with the Premium Enviro Blend Ice Melter. It’s made for extreme cold and has a chemical composition designed with the environment, pets, and people in mind.

This blend has an anti-corrosion agent that helps it break down easily while minimizing damage to concrete, asphalt, and yards. It also has a green dye that makes monitoring its performance and presence on the ground easy. When the green coloring fades, it’s time to add more. This formulation did an excellent job melting ice and maintaining clear walkways. We also had a property management company test it, and they were impressed.

Though some may prefer ice melt that comes in a bucket or ice melt shaker, we found the durable bag-style packaging of this Snow Joe eco-friendly ice melt easy to reach into and move around. Be aware, however, that if the open bag gets wet, the contents will bind together and consolidate into a giant rock. We kept ours in the garage, and it was fine.

Get the Snow Joe Enviro Blend ice melt (various sizes) at Amazon, The Home Depot, Walmart, Best Buy, or Snow Joe.

Since almost all ice melt formulations contain salt or chlorides, this salt-free option from Safe Paw is quite unique. It’s a great choice if your household is sensitive to salts or if using anything corrosive is not viable (such as around a classic car, near expensive equipment, or on a newly paved surface). It’s also nonconductive, making it safe around electrical components.

This product comes in a granular form and doesn’t have sharp edges like rock salt. Thanks to its nonabrasive texture, our dogs had zero issues walking through it. They even played right where we tested this product and showed no adverse effects. That’s also likely partly due to the blend’s chemical composition, which isn’t as aggressive as other formulas. While that means it doesn’t melt ice as quickly as some of the heavier hitters we tested, it’s still effective.

In addition to melting a bit more slowly, it also doesn’t work at quite as low temperatures. In our tests, it melted ice in as low as 15 degrees Fahrenheit but struggled if it was colder. Though the label claims it works at -2 degrees Fahrenheit, the manufacturer only guarantees it down to 10 degrees Fahrenheit. We think 10 degrees is accurate—any lower than that, and we’d say all bets are off. So long as you know when and where to use it, you can rely on this salt-free formula around your sensitive family members and in spaces where you want to ensure the integrity of your equipment and surfaces.

What our tester says: “We really liked testing this product because it spread quite easily. We used an old cup to scoop and spread it without worrying about getting it on our skin. In fact, it spread nicely and didn’t cause a reaction even when we used our hands instead of the cup.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Safe Paw ice melt (various sizes) at Petco.

Don’t let this ice melt’s small bag fool you: This Redmond’s Nature’s Blend is packed with concentrated dye-free, urea-free, and polymer-free nontoxic ice melt chemicals that effectively bust ice and slush over an up to 400-square-foot area. The all-natural blend is certified by the Organic Materials Review Institute (OMRI), making it one of the best snow melts for use around children, pets, vegetation, and waterways. It’s safe and easy to apply via hand, shovel, or cup.

This pick’s unique formulation can melt snow quickly in temperatures approaching 0 degrees Fahrenheit. It works a bit more slowly at more extreme temperatures, but we were impressed by its overall melting capabilities in our tests. The fact that the mild formula is also easy to handle and safe around snow blowers, vehicles, and other sensitive items makes it ideal for residential use.

The Redmond Ice Slicer works well in climates with occasional storms and freezes. If you need something for a more extreme environment, you’re better off choosing another product, as overapplication of this melter can lead to red spots and smears on driveways and walkways. While we didn’t notice any spotting or staining during testing, Redmond’s more aggressive commercial- and industrial-grade ice melts might be better in colder and snowier climates.

Get the Redmond ice melt at Amazon or Ice Slicer.

When people think about removing snow from roofs, they often imagine doing so manually. That’s because few ice melt products are made to address ice buildup on roofs—which is what makes this ice melt such a unique product. The tablets are composed of calcium chloride and designed to be thrown onto roofs to prevent snow and ice buildup from wreaking havoc on gutters and adding weight to vulnerable areas. For those living in areas with heavy snowfall where ice dams often form, they are a worthy investment.

During testing, we aimed for problem spots and tossed the tablets up. While snow began to slough off the roof relatively quickly, we struggled to verify the exact rate at which the tablets melted the ice since we couldn’t see it happening from the ground. Still, for their intended purpose, they worked well.

The Roof Melt tablets aren’t granular or spreadable, so they aren’t compatible with larger surface areas like driveways. You could probably use them on the ground where drainage is constricted and problematic, but other options will be more economical for that purpose. If you deal with dangerous ice dams on your roof, however, these tablets are worth having around to quickly and easily resolve the issue.

The best way to determine how effectively various ice melts perform is to fully test each product. As residents of Montana, we began our testing in the aftermath of a winter snowstorm that turned bitter cold. We applied the products to gravel, pavement, and grass in temperatures as low as -6 degrees Fahrenheit.

As the snow went through several melt/freeze cycles over the coming days, it formed icy spots under our rooflines and in several low spots. We tested the ice melts in freezing temperatures on water drips and overnight freezes that created walking hazards each morning. We analyzed how long it took to apply each product, how quickly they melted ice and snow, their degree of pet friendliness when used around our dogs, and a number of other hands-on factors. Lastly, we compared pricing, packaging, and ease of application.

Ice melt products are designed for use either before or after snow or ice has fallen. Their application prevents ice from forming or melts it into a slush that’s easier to clear with a standard snow shovel. Each type of ice melt will perform differently depending on its form and chemical composition. Other variables, such as temperature, ground type, melting time, and environmental impact are essential to consider before purchasing an ice melt product.

Ice melt is available in solid and liquid formulations, each with pros and cons. Solid ice melt typically comes in pellets and granules. It works well for many applications and is typically the go-to solution for road crews dealing with icy and snowy weather. Pellets and granules are generally less expensive and easier to store than liquid formulas, and they add a “crunchy” texture on surfaces that adds grip for walking and driving. Their main downsides are that they scatter more easily across icy surfaces, making them harder to apply with precision, and that they tend to be slower acting and more likely to clump together, which sometimes makes them less effective.

Liquid ice melt is a wise choice for lower-temperature situations and times when faster results are necessary. That said, some products must be applied before ice forms rather than after. When applied, liquid is less likely to scatter, staying in place for longer-lasting results. Liquid de-icers, which tend to cost more, can be more challenging to transport and store because of their weight. Plus, if heavy rain ensues, the product can get washed away.

Self-heating ice melt, which comes in pellet and granular form, generates its own heat when in contact with ice and snow—a process known as an exothermic reaction. Unlike other products that must absorb moisture to create a brine to melt the ice, self-heating ice melt can get right to work.

Ice melts work by absorbing the moisture on the top of the ice, creating what’s called brine, and working its way down to break the bond between the ice and the surface. This creates cracks and flakes that are safer to walk on and easier to remove. All of these products have a temperature limit. If temperatures plummet beyond a product’s ice melting point, the chemicals will no longer be effective. Here’s what to expect from the various ice melt types available:

Many of the chemicals in ice melts can potentially damage surfaces, so it’s important to consider where the product will be used. The most common areas—driveways, sidewalks, decks, and porches—can be composed of different materials, such as concrete, asphalt, wood, and metal. Packaging and product descriptions of the best ice melts will reveal what materials they can be used on safely, so be sure to read this information prior to purchase. It would be unwise to apply a product that could corrode concrete, rust metal, or damage wood on those surfaces around the home.

The quest for comfort and convenience in frigid weather has led to the invention of such products as heated jackets, heated gloves, and electric snow shovels. Similarly, certain ice melts have been developed to work in colder climates. Some products won’t work in temperatures lower than 20 degrees Fahrenheit. This is acceptable if the temperature in an area seldom gets that low, but these products won’t get the job done if you live in a colder spot. For locations where temperatures can reach less than 20 degrees Fahrenheit, you’ll want to purchase a product specifically made for lower temperatures.

The time it takes a product to melt ice and snow depends on several factors. Liquid ice melters and self-heating ice melters act fairly quickly. Unlike solid melters that take time to absorb moisture and create the brine, liquid products are already a brine. Self-heating ice melters have a similar advantage: Instead of absorbing moisture, the pellets will heat up more quickly and melt the ice and snow faster than other ice melters. Regardless of which form you choose, there will still be some downtime while you wait for it to work, which you put to good use cleaning your windows with an ice scraper.

Longevity refers to an ice melt’s ability to keep working beyond the initial application period. A long-lasting ice melter is especially helpful when snowstorms or icy rain continue throughout the day. Although long-lasting ice melt tends to be more expensive, the cost can even out since smaller amounts of product tend to get the job done.

The chemicals in some ice melters can be hazardous to pets and plants. According to Alex Blutinger, Medical Director of Veterinary Emergency Group in Greenwich, Connecticut, “Melting ice can be very dangerous to animals, specifically because of the harsh ingredients in ice melt products. Ingestion of these chemicals can cause stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea. It may also irritate the paw pads and exposed areas of the limbs.” Dr. Blutinger says that, if you suspect your pet has been exposed to unsafe deicing chemicals, you should wipe your pet’s paws with a damp cloth or baby wipe to minimize ingestion through liking and reduce the risk of skin irritation. While using a pet-safe ice melt is smart, you can also reduce exposure using paw was or booties.

Certain elements in ice melters can also do environmental damage, such as killing wildlife that may ingest the pellets or aquatic life if the chemicals reach waterways. Many people are concerned about the impact of using large amounts of these products outdoors, so it’s important to read product information carefully to understand the dos and don’ts of using ice melt.

To ensure you get the best performance out of your purchase (or even a homemade ice melt), try the following de-icing tips and tricks.

If you’re not keen to try to melt ice without salt and want more information about ice melts, here are answers to some commonly asked questions.

Ice melters absorb moisture and create a brine that then melts snow and ice. This eventually breaks the bond between the ice and the surface, creating a slush.

Both. Applying ice melt before and after it snows allows the product to work at its best.

A solid, noncorrosive choice for concrete is the Natural Rapport ice melt. This ice melt is made with calcium chloride, which will not corrode concrete no matter how many times it is applied to outdoor surfaces.

It depends. Some but not all ice melt products are formulated to avoid damaging wood, so read product descriptions carefully.

Generally speaking, calcium chloride is better for ice melt. It’s effective at low temperatures, is a good choice for concrete, and comes in pellet, granule, and liquid forms. Since both types can be unsafe for use around plants or waterways, you may want to refer to the Type section above for more information, especially if you intend to use them around pets or kids.

#7819. I Tried To Renovate Everything at Once. Here’s What Went Wrong…

Taking on too many renovation projects at once can leave everything half-finished. Here’s how to know when it’s time to slow down.

Home improvement isn’t the classroom: there’s no extra credit for taking on more work, and you’re not going to make the honor roll for having the most unfinished projects.

It can be easy to fall into the familiar cycle of jumping from one major renovation to another and finding your to-do list growing day after day without actually whittling it down. I know because I’ve done it. One project turns into two, then something else suddenly feels more important, and before long, several rooms are half-finished at once.

At one point during my current fixer-upper I had so many projects going that the house felt less like a home and more like a construction site.

Before you hit a metaphorical wall (continue as planned if you’re doing demo), take a step back and see if this is starting to sound familiar:

You’ve got several rooms torn apart, tools and materials everywhere, and you keep starting new jobs before finishing old ones. Or maybe working on the house just isn’t fun anymore and every weekend feels like another shift.

It’s much easier to fix a bad plan early than it is after you’re already in way over your head. Spacing projects out gives you time to finish, clean up and actually enjoy the work you just did before starting all over again.

I consider myself a bit of an expert in this area because, well, I’ve been guilty of overcommitting to projects more times than I can count. While I still find myself occasionally doing too much at once, I’m in a better position to recognize those warning signs/red flags earlier.

Recently, I wrote a column for Family Handyman about how I’m adding a 95% day to my DIY routine. Basically, I set aside a day every few months to finish all those little things I’ve been putting off. Missing trim, nail holes, outlet covers and other jobs that keep a “finished” project from actually being finished all go on the list.

I’m also getting better at utilizing my project planner to see projects through and stay on schedule. Writing everything down makes it pretty obvious when I’m trying to cram too much into one week and helps me decide what actually needs to get done first.

Learning how to triage projects will also go a long way. What do I mean by that? Instead of doing a little bit of each project every day, focus on finishing one and then move on to the next one. You can either pick the one that takes the least amount of time to complete so you can check things off your to-do list quicker, or the project that has a more time-sensitive deadline.

For people who think in financial terms, this is like the snowball vs. avalanche debt payment strategy. Or for a sports metaphor, decide whether you need the easy points or should focus on the bigger play first. I’m out of metaphors, but I think you get the general idea.

Also, remember there’s no shame in hiring a professional to finish a job you’ve started. Life gets busy and contractors are often happy to take an easy paycheck on a job that’s already been started. They might even appreciate that some of the early legwork is already done for them. If bringing in someone to do one or a few jobs allows you to finish other things, it might be worth it.

An important DIY skill is learning when to walk away. If you’re currently in this situation, or find yourself overcommitted down the road and are thinking back to this column, just remember it’s totally normal and you’re certainly not alone. If anything, it means you’re working on making your home a little better, and that’s definitely something to celebrate.

But not for too long… there are still projects to finish, after all.
