#7818. Court Blocks W. Va. AG's Subpoena to Environmentalist Nonprofits

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Part of the AG's argument was that the nonprofits relied on a climate change scenario, RCP8.5, that has been recently "retired."

From yesterday's decision by Judge Joseph Goodwin (S.D. W. Va.) in W. Va. Rivers Coalition, Inc. v. McCuskey:

The Attorney General of West Virginia has used the State's power to compel two citizen organizations to open ten years of their files: their drafts and internal arguments, the groups they have funded, the people who serve on their boards, the coalitions they have joined, and what they have told the agencies they petition. Neither organization markets goods nor services relevant to the subpoenas. The Attorney General identifies no consumer who was cheated, no sale, and no purchase made in reliance on anything either group said.

What these organizations do is argue in public about what coal, oil, and gas do to West Virginia's waters and climate. The State's chief legal officer, who has publicly condemned that advocacy, now demands to know how they reached their views and who stood with them.

The First Amendment forbids a State from using its investigative power that way, and I will not allow it while this case is pending.

The country was founded on the premise that a citizen owes the government no account of his opinions or of the people he holds them with. The Attorney General has demanded that two citizen organizations hand the State their working lives.

The State wants a decade of what they published, down to a note sent to a single person outside the organization, along with the unreleased drafts and the internal arguments over what to say. He demanded the names of the organizations that fund them and what each gave, and he has now withdrawn that demand. He still wants the groups they paid, the board members they share, the coalitions they joined, and the comments they filed with the agencies they were petitioning. Because the demand period runs to the date of compliance, the subpoenas reach new communications written while they remain outstanding. No demand identifies a consumer, a sale, or a statement anyone relied on. The subpoenas go into how these citizens arrived at their positions on public questions and who helped them get there.

The Plaintiffs in this case, West Virginia Rivers Coalition, Inc. ("WVRC") and 350.org, promote clean waters, reduced carbon emissions, and healthier lives for the people of West Virginia and beyond. They do not sell any service. They do not advertise a certain product of their own. Instead, they promote ideas. Some of that advocacy and some of those ideas are based, in part, on one model. For that, they have been subpoenaed and asked to turn over ten years' worth of information far beyond any use of that one model.

AG McCuskey's actions violate the protections afforded by the United States Constitution. The Plaintiffs, on this record, have only engaged in protected advocacy speech, not commercial speech. The subpoenas issued on the Plaintiffs trespass on their freedom of association, chill their exercise of the First Amendment, and deter others from engaging in similar conduct.

Because Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their claim that the subpoenas violate their First Amendment freedom of association, and because the remaining injunction factors also favor Plaintiffs, their Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order, is GRANTED.

Attorney General McCuskey is enjoined from enforcing these investigative subpoenas for the next fourteen days as set out in the Conclusion of this Memorandum Opinion and Order….

Plaintiff WVRC is a river advocacy nonprofit corporation organized under the laws of West Virginia, and its "mission is to promote clean and healthy West Virginia waters for all." The nonprofit is committed to "clean water and healthy rivers through research, public education, policy advocacy, citizen water-quality monitoring, and engagement with state and federal agencies." It has a modest staff of 15 and an annual budget of approximately $2 million primarily funded by foundations and other organizations. WVRC regularly submits comments on proposed legislation, permits, and rules concerning water quality. And as this court is familiar, WVRC is a party litigant in multiple cases across the Fourth Circuit that challenge permits and approvals for infrastructure projects, pipeline projects, injection wells, and toxic discharges. Because of its litigation efforts, WVRC coordinates "with other organizations through shared counsel" about litigation strategy.

WVRC also engages in public education and information campaigns, including "statements about the effects of climate change in West Virginia's waters and communities, and about the environmental effects of fossil-fuel extraction, transport, and combustion." It is a member of multiple different coalitions committed to similar goals. To fund ts work, WVRC "solicits charitable contributions from the public through its website, mailings, emails, and events," but it does not publish the identities of its funders.

Plaintiff 350.org is a nonprofit corporation, and its "mission is to build a grassroots movement to end the use of fossil fuels and to accelerate the transition to renewable energy." The organization publishes information about climate change, organizes public demonstrations, and coordinates with other organizations with similar goals. 350.org also "solicits charitable contributions from the public through grant applications and through its website, mailings, emails, and events." Those grants and contributions are subject to opt-in confidentiality in some cases and agreed upon confidentiality in other cases.

And an excerpt from the court's First Amendment analysis (for more on RCP8.5, see this N.Y. Times article):

[T]he Court applies "exacting scrutiny" to compelled disclosures of protected First Amendment speech and association. To be a permissible intrusion on the First Amendment, "there must be 'a substantial relation between the disclosure requirement and a sufficiently important governmental interest.'" …

The subpoenas … "… concern[ ] an investigation into alleged unfair or deceptive acts or practices and other possible violations of the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act ('WVCCPA')." State code authorizes the Attorney General, if he "has probable cause," to "subpoena witnesses, compel their attendance, adduce evidence, and require the production of any matter which is relevant to the investigation."

Under West Virginia law, "[u]nfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are … unlawful." Trade or commerce "means the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of any goods or services and shall include any trade or commerce, directly or indirectly, affecting the people of this state." "Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices" includes 16 different definitions including "[e]ngaging in any other conduct which similarly creates a likelihood of confusion or of misunderstanding."

Deploying these broad definitions, AG McCuskey's theory is that the Plaintiffs, environmental advocacy groups, published information, made comments, and advocated based on a study, the RCP8.5, that has been determined "implausible." According to AG McCuskey, this reliance, and subsequent advocacy, is a deceptive act or practice that affects the energy marketplace of West Virginia.

Begin with common sense—in what way could WVRC and 350.org violate the WVCCPA? They are not financial institutions, lenders, or creditors. They are not businesses seeking to make a profit by engaging with consumers. In fact, both are 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations. They do not sell services of any kind. As explained, Plaintiffs are advocacy organizations committed to climate issues. Their missions are public education, dissemination of information, advocacy in support of their ideals, and public support of those who align with their beliefs. What little items they sell are merchandise bearing their names and logos. Surely these minimal sales from advocacy organizations are not the transactions the West Virginia legislature sought to protect consumers from….

Plaintiffs do not engage in commercial speech. By virtue of their missions as nonprofit environmental advocacy groups, their interests are not economic. Their interests include public education, funding environmental projects, modeling and projecting the effects of climate change, and contributing to a society that values clean air, clean water, and healthier lives. The fact that their advocacy touches on the economy is insufficient to be commercial speech. Therefore, Plaintiffs' protected speech and advocacy alleged in this case cannot be regulated under the WVCCPA.

Accordingly, I find that the WVCCPA cannot supply a "sufficiently important governmental interest" under the "exacting scrutiny" applied to freedom of association claims. I next turn to the severity of the "disclosure requirement" under the "exacting scrutiny" analysis….

As discussed, the subpoenas broadly assert that a violation of the WVCCPA might have occurred. And in his response, AG McCuskey admits that there may not be any WVCCPA violation. He does, however, have authority to issue subpoenas to investigate "whether a violation … has, in fact, occurred."

That violation, AG McCuskey argues, arises from only a few instances of Plaintiffs using a certain climate projection model, RCP8.5. Any publication born from that model, he asserts, is potentially unfair or deceptive. So to assess the breadth of the subpoenas and the compelled disclosure Plaintiffs are subjected to, the court turns to the subpoenas' demands. It is reasonable to assume that the demands would roughly track the RCP8.5-related violations and the allegations of unfair or deceptive trade practices.

Not so. The subpoenas ask for much more. The 16 categories of demands include every statement Plaintiffs have ever published about a West Virginia energy business with a "Climate Claim." But that demand is not limited to climate-related statements supported by the RCP8.5 model. It includes every climate-related statement that names a West Virginia energy business which is published and supported or informed, at least in part, by any model, study, project, plan, projection, or paper. Demand No. 4 is similarly broad: the subpoena demands every published projection concerning West Virginia and all documents related to those projections, without narrowing it down to those supported by the RCP8.5.

The rest of the demands do not even try to mask their broad and sweeping intentions. Donation requests, payments to third parties, and licensing and funding documents of all projects concerning West Virginia are demanded. Every document projecting costs and damages is demanded, as well as every report, study, model, or paper that the Plaintiffs directly or indirectly supported. Documents pertaining to internal considerations are demanded wholesale. So, too, are all documents pertaining to third-party communication and coordination in any fashion. And even with AG McCuskey's last-minute withdrawal of certain demands for donor information, Plaintiffs will still be obligated to disclose "board affiliation, coalition partners, grantees, agency submissions, internal deliberations and drafts, solicitation totals and targeting."

Plaintiffs call this a fishing expedition. In part, I agree. The subpoenas demand a large share of documents in Plaintiffs' control for the last ten years. But even on a fishing expedition, hoping to just get one bite in the vast and quiet water, a person brings a fishing pole. And in other cases, perhaps, a net. Here, AG McCuskey has abandoned both the fishing pole and the net. Instead, he has brought dynamite to the lake. Tossing a couple in, he hopes to catch something.

As stated, compelled disclosure that invades First Amendment protections can only stand if there is a substantial relation between what must be disclosed and a "sufficiently important governmental interest." Here, I find neither a sufficiently important government interest nor do I find a substantial relationship between the compelled disclosure and the government interest….

And the court also briefly notes plaintiffs' retaliation claim, without resolving it:

Plaintiffs have alleged substantial evidence to support their [retaliation] claim. AG McCuskey has publicly disparaged pro-environmental groups and has called for the DOJ to investigate similar groups. He has joined contentious litigation against environmental advocacy organizations. And the chasm between the subpoenas' demands and the purported basis for investigation suggests a retaliatory motive.

This phenomenon of state and federal investigation into the affairs of advocacy non-profits has begun to permeate our culture. The courts have enjoined civil investigative demands on comparable records. [Citations omitted. -EV]

However, because retaliation concerns the Attorney General's motive, I will reserve judgment on Count One until he can present evidence at a hearing for a preliminary injunction. Having already determined that an injunction is warranted on the basis of Count Two (freedom of association), the court declines to address the remaining counts….

Derek Teaney and Amanda Demmerle (Appalachian Mountain Advocates, Inc.) represent plaintiffs.

NEXT: Short Circuit: An inexhaustive weekly compendium of rulings from the federal courts of appeal

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

What would the holidays be without Christmas lights? While nothing brightens a dark winter night quite like a twinkling display, finding the right set can feel overwhelming when strands with so many bulb shapes, lengths, and extra features are available,

To help you find the right options, we researched dozens of popular sets, eventually choosing the JMEXSUSS 33-Foot 100 LED Indoor String Lights as our favorites for their energy efficiency, gorgeous warm white glow, and built-in memory function. Read on to learn more about these and the rest of our picks for the best indoor Christmas lights.

Bottom line: Explore a range of indoor Christmas lights, from energy-efficient LEDs to vintage styles, ensuring a festive and personalized holiday display.

The top picks listed here feature different styles and types of Christmas lights. Durable enough to last several holiday seasons, they fall within different price ranges. These lights meet the criteria previously listed, but they are also attractive and offer a positive user experience.

The JMEXSUSS string lights offer 33 feet of clear-wired holiday illumination. Each string is equipped with 100 LED lights, which emit a warm-white light. The clear wire blends in with different backgrounds like mantels, Christmas trees, banisters, or garlands.

A button on the electrical plug switches through eight lighting modes, which include combination, waves, sequential, flash, slow fade, chasing, slow glow, and steady. If the strand is unable to reach a convenient electrical outlet on its own, this string has a 10-foot lead wire that provides extra length. Finally, the lights include a memory function, which means that when they’re turned on, they revert to the last used lighting mode. However, they can’t connect to another string of lights.

Get the JMEXSUSS indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

The Lidore indoor string lights go back to basics with white wire and traditional incandescent bulbs. These mini lights are strung on a 21-foot wire with a 16-inch lead and 4-inch tail, so most of the wire is devoted to the 100 lights. The white wire option blends with flocked trees or white Christmas ornaments. It can also mix well with tulle and other Christmas fabrics.

Designed so that the entire string will stay lit if one of the traditional incandescent bulbs goes out, the set includes two replacement bulbs. Multiple strings connect to create a continuous light display. The incandescent bulbs aren’t as energy efficient as LED lights, but they emit a traditional warm light. However, these lights may not last as long as standard LEDs, especially if used constantly over several weeks.

Get the Lidore indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

Plugging in and unplugging Christmas lights is a thing of the past with the Brizled LED Christmas lights. All 200 of these warm white and multicolored LED lights are remote controlled, can be used indoors and outdoors, and come with 11 lighting modes to provide any ambience desired. Plus, these lights come with four different dimmer settings to emit a warm glow or bright spectacle.

To make Christmas morning even more relaxing, shoppers can rely on the 26.25-foot range of the remote control for quick adjustments and the programmable timer so the lights stay lit as long as needed. Plus, this 82-foot strand of lights can be connected to two other strands of Christmas lights, extending the lighting effects to more than 246 feet.

Get the Brizled LED Christmas lights at Amazon.

These Loende battery-operated string lights provide versatile decor options and reduce presence of wires and cords. The LED lights operate on three AA batteries and include a built-in timer to help conserve battery power. The lights follow a 6-hour-on, 18-hour-off schedule. The battery pack has a small loop to hide it on wreaths or other decorations.

The Loende lights also come in multicolor and white with a white wire option as well. Each type has eight lighting modes, including combination, slow glow, flash, slow fade, sequential, waves, twinkle, and steady. These lights are waterproof for indoor or outdoor use.

Get the Loende indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

Whether it’s for a 10- to 12-foot tree, a very long stairway banister, or even for hanging around the ceiling, the MZD8391 105-foot Christmas lights can fit the bill. This option has eight different light modes, a copper wire in PVC construction, up to 20,000 hours of life, and LED bulbs to help lower holiday energy consumption. Plus, each of the 300 LED lights stays cool to the touch, no matter how long they are in use.

These Christmas lights also come with the benefit of a memory function and an IP65-rated waterproof construction to double for outdoor use. The end-to-end design supports connecting up to four strings of lights together for a maximum length of 420 feet. Finally, this option comes in multiple colorways and has an easy-to-use remote control.

Get the MZD8391 Christmas lights at Amazon.

Made to resemble authentic vintage decorations, these Abeja bubble lights have a retro vibe straight from the 1940s. Each string is 11 feet long and contains eight lights and can connect to an additional 11 sets for a total of 12 strands.

The Abeja lights contain traditional incandescent bulbs, so their soft, warm light feels vintage, too. Replacement bulbs can be purchased separately.

Get the Abeja indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

At almost 160 feet long, the Twinkly multicolor LED string holds 600 LED lights. It comes with a free app that lets users map the lights using the camera on the connected device. From there, map out the lights’ location and set colors and effects by section.

The app can connect to other devices and control several smart light strings at once. Smart capabilities allow users to set timers, turn the lights on and off from anywhere, and create custom effects. These lights can sync with music and connect with another set of string lights. However, all the cool effects come with a relatively high price, and the app may have connectivity issues.

Get the Twinkly indoor Christmas lights at Amazon or Best Buy.

These Twinkle Star lights bring the Christmas star front and center. They can connect to a maximum of 10 strings. Those connections stay close together with an adaptable design that lets users remove the 16-foot lead wire when connecting strings.

Eight lighting modes are available, including sequential, combination, flash, twinkle, stead, slow fade, and waves. While these lights are white, they are definitely a cool white. They’re indoor-outdoor lights, but the transformer must be kept inside, limiting the number of ways the lights can be hung outdoors.

Get the Twinkle Star Christmas lights at Amazon or Target.

Suitable for indoor and outdoor use, the Holiday Essence mini Christmas lights come with 16 feet of LED Christmas lights with more than 60 LED lights per strand for ample light during the holiday season. These mini lights come in six colorways including blue, cool white, green, multicolored, red, and warm white to suit multiple preferences, and they can be connected to more than 45 other strands of lights at a time.

As for durability, these mini lights are listed as indoor and outdoor lights and should last for greater than 25,000 hours of use. Plus, these lights come at an affordable price point, which makes buying multiple units a cinch.

Get the Holiday Essence Christmas lights at Amazon.

The Louis Choice shatterproof LED bulbs save energy, but they’re also equipped with a built-in timer that runs on a 6-hour-on, 18-hour-off schedule. A 49-foot string provides adequate length to use on a large Christmas tree or banister. However, 16 feet is devoted to the lead wire to help the string reach an outlet.

This model can extend by an additional nine light strings to lengthen its overall reach. A memory feature turns the lights on in the same mode in which they were turned off. Eight modes are available, including slow fade, twinkle, steady, combination, sequential, waves, slow glow, and flash. The package includes 10 twist ties for installation. The globe portion of the light is attractive, but it’s plastic, which can be quite fragile.

Get the Louis Choice indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

We researched more than 90 indoor Christmas lights from almost as many brands. Specifically, we looked at user experience, reliability, and durability. LED lights were more likely to make this list because of their energy efficiency and ability to work with smart technology. However, incandescent bulbs also made the list for their soft, warm light and affordability.

Finally, we considered design. Bulbs, both large and small, globe and novelty, made the list, but they had to have the durability and reliability to warrant their inclusion. We tried to represent a wide range of options and brands to fit different preferences.

Everything from the string length to the bulb size and power source can affect the look and feel of Christmas lights. The following considerations are important to take into account before starting to browse for the best indoor Christmas lights for the home.

Traditional incandescent bulbs work by creating enough heat to make a filament inside the bulb light up. Consequently, these lights use a lot of energy and release a significant amount of heat. However, they’re less expensive than LEDs and have a warm white glow that LEDs don’t.

LED Christmas lights have diodes that emit light via the movement of electrons within the semiconductor. LED bulbs are significantly more energy efficient and durable than traditional incandescent bulbs. They also release far less heat. LED bulbs are used in most smart lights, offering up to several million color choices.

Distance to a power source is a concern when buying and installing Christmas lights. For indoor lights, power must come from electricity or batteries. Lights with an electric plug require access to an electrical outlet or an extension cord. Electricity provides consistent power that never runs out (unless the power goes out). Several strings can connect to each other to use power from a single outlet. However, outlets can get crowded with all the light plugs.

Battery-powered Christmas lights are less common, though they are convenient. They can hang almost anywhere without proximity to an outlet. However, battery-powered lights have a short runtime and will dim as the power runs out.

Wire lengths vary from short 10-foot strings to 66- to 100-foot strings. A longer cord means fewer outlets and connection points between strings; however, experts recommend using strings in lengths appropriate for the decor job at hand. Use a tape measure to estimate the distance required to wrap around the tree or run down the banister.

Bulb size should be to scale with the rest of the holiday decor. Delicate ornaments may get overpowered by large bulbs. If unsure of the right size, mini lights blend into the background no matter the style or theme.

White, single-color, and multicolor sum up the Christmas light color options. Whites can be warm (yellowish) or cool (bluish), and single colors can be red, green, blue, orange, purple, and various hues in between. Pick a color or several colors that complement holiday themes. White makes an ideal neutral when unsure of which color to choose.

Shapes range from globes and small teardrop lights to vintage bulbs shaped like candleholders or snowmen. The shape should complement the rest of the decor, just like the color and style.

A few lighting modes include twinkle flash, slow glow, chasing flash, slow fade, and steady on. Smart LED Christmas tree lights offer the most lighting options. Some allow the user to set the colors by section or offer variable brightness adjustments. Lights that feature lighting modes may cost more than a typical string of Christmas lights, especially if they’re smart lights, because they usually cost more.

Choosing the right lights with the perfect length, color, and style isn’t an easy decision. We’ve answered the most common questions to help make your choice easier and get those twinkling Christmas lights up and running.

The Christmas lights used by professionals are usually LED lights with coaxial connectors, which are a little more hard-core than domestic lights. The wiring may be different, but the lights are not.

Color depends on the decor theme and personal preferences. White offers a clean, classic look, while a single color adds mood. Cheerful multicolor lights bring fun to the holidays. Think about the look you want to create, and go with a color that supports your decor.

Incandescent bulbs are approved for safe use on Christmas trees. However, LED Christmas lights don’t get as hot, which probably makes them a safer option for a live tree.

Remove each bulb one at a time, placing a piece of foil in the socket after removing the bulb. If the lights turn back on, you’ve found the bad bulb.

Longevity and durability vary by brand, but incandescent bulbs typically last two or three seasons, and LED bulbs typically last six or seven seasons. Both can last longer if cared for and stored appropriately. Certain conditions, such as living near the ocean or in an area that experiences extreme heat, can shorten their lifespan.

#7815. When Should You Actually Use Your Hazard Lights? You May Be Using Them Wrong

Hazard lights can warn other drivers when a vehicle is stopped or disabled. Here’s when to use them, and when to leave them off.

Drivers are notorious for forgetting common traffic rules, and that can be especially true during extreme weather. A perfect example is knowing when to use hazard lights while driving.

Hazard lights are one of the simplest controls in a car, but drivers don’t always agree on when they should be used. Seeing hazard lights while driving is especially common during heavy rain, fog, sudden traffic backups, and other situations where drivers want to make their vehicles more noticeable. But should they be used during extreme weather?

Learn when hazard lights make sense, when drivers should leave them off, and what to do when bad weather makes it difficult to see.

There isn’t one nationwide rule for using hazard lights while a vehicle is moving. Some states allow them in certain situations, while others limit or prohibit their use.

AAA notes that hazard-light laws vary by state, so drivers shouldn’t assume the same rules apply everywhere. Anyone unsure about using flashers while driving should check the current driver handbook or motor vehicle agency guidance for the state where they’re traveling.

Hazard lights, also called emergency flashers or four-way flashers, make a vehicle’s turn signals flash at the same time. Their main purpose is to warn others about a stopped or disabled vehicle.

After a breakdown, flat tire, or similar problem, the driver should move as far from traffic as safely possible and turn on the flashers. The same applies after a crash if the vehicle has to remain near traffic. If it can move safely, getting out of an active travel lane should come first.

Extremely poor visibility is one situation where hazard lights may also help while a driver gets off the road.

“In extremely dense fog where visibility is near zero, the best course of action is to first turn on your hazard lights, then simply pull into a safe location such as a parking lot of a local business and stop,” according to the National Weather Service’s resources for driving in fog.

Hazard lights shouldn’t serve as a substitute for headlights during bad weather. AAA specifically advises against switching them on simply because heavy rain makes it harder to see.

“Do not drive with your hazard lights on,” according to AAA. “Hazard lights are meant to signify that your vehicle is disabled. Using them while driving could confuse other motorists.”

The flashing lights can also make a moving vehicle harder for other drivers to read. During heavy rain, drivers should instead turn on their headlights, slow down, and leave more space between vehicles.

“Hazard lights can actually reduce visibility making other drivers think you are stopped or stalled,” according to AccuWeather. “They make it difficult to see if motorists ahead are tapping on the brakes and they don’t allow you to use your turn signals.”

Avoiding dangerous road conditions can be safer than trying to manage them after a trip has already started.

“Check your local weather and traffic reports before heading out,” according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s winter driving tips. “If your roads are not in good shape, consider postponing non-essential travel until the roads are cleared. If you do have to go out, make sure you are prepared in case you become delayed while traveling.”

#7814. A Libertarian Perspective on the 2026 Election

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Why we should vote "Democrat by Default" for federal offices - with a few rare exceptions. I build on a post by political philosopher Dan Shapiro.

I was going to write a post about why, in this election, the right thing for libertarians to do is vote for Democrats for all federal offices, unless either 1) the Dem candidate is DSA, or 2) the GOP candidate is one of those very rare Republicans who oppose all or most of Trump's awful policies. But libertarian political philosopher Dan Shapiro beat me to it, in an excellent post at the Bleeding Heart Libertarian substack. I agree with the vast bulk of what he says. But I have a few additions and caveats that I will append after quoting a few key passages from Dan's post. Before getting into detail, I will note that I generally believe in voting for the lesser evil among those candidates with a realistic chance to win. Thus, unlike Dan, I don't usually vote for third party candidates, even in more normal times. If you're opposed to "lesser evil" voting on principle, we have a disagreement that goes  far beyond the present election. But I would urge you to check out my defense of that practice, where I explain why you should even vote for the evil Queen Cersei over the even more evil Sauron, if those are the only available choices.

I don't expect this post or Dan's will change the outcome of the election. They almost certainly won't. But they might still be helpful in thinking through big issues we face in the current political moment.

Most of my voting life I voted for the Libertarian Party when they advocated classical liberal/libertarian policies. Now those who care about and prioritize liberty and a free society—however they label themselves—should vote Democratic unless the candidate is a Democratic Socialist….

There's been so much criminality and misdeeds in the Trump administration that it's exhausting to cover it all, but keeping "the land of the free and the home of the brave" means remembering the essentials. I provide links when the points I make are not common knowledge and/or might be controversial.

January 6: Trump is the only presidential candidate in the US who refused to concede that he lost. He told a crowd to "fight like hell," and the mob then stormed the Capitol to try to overturn the results. The House impeached him for "incitement of insurrection," and 57 senators, including seven Republicans, voted to convict—short of the two-thirds required. After his campaign of lies and deception and pressuring election officials to falsify the results failed to overturn the election, he later pardoned all the perpetrators of the violence.

ICE: masked secret police who kidnap people and send them to hellholes in El Salvador, where they were subject to constant beatings, sexual abuse, and torture; to the Central African Republic, in the midst of a brutal civil war with severe human rights abuses; to Florida's "Alligator Alcatraz," where large numbers of detainees were held in cages the size of phone booths; and to Fort Bliss, Texas, where guards grabbed detainees' testicles while beating them. There've been zero consequences for this; indeed, Trump says they are "immune."

Not only were the deportations done without any notification to families or lawyers, but ICE has disappeared from databases those they seized so lawyers and families can't find them.

ICE and CBP have rammed people in their cars, dragged the occupants out, and rammed into houses without warrants. They have murdered, wounded, and assaulted protestors and ICE monitors—Alex Pretti and Renee Good, during the ICE occupation of Minneapolis, being the most publicized—but there have been many others.

There is now "expedited removal" for anyone undocumented, which means no hearing before a judge. (And this is even though immigration judges are—wrongly—a part of, and not independent of, the executive branch.) Indeed, Trump fired any immigration judge who disagreed with him or whom he perceived as not being deportation-friendly enough, and replaced the Board of Immigration Appeals, which has denied appeals for almost all deportation orders.

The administration removed TPS (temporary protected status) for immigrants fleeing violence and is deporting them to the very countries the State Department has declared unsafe—e.g., Haiti.

ICE apprehended immigrant parents after they dropped their kids off at school (see here, here, and here), as well as apprehending children and toddlers and using them as bait (the Liam Conejo Ramos incident)….

Trump sent Marines to LA, and National Guard troops to Chicago and DC. This violates a basic norm since the Founding and violates Posse Comitatus, a statute banning the military from policing.

Trump and FCC chairman Carr threatened talk shows and networks for dissenting political opinions.

As mentioned, ICE murdered, assaulted, and wounded protestors and ICE monitors.

The administration targeted people for their political views and for writing op-eds. Rochester resident David Streever sent a critical email to the director of ICE, and five months later, federal officers tracked his movements and staked out his New York City hotel as he returned from an overseas trip….

There is much more, including explanations of why the Democrats (with the notable exception of DSA types) are far less bad than this, despite their considerable flaws. I myself have written about the evils of the DSA here, explaining why they are comparable to MAGA nationalist Republicans.  In addition to the harm individual DSA members might cause if elected to office, it is important to reduce their numbers as much as possible, so as to minimize the chances that socialists could take over the Democratic Party, as MAGA nationalists have done with the GOP.

I have a few additions to Dan's arguments.

First, it is essential to consider the enormous scale of Trump's harmful and unjust immigration and trade policies. When it comes to setting issue priorities, scale matters a great deal. Even under normal administrations, immigration restrictions threaten the economic and civil liberties of American citizens (to say nothing of those of immigrants themselves) more than any other federal policy. Trump's vast expansion of exclusion and mass deportation has made things a lot worse. The liberty and well-being of millions of people are at stake.

Trump's trade policies seek to impose the highest tariff levels since those that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression, and also are a grave menace to the rule of law. Here too, we're talking about massive effects on the liberty and welfare of millions. Judicial review can and has helped curb these abuses (more on the tariff front than immigration). But there is much Congress can do to help, including curbing funding to ICE and other agencies complicit in wrongdoing. Congressional Democrats also plan to cut back executive tariff authority. That may not succeed while Trump remains in office, but can help set the stage for later progress.

Dan raises the issue of whether non-DSA Democrats might be worse than the Trump-era GOP on economic liberty issues. This becomes an easy issue if you recognize that immigration restrictions and tariffs are also violations of economic liberty. Due to their massive scale, Trump's actions in this area easily outweigh the very real economic policy flaws of non-DSA Dems. And then we have such things as his acquisition of federal government stakes in numerous private firms, something that even the most left-wing recent Democratic presidents didn't attempt. It's a dramatic example of how MAGA nationalists have dangerous economic policies similar to those of socialists.

It is also important to remember that a Democratic Senate could block Trump's horrible executive and judicial nominees. I don't want to see any more Pete Hegseths and RFK, Jrs. In Trump's first term, he had some good judicial nominees. In the second, he has mostly  bad ones (Emil Bove is a particularly egregious example). From a libertarian perspective, I'd rather have a standard liberal nominee fill the next Supreme Court vacancy (despite all the flaws such jurists have) than the type of right-winger Trump II is all too likely to nominate. Such a person would probably be selected for his willingness to turn a blind eye to executive abuses of power, trample civil liberties, and bulldoze constitutional obstacles to MAGA nationalist policies, such as federalism and separation of powers. There may well not be any Supreme Court vacancies, of course. But lower court nominations will arise, and they matter too.

Finally, I'm more hawkish than the average libertarian, and I think it's important to counter Trump's policies of undermining the Western alliance, and coddling mass-murdering dictators like Vladimir Putin and (to a lesser extent) Xi Jinping. We should care about defending liberty worldwide, not just in one country, especially since the two are interconnected. The Democrats (except for a few far-leftists) oppose this awfulness and could use control of Congress to help curb it.

In these and other areas, a Democratic-controlled Congress could not fully stop Trump's abuses. The executive has accumulated too much power for that, often in constitutionally dubious ways. But congressional control of nominations and purse strings can do much to constrain the executive at the margin. And electoral repudiation of Trump's abuses can reduce the risk that future presidents will imitate them.

I do have a few caveats to attach to Dan's otherwise compelling points:

First, Dan doesn't differentiate between elections for federal offices and those for state and local ones. I do. Beating the GOP in federal races is vital for countering Trump's awful agenda. At the state and local level, other issues are dominant, and Republicans are often better than Dems on the crucial issues of housing, state-level taxation, and state and local economic regulation. Which party is better on these and other state and local issues will vary from state to state. For example, red state Republicans are much better on the crucial issue of housing deregulation than blue state ones (who often back exclusionary zoning against Democratic reform efforts). Thus, it might make sense to vote for Republican candidates in some state and local races, but not others, depending on the issues involved.

Second, when it comes to the DSA problem, there can be difficult questions about what to do with Dem candidates who are not actual DSA members, but seem closely adjacent to them. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is a notable example. He says he's not a socialist, but also is closely aligned with socialists like Bernie Sanders, and "influencer" Hasan Piker, the guy who - among other things - praises communist mass murderers like Mao Zedong.

In this post, I'm not going to try to adjudicate each individual candidate and race. I will merely say that if you're trying to figure out whether a non-DSA member is actually a socialist, two noteworthy indicators are 1) whether he or she supports government control of all or most of the economy and 2) whether they praise socialist despots abroad, such as Mao, Fidel Castro, and others. If the answers to one or both questions are "yes," that's a strong indication they might be socialists, and therefore not worth voting for, except perhaps against the very worst Republicans.

There is a similar calculation in identifying the few Republicans who have opposed Trump's worst policies. Here, key indicators are whether they have opposed his tariffs, his mass deportations, his kowtowing to Vladimir Putin, and his attacks on civil liberties. Sadly, Republican candidates with consistent strong records on all or most of these issues, are few and far between, though Republican criticism of the tariffs and policies towards Russia have picked up in recent weeks.

Finally, as Dan would agree, voting for Democratic candidates does not imply supporting everything the Democratic Party does, or abstaining from criticizing Democrats on the many occasions when they do bad things.

Elsewhere, I have argued that libertarians, in the current political moment, should seek an alliance with "abundance liberals." But alliance is not the same thing as total agreement. And the Democratic Party obviously includes various factions who are much worse than the abundance types. We should keep that in mind, even as we recognize that right now the Republicans are much worse.

City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7812. Fix Your Fridge: All Your Questions About Refrigerators Answered

Frustrated by refrigerator issues? Use these tips to handle common problems and routine maintenance.

Not usually. In older refrigerators, water is often stored in a reservoir near the crisper drawers. But in many modern models, water flows through tubing that runs up the back of the refrigerator to the water filter, then down to coiled tubing that serves as a storage tank, and back up to the door dispenser. Along the way, it’s exposed to warmer parts of the refrigerator. Because the water is constantly flowing through the tubes instead of chilling in a reservoir, it may not be as cold as you’d like. Here are a few ways to enjoy colder water:

If the ice from your refrigerator has an unpleasant smell or taste, it’s probably time to clean the ice maker. Do this once or twice a year, depending on how often you use it:

We all learned in school that water freezes at 32 degrees. While that temperature is fine for making ice cubes, it’s too warm for safely storing frozen food because mold and bacteria can continue to grow on food surfaces. According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the ideal freezer temperature is zero degrees. This is also the recommended factory setting for most major refrigerator brands, helping keep food safely frozen while conserving energy and extending the life of the appliance.

Dirty condenser coils are a common culprit. When they’re clogged with dust, the refrigerator can overheat, causing the compressor’s overload protector to shut it down. The refrigerator may restart automatically once the compressor cools, but by then your food may already be warming up. Vacuum the coils regularly to clear debris and prevent overheating.

Also check the condenser fan. If it’s blocked by debris or not spinning freely, the fridge can’t release heat efficiently. Remove any obstructions and clean the fan thoroughly.

Finally, check the interior light. A stuck or misaligned door switch can leave the light on even when the door is closed, raising the temperature inside the refrigerator. To test it, close the door and use a butter knife to pull the door gasket slightly away from the frame. If light shines out, the switch may be faulty or out of alignment.

Dish soap is a trusty staple. Put a drop on a microfiber cloth with warm water and wipe with the grain of the metal. Wipe again with a clean damp cloth, then towel-dry to prevent water spots and soap residue.

For tough grease or fingerprints, use a stainless steel cleaner. These products are formulated to cut residue without leaving streaks, making them a good step up when soap and water aren’t enough.

For a quick polish after cleaning, a little olive oil can help restore shine. Apply it with a microfiber cloth and buff with the grain until smudges disappear. Follow with a dry microfiber cloth to remove excess oil and prevent a greasy finish; this leaves behind a thin protective layer that resists fingerprints.

Dust and debris can easily accumulate on refrigerator coils, forcing the appliance to work harder and use more energy. Fortunately, cleaning the coils is simple. First, unplug the refrigerator and access the coils (they’re usually behind the front kickplate or on the back of the unit). Use a shop vacuum to remove dust and debris. For hard-to-reach places, use an air compressor with a blower nozzle to loosen the dust, then vacuum it up. Remove any stubborn dirt with a soft-bristled brush or duster, then vacuum again. Finally, clean the floor around your work area, reattach any panels and plug the fridge back in.

First, listen. Do you hear anything? There should be a rumbling from the auger inside the ice bin. If there’s a rumble and no ice, ice is likely stuck in the door chute and needs to be cleared out. If you hear a hum but no rumble, the auger is probably stuck and can’t spin; emptying the bin and reloading the ice may fix it. If you don’t hear any sound at all, the dispenser switch may be broken and will likely need to be replaced by a pro. If you hear the auger turning and nothing’s clogging the chute, move on to these steps:

A great place to start is with the handles, which tend to yellow and collect grime over time. Instead of replacing them, clean and repaint for a quick, budget-friendly refresh. You’ll need spray paint formulated for plastic, plus a degreaser and a scrubbing pad.

Pry off the caps that cover the side screws, then open the door and remove the remaining screws. Take off the handles and wash them with degreaser and hot water, scrubbing any textured areas to remove buildup. Wipe them with a dry cloth and let them air-dry completely. Mask off any emblems or chrome trim, then spray-paint, coating the sides first, followed by the flat surfaces. Once the paint has dried, reinstall the handles.

Baking soda is a highly effective odor neutralizer. As bacteria break down food, they release smelly molecules that can be either acidic or alkaline (basic). Baking soda, aka sodium bicarbonate, reacts with these compounds to help reduce odors. Stash an open box in the refrigerator and replace it about every three months. Tip: Date the box so you know when to replace it.

If your refrigerator isn’t cooling properly, start with these quick checks. You may be able to solve the problem yourself before calling a pro.

#7811. 2026 Heating Oil Prices: Are They the Worst They’ve Ever Been, and Is There Any Way to Keep Costs From Skyrocketing?

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Nov 2, 2026 2:27 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you are one of the 4 million households in the United States that rely on heating oil to power furnaces, boilers, and water heaters, you might be experiencing sticker shock when it comes to heating oil prices this season. The price has risen to about $6 per gallon compared to last year’s $3 per gallon.

According to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, the cost to heat a home using heating oil is expected to rise by at least 50 percent across the region, including states like Maine, Massachusetts, and New York. In fact, Maine has been getting a lot of attention lately since the state relies heavily on this type of fuel, and prices have already reached 80 percent higher than just a year ago. Learn why heating oil is so expensive this year and what you can do to manage the “pain at the tank.”

Heating oil prices typically rise during the winter as demand increases heading into the heating season, says Lowell Richard, director of fuel operations at Townsend, a home service company based in New England that offers fuel delivery as well as HVAC and electrical services. “Over the past several months, global events and geopolitical uncertainty have driven significant increases in the cost of heating oil, propane, gasoline, diesel fuel, and other forms of energy,” he explains. With a shift in shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war with Iran, the cost of heating oil has gone up. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine has also impacted the global supply, leading to price hikes.

By comparison, propane prices are relatively unchanged from last year because propane has a different supply structure than heating oil. “Propane is a byproduct of both crude oil and natural gas processing, so its price is linked to both—natural gas prices tend to be steadier, while crude oil does fluctuate,” says Richard. “Additionally, propane has lower wholesale prices and adequate inventories. As a result, propane prices are typically steadier than heating oil prices.” It’s worth noting that propane prices vary by supplier and delivery volume, so Richard recommends checking with your local supplier for the current price.

If you are struggling to pay your heating bills, consider tapping into available resources in your area. “Every supplier is unique, but at Townsend, we offer several ways to help our customers spread out or control their costs,” explains Richard. “We have a variety of budget plans to help fit our customers’ financial needs. For example, automatic delivery is something we encourage because it typically offers better pricing and helps homeowners avoid emergency delivery fees.”

Fortunately, there are several ways for you to help offset high heating oil prices on your monthly bill. Try making one or more of the following changes in your home to keep heating costs manageable, and if suspect damage to your oil tank, have the tank checked and replaced if necessary.

Set your thermostat to a comfortable temperature, but keep in mind that setting it even a few degrees lower can save a noticeable amount on your energy costs, says Richard. “Intentionally setting your thermostat 7 to 10 degrees lower when you are sleeping or away can save up to 10 percent on annual heating costs,” Richard explains. Investing in a programmable or smart thermostat will help you set temperature preferences and schedules, even when you are not home.

Check all the doors, windows, and exterior walls for drafts, since your home can lose heat if ‌air is leaking out. “Replace old or missing weatherstripping around doors, windows, and pipe entry points, and seal cracks in your foundation if you have any,” suggests Richard.

Use a space heater so you can lower your thermostat a few degrees. Choose an energy-efficient model that has a thermostat, adjustable heat settings, sleep mode, and auto-off timers to avoid wasting energy. Always turn a space heater off when you leave the room.

Featuring three heating modes, quiet operation, and an attractive look, this efficient space heater earned “best overall” in our hands-on testing.

“Change your air filter every 30 to 90 days,” says Richard. “A clogged air filter will significantly impact how efficient your system is, so make this a regular habit.”

Maintain your heating system to ensure it is running as efficiently as possible, which in turn requires less energy to heat your home. “Get a fall tune-up to catch small problems before they become bigger, and therefore pricier, problems,” says Richard.

“If your water heater runs on heating oil, keep it set to 120 degrees Fahrenheit for safety and to save on energy costs,” notes Richard.

#7810. Does Every Home Need a Bathtub? The Pros and Cons of Going Tub-Free

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Updated Nov 2, 2026 2:35 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

There are shower people, and then there are bath people. While these two groups may be able to debate the advantages and disadvantages of having a bathtub in a home from sunrise to sunset, not every home needs a bathtub and some can’t do without.

Even though a bathtub may simply be nice to have, there may be other reasons to include or exclude a bathtub if you are thinking about future resale value and your investment. With luxury showers growing in popularity, homeowners’ needs for tubs are changing.

https://secure.money.com/embeds/embedder.js?v=1

Rachel Moussa, founder and Realtor at Blushwood Realty Group in Texas, says that when she first got into he unwritten rule was that there should be one bathtub on each floor that has a bedroom. For two-level homes with bedrooms upstairs and downstairs, there should at least one tub on each floor. We get that. If you love a good tub soak, you don’t want to have to schlep your bath salts, book, beverage, candle, and other gear to another floor.

This tub-per-floor rule, Moussa says, is no longer hard and fast. Whether you’re remodeling a bathroom or contemplating a home without a bathtub, here’s what to consider if you’re thinking about ditching the tub.

From a time and water waste perspective, showers have the upper hand. The average shower in the U.S. lasts approximately 8 minutes and uses approximately 16 gallons of water. A bath is a more languid affair. Sometimes soaks can last more than a half an hour and use around 70 gallons of water, which doesn’t include the water you might use to rinse off after a bath. The less water you use bathing, the more money you can save on your water bill.

The Keenray bucket towel warmer heats up in just 6 minutes and holds up to 2 bath towels measuring 70 x 40 inches. See our full review.

Shower people may not want a bathtub of any kind in their home, and might go as far as to remove a tub from their primary suite and put in a walk-in shower. If you plan to stay in the home long-term, nixing a tub really isn’t much to worry about. However, if you plan to put your house on the market in the near future and your floor plan doesn’t include a tub, understand that you’re automatically excluding some percentage of potential buyers.

After hundreds of sales and experience in renovating and flipping houses, Moussa says there are people who will not buy a house without a bathtub. In contrast, having a bathtub in a home is highly unlikely to tank a real estate transaction. So erring on the side of at least one tub in the house could make a difference in your ability to sell your home.

Moussa points out that jetted tubs can be pretty gross if they’re not taken care of properly. The interior pipes of jetted tubs that are not filtered or cleaned with appropriate chemicals can develop bacteria and microbial growth. When the jets turn on, this bacteria shoots into the tub along with the water, which can result in adverse health effects, including urinary tract infections and skin irritations or infections.

Families with young children or pets tend to rely heavily on tubs; many would consider a quality bathtub essential. Washing little ones in the kitchen sink may work while they are really small, but there comes a point when that doesn’t work anymore; tub baths, unlike showers, can get the kids clean while you stay dry. Similarly, a bathtub is often the easiest place to scrub dogs and other pets clean after they play outdoors.

RELATED: The Best Tub-to-Shower Conversion Kits to Update the Bathroom

Walk-in showers are generally better than tubs for seniors or those with mobility issues. Showers are easier to get into and out of than tubs are, and are thus usually preferred by those who are aging in place.

However, as Moussa mentions, houses do shift a little over time, so a curbless shower built at the right angle now may create an opportunity for water to pool years down the road. A shower that has even a small lip or curb can contain water better and eliminate future stress. Accessible walk-in tubs, which have with a side door to the bathtub for easy entry, are another option.

How often you plan to have a long, luxurious bath is another factor. If you don’t have a hot tub at your home, a hot bath is the next best thing. Creating a spa-like environment is a benefit many homeowners seek out when looking for a primary suite with a bathroom. A bathtub with a ledge around the top or near a source of natural light is another benefit that adds to the ambiance.

Many adults like baths because of the luxury associated with them, but Moussa points out that modern showers can be extravagant too. Large showers with frameless glass elevate the aesthetic of a bathroom. These showers often have multiple shower heads and settings, built-in seating, and plenty of space to shower without feeling cramped. The steam keeps you warm, and you get a constant water supply at your preferred temperature, unlike a tub where the water gets gradually cooler.

#7809. What Is “House Blindness”? I Think I Have It

House blindness makes clutter, half-finished projects and little repairs fade into the background. Here’s how to spot it in your own home.

Hear no mess. See no mess. Speak no mess.

If only that actually made the mess go away. Sometimes in the life of a DIYer, you get a little too comfortable with living in a half-finished house.

For me, I often see straight through the small mountain of tools and materials stacked in the corner of the room where we’re currently (…have been for a while…) renovating. And the spackle on the wall that needs to be sanded down and painted? Invisible to my eyes.

The missing trim in the kitchen, sticky door to the basement, loose handle on the trash can are all obvious to anyone stepping foot in my home, but not so much to me and my family.

House blindness is simply when you get so used to the mess, clutter or unfinished jobs around your home that you stop noticing them. Think of it like going nose blind, but with imperfections in your home. It can also be referred to as “clutter blindness,” “mess blind,” “clutter creep”, or something similar.

A post shared by Emma Shoemaker | DIY & Home (@shoemakesnew)

Once I heard the term, it immediately made sense. I’m not purposely ignoring the pile of tools in the corner or that missing piece of trim. I’ve just walked past them so many times that they’ve basically become part of the room.

The concept of house blindness isn’t overly complex. However, it might be confronting or hard to realize that it’s something you’re doing too.

For me, the biggest giveaway is when I suddenly notice something that’s been sitting there for weeks or months. If guests are coming over, I take a photo of the room or I simply look at it from a different angle. All of a sudden, that pile I’ve walked past 100 times is impossible to miss. If that sounds familiar, you might be doing it too.

Now, for solutions. Here are some things I’ve discovered that help.

Because our house is usually a revolving door of major renovations, there’s almost always at least one major project going on. To help with construction mess spilling into other rooms, I keep a designated tool and materials box that everything goes into once the work is done for the day.

I’ve also prioritized 95% days, which are days I set aside specifically to finish all those little jobs I’ve been putting off instead of starting something new. Think missing trim, nail holes, outlet covers and all the other annoying final steps that keep a project at 95% instead of actually done.

Another one that might seem silly but does work is to look at your home from angles you don’t normally see from. If you’re tall, try kneeling or sitting on the ground and looking around. Or if you’re short, get a step ladder for a new perspective.

One trick I recently learned but haven’t tried is to take photos around your home and look at them on your phone later. Viewing them through this new lens helps strip away the usual filters your brain uses to block that clutter noise and can help you see more clearly.

Try one, or multiple, of these approaches and see what works best. Thankfully, clutter is usually a pretty easy issue to fix and if it’s something you’ve gone house blind to, it doesn’t take much to start noticing it again.

#7807. 50 Haunted Buildings That Show Every State Has a Ghost Story

From old hotels and historic homes to former prisons, every state has a building with a past and a few lingering ghost stories.

Spooky season is right around the corner, and what better way is there to celebrate than to learn a little history and some fun facts about some of the most haunted places across the country?

Each state is home to unexplainable stories, whether that’s at historic hotels, residences, prisons, and more. Many of the buildings still welcome visitors today, giving anyone interested in old architecture and local lore a chance to see them firsthand.

Learn about famously haunted buildings from every state.

Built in 1837, Selma’s St. James Hotel has spent much of its life welcoming travelers, some of whom say the historic hotel has a few guests who never checked out.

The Red Onion Saloon opened in Skagway in 1898 during the Gold Rush, and stories about former occupants still follow the historic building today.

Built in 1895, the Victorian-era Rosson House is one of Phoenix’s best-preserved historic residences and has inspired local stories about strange sounds and unexplained happenings.

The Crescent Hotel has overlooked Eureka Springs since 1886, and its unusual history has helped make it one of the state’s most famous spots for ghost stories.

Built in San Diego in 1857, the Whaley House served as both a family home and courthouse before becoming known for reports of strange sights and sounds.

The Stanley Hotel opened in Estes Park in 1909, and its grand halls have since become nearly as famous for ghost tales as for overnight stays.

Samuel Clemens and his family moved into Hartford’s Mark Twain House in 1874, and visitors today occasionally report footsteps and other odd happenings inside.

Built in the 1850s on Pea Patch Island, the former Civil War fort has a long history as a military prison and is now a popular setting for stories of unexplained activity.

The famous pink hotel opened in 1928 and is associated with stories about its founder, Thomas Rowe, whose ghost is reportedly seen around the property.

Since opening in Americus in 1892, the Windsor Hotel has hosted generations of guests and gathered its share of ghost tales along the way.

Built in 1882, ʻIolani Palace was the residence of Hawaii’s last ruling monarchs. There are stories about apparitions of Queen Liliʻuokalani and unexplained sounds, including reports of a piano playing.

The Old Idaho Penitentiary opened in Boise in 1870, and its years as a prison left behind plenty of stories about strange noises and shadowy figures.

Opened in 1858, the former prison has a dramatic history and is now open for tours.

This 19th-century inn is associated with the “Blue Lady,” reportedly seen in rooms and hallways and sometimes accompanied by the smell of cherry tobacco.

Built in 1868, the Villisca Axe Murder House became infamous after the 1912 killings there and later gained a reputation for unsettling experiences inside.

The current Eldridge Hotel building opened in Lawrence in 1925, continuing a hotel tradition on the site that stretches back much further and includes several ghost tales.

Louisville’s Waverly Hills Sanatorium opened in 1926, and the former hospital has since become closely associated with stories of strange figures and unexplained sounds.

Built in St. Francisville in 1796, The Myrtles now welcomes overnight guests, many of whom arrive already familiar with the home’s long haunted reputation.

The Kennebunk Inn began as a private home in 1799, and stories about former residents and workers have followed the property through its later life as an inn.

Baltimore’s Lord Baltimore Hotel opened in 1928, and guests over the years have shared stories about unexpected elevator rides, unexplained noises, and unusual sightings.

The Lizzie Borden House, built in Fall River in 1845, became famous after the 1892 murders and now attracts visitors interested in both the case and the home’s ghost stories.

The iconic 1887 hotel has long been associated with reports of apparitions and unexplained activity.

These former sandstone caves date to the 19th century and have accumulated stories of ghostly activity.

King’s Tavern dates to the 1700s and began serving travelers in Natchez in 1789, with ghost tales becoming another chapter in the building’s long history.

The former prison operated for 168 years and is now open for history and paranormal tours. Its enormous cellblocks and long institutional history add to its spookiness.

Fort Benton’s Grand Union Hotel opened in 1882, and its long life on the frontier has produced more than a few stories about strange sounds and sightings.

The Argo Hotel was built in Crofton in 1912 to serve railroad passengers, though today its history also includes stories of unusual encounters reported by guests.

Opened in Tonopah in 1907, the Mizpah Hotel is best known in ghost lore for a mysterious figure commonly called the Lady in Red.

The Mount Washington Hotel opened in Bretton Woods in 1902, and one of its best-known stories involves the supposed appearance of a former owner’s wife.

The 1923 hotel is associated with the “Lady in White,” reportedly seen wandering the hallways and accompanied by stories of singing, laughter and unexplained activity.

The current La Fonda on the Plaza opened in Santa Fe in 1922, continuing a long history of lodging on the site and adding a few ghost stories over the decades.

The Morris-Jumel Mansion, built around 1765, served as George Washington’s headquarters during the Revolutionary War and later became known for reports of ghostly figures.

Asheville’s Grove Park Inn opened in 1913, and its best-known ghost story centers on a mysterious guest remembered simply as the Pink Lady.

The 1880s mansion built by the Marquis de Mores is one of North Dakota’s most distinctive historic buildings. It has also been included in the state’s modern haunted-location lore.

The Ohio State Reformatory opened in Mansfield in 1896, and visitors to the former prison often hear stories about strange sounds and figures inside its cellblocks.

Oklahoma City’s Skirvin Hotel opened in 1911, and a century of guests has produced a steady collection of stories about unusual noises and sightings.

Completed in Portland in 1914, Pittock Mansion now operates as a historic house museum, where visitors have occasionally reported unexplained sounds and movement.

Philadelphia’s Eastern State Penitentiary opened in 1829, and the abandoned prison blocks have inspired ghost stories for decades.

Newport’s Belcourt was completed in 1894, and the Gilded Age mansion has become associated with stories about strange sounds and unexpected figures inside.

Charleston’s Francis Marion Hotel opened in 1924 and has since gathered stories of unexplained footsteps, flickering lights and a mysterious figure said to linger inside.

The Bullock Hotel opened in Deadwood in the 1890s, and local stories claim former owner Seth Bullock still makes the occasional appearance.

Nashville’s Ryman Auditorium opened in 1892, and more than a century of performances has also produced stories about mysterious figures and sounds after the crowds leave.

The Menger Hotel opened beside the Alamo in 1859, and generations of guests have contributed stories about former visitors who supposedly still wander its halls.

Built in Salt Lake City in 1901, the McCune Mansion has served several purposes over the years and has also become known for reports of ghostly figures inside.

The Green Mountain Inn has welcomed guests in Stowe since 1833, though some visitors say footsteps and tapping sounds continue after everyone has settled in for the night.

The 1927 hotel has a long history of celebrity guests and Prohibition-era stories, along with reports of apparitions and unexplained activity.

Built in Port Townsend in 1892, Manresa Castle began as a private home before becoming a hotel with stories about unexplained sounds and sightings.

The Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum began receiving patients in Weston in 1864, and today its tours cover both the former hospital’s history and the ghost stories that followed.

Milwaukee’s Pfister Hotel opened in 1893, and guests over the years have reported unusual sounds and sightings in the historic hotel.

The current Occidental Hotel in Buffalo dates to the early 1900s, and one of its best-known stories involves the ghost of a young girl seen around the property.

“With subtle yellow undertones, this soft, muted green strikes a perfect balance between an airy pastel and a grounded, herbal hue,” according to Sherwin-Williams.

Behr selected Grounded (T27-01), a dark olive green with brown undertones inspired by nature.

“The shade’s organic warmth creates a sense of calm and renewal, making every room feel inviting and effortlessly livable,” said Kayla Kratz, Head of Color at Behr Paint Company, in a company release.

Behr recommends Grounded for interior and exterior projects, including living rooms and kitchens.

Valspar chose Cottage Door (8004-38E), a muted blue-gray with warm undertones.

“A cultural shift toward intentional living and self-reflection calls for authentic and heartfelt hues,” according to Valspar.

The color pairs with light neutrals and natural wood, making it suitable for bedrooms and living rooms. It also works on exterior siding and front doors.

Glidden selected Artifact (PPG10-16), a smoky blue-gray with hints of aqua.

“A calm, fresh aqua that feels like a reset for your whole space,” according to Glidden.

The shade works in bedrooms, bathrooms, and living rooms. Glidden also pairs Artifact with lighter blues and earthy greens.

Dunn-Edwards chose French Press Coffee (DEBN07), a dark brown with subtle purple undertones that resemble dark roasted coffee.

“The overall effect is one of layered, lived-in luxury,” according to Dunn-Edwards, describing its 2027 color trends.

The brand recommends French Press Coffee for powder rooms, home offices, and entryways, where its darker color can stand out against lighter finishes.

Dutch Boy selected Deep Rooted (311-7DB), a warm orange that resembles terracotta.

“As paint trends show people seeking more grounding, authenticity, and connection, Deep Rooted brings stability and a sense of calm to the home,” according to Dutch Boy.

The brand suggests pairing the color with soft whites, blues, or greens on walls and furniture.

Clark+Kensington, available at Ace Hardware, selected Vantage Point (38B-4), a rich blue with muted undertones.

“Vantage Point brings a sense of warmth and character to interiors,” said Kim Lefko, Chief Marketing Officer at Ace Hardware, in a company statement.

The brand pairs it with warm neutrals and lighter colors through its Drift and Mellow palettes.

Graham & Brown chose Rose Earth, a soft pink with earthy undertones.

“Rose Earth takes its cue from the natural mineral pigments traditionally sourced from clay deposits in Italy,” according to Graham & Brown.

The brand designed it to complement its Roselle Grove floral wallpaper, though the color also works with greens and warm neutrals.

C2 Paint selected Pueblo (C2-510), a warm shade between dusty pink and terracotta.

“For 2027, we’re looking outward again, toward the things that make us feel alive,” according to C2 Paint.

Pueblo changes with the light, appearing pinker during the day and darker in the evening. C2 Paint suggests pairing it with deep browns, muted greens, and natural materials.

Minwax chose Pickled Oak, a light wood stain with warm undertones, as its 2027 Color of the Year.

“As homeowners gravitate toward more organic interiors, Pickled Oak answers the call for clarity and connection,” according to Minwax.

Unlike paint, the stain lets the wood grain show through. Homeowners can use it to lighten the appearance of old furniture, shelving, and other wood projects.

#7802. Previous Homeowners May Still Have Access to Your Smart Home — Here’s How To Check

Smart cameras, locks, and thermostats may still be linked to former owners. Experts explain how to check access and secure each device.

Moving into a new property can be a scary and intimidating process. There are so many new things to learn, and the last thing a new homeowner wants to worry about is home security. And while you should absolutely change the locks after moving in, proper safety measures don’t end there.

It’s possible for previous homeowners to still have access to smart home tech they left behind. Security cameras, thermostats, and other smart devices can remain linked to the previous owner’s account without the new homeowner realizing it.

Learn which devices need resetting, and what new homeowners should do to keep their homes secure.

Unfortunately, there’s no easy way to tell just by looking at a device.

“It is much safer to just assume the old owner can still access them,” says Kurtis Baron, an offensive security specialist at the cybersecurity company Echo Secure.

Nathan Connell, founder and editor of Future Technology, recommends trying to register each device through its manufacturer’s app. If the app says someone else already owns it, the previous account may still be linked. For example, Ring has an ownership transfer process for previously registered cameras and doorbells. Connell also recommends checking the app’s shared users list for unfamiliar accounts.

“The previous owner, or anyone they shared access with, can still unlock doors, open the garage or watch camera feeds remotely,” Connell says.

Baron recommends resetting all inherited smart devices, including cameras, alarms, locks, thermostats, and connected appliances. Some might be harder to identify than others. According to the Federal Trade Commission, “light bulbs or security systems may be difficult to detect as ‘smart’ devices.”

Homeowners should follow the manufacturer’s instructions to remove the previous account, factory reset each device, and register it under their own account. Google’s moving guide explains how to transfer Nest devices, some of which require the previous owner to remove them first.

“Old PIN codes on keypad locks and alarm panels often stay active too,” Connell says.

Baron recommends getting a new router rather than reusing the previous owner’s equipment. Homeowners should also set up their own Wi-Fi password and check for unfamiliar connected devices.

Some older smart devices may need replacing, especially if the manufacturer no longer provides security updates. Baron recommends replacing anything that can’t be fully factory reset or has become outdated.

A device linked to a previous owner’s account doesn’t always need replacing, though. Some manufacturers offer ownership transfers or can help new homeowners regain control. Until then, homeowners shouldn’t rely on an inherited smart lock or security camera for protection.

Connell recommends asking sellers for a list of every connected device included in the sale, along with manuals, hub information, and account transfer instructions.

The FTC also recommends leaving behind manuals that explain smart features, particularly those that might be difficult for new homeowners to identify. Sellers should confirm they’ve removed their accounts and revoked access for anyone previously authorized to use the devices.

Baron suggests including a requirement in the closing paperwork confirming that the seller has removed access to all smart devices included in the sale. That gives new homeowners a chance to set up their own accounts and passwords without leaving access in someone else’s hands.

Kurtis Baron, offensive security specialist at Echo Secure, a UK cybersecurity and penetration testing company Nathan Connell, founder and editor of Future Technology

Federal Trade Commission, “Buying or Selling a “Smart” Home? Read This” Federal Trade Commission, “Securing Your Internet-Connected Devices at Home” Ring, “Transfer Ownership of a Ring Device” Google Home and Nest Help, “Moving Guide for Google Home and Nest Devices”
